Historically, legislation and regulatory texts frequently include provisions that affect large Wall Street banks, so claiming there are none is unlikely and requires exhaustive proof. The phrase “substantially affect or advantage” is also subjective and hard to substantiate without context.

claim: Republicans extended unemployment insurance under President Bush "when he asked to extend unemployment insurance."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While unemployment benefits were extended during President Bush’s tenure, extensions are enacted by Congress and were achieved through bipartisan votes and compromises rather than simply Republicans unilaterally extending benefits whenever he asked. The statement omits which President Bush and specific legislative actions, and overstates GOP sole credit for extensions.

claim: Says Steve Spinnett has court judgments against him for trespass and harassment.
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence in my available knowledge that a person named Steve Spinnett has court judgments for trespass and harassment. Because I have no access to current court databases and no reliable reporting or public-record sources corroborate the claim in my training data, the assertion is unverified and treated as false. If accurate court documents exist, they would need to be cited for confirmation.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that South Korean police routinely spray protesters with dye to mark them for later arrest. While dye-marking and colored water cannons have been reported in other countries (e.g., Hong Kong, Brazil) as a crowd-control tactic, reputable coverage and official sources do not document this as a standard South Korean practice; the claim likely confuses South Korea with those cases or refers to an isolated, unverified incident.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: There is no clear record that Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker personally received a discrete $7,300 pay raise; gubernatorial pay is set by statute/commission and any adjustments are public. Claims of a $7,300 raise likely misstate changes in benefit formulas, cost-of-living adjustments, or refer to a different person or time, not a one-time pay increase to Walker.

claim: Says there are half as many students in one Georgia technical college than there were two years ago.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented because it does not identify which Georgia technical college or the specific two-year period. Enrollment changes must be confirmed with institution or state system enrollment reports; without that data the assertion that enrollment is half of what it was two years ago cannot be verified. Therefore the claim is treated as false in the absence of evidence.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: Both Luke Messer and Todd Rokita voted in favor of the 2015 Trade Promotion Authority (commonly called 'fast-track') bill, which authorized expedited congressional consideration of trade agreements negotiated by President Obama. Thus the statement that they 'voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals' is accurate in that they supported the procedural authority enabling those deals.

claim: Says Amber Alerts are issued for white kids "but not Black kids in Milwaukee."
rationale: The claim asserts a categorical practice that Amber Alerts are issued for white children but not for Black children in Milwaukee. AMBER Alerts are issued by law enforcement based on objective criteria (age, abduction confirmation, imminent danger, and sufficient descriptive information), not race. While there have been critiques and documented instances of uneven media attention or delayed alerts in some cases, there is no established policy or consistent practice formally withholding Amber Alerts for Black children in Milwaukee.

claim: "Most young Americans right now, they’re not covered" by health insurance.
rationale: This claim is false. Recent U.S. data show that while young adults have higher uninsured rates than older adults, a majority of young Americans have health coverage through employers, parental plans (coverage up to age 26), Medicaid, or the ACA marketplaces, so uninsured young people are a minority rather than "most."

claim: "Right now we’re the highest taxed country in the world."
rationale: The United States is not the highest-taxed country in the world. Measured by common metrics such as total tax revenue as a percentage of GDP or by typical top combined tax rates, many countries (notably Nordic and some Western European states) have substantially higher tax burdens than the U.S. Even combining federal and state taxes, the U.S. tax-to-GDP ratio is below that of countries like Denmark, France, and Sweden.

claim: "IDC members also get tons of campaign money from real estate, charter school, and health care lobbyists, some of whom are Republicans with connections to Trump"
rationale: Contemporary reporting and campaign‑finance analyses showed New York's IDC members accepted substantial contributions from real estate interests, charter‑school backers and health‑care industry donors during their tenure. The contributor lists and lobbying disclosures also included some donors and lobbyists with Republican ties or past support for Trump, supporting the claim in broad terms, though exact amounts and the strength of "connections to Trump" vary by donor and year.

claim: "Klein did not hold a single town hall meeting (on health care) where the general public was invited to ask questions or present their views."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it does not identify which 'Klein' (which office, jurisdiction, or timeframe) is meant. Many public officials with the surname Klein have held public forums or town-hall style meetings, so a blanket assertion that 'Klein did not hold a single town hall' is implausible without specific identification and evidence. Given the ambiguity and lack of supporting documentation, I judge the claim false pending clarification and sourcing.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Julia Roberts ever made this statement; a comment this extreme would have been widely reported by mainstream outlets and fact-checkers. The quote appears to be a fabricated or misattributed viral claim circulated on social media and partisan/satirical sites rather than a verified remark by the actress.

claim: "The (health reform) legislation which Washington passed last year has made it more difficult to hire" because it’s increased costs for employers.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and is likely false as a generalization. It fails to specify which "health reform" or whether "Washington" means the federal government or the state, and empirical studies of major recent U.S. health reforms (e.g., the Affordable Care Act) found little net effect on overall employment—while some firms face higher costs, many employers were exempt, received offsets, or adjusted in ways that did not meaningfully reduce hiring. Therefore the blanket assertion that the law "has made it more difficult to hire" because it increased employer costs is unsupported without specific evidence by sector, firm size, and jurisdiction.

claim: "Florida is one of only 10 states that totally prohibit a (firearm) registry."
rationale: The statement gives a specific count that isn’t reliably supported: state laws vary and the number of states that ban firearm registries depends on how “totally prohibit” is defined and on timing. Florida does have statutory limits on creating a registry of law‑abiding gun owners, but authoritative trackers (which classify statutes differently) do not consistently identify exactly 10 states with an absolute, total prohibition. Because of that ambiguity the precise claim that Florida is “one of only 10” is not reliably true.

claim: Says Paul Ryan’s budget plan "ends Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan’s budget proposals did not immediately abolish Medicare for current beneficiaries; they proposed replacing traditional Medicare for future enrollees with a premium‑support (voucher‑style) system that would shift more costs to beneficiaries. Critics called that an 'end' of Medicare as currently structured, but the plans preserved an altered federal program rather than terminating Medicare outright.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsubstantiated: there is no clear evidence that Charlie Crist enacted a specific law or regulatory change that directly "made it easier for Duke to take your money." Utility rates and practices in Florida are controlled by the Public Service Commission and specific legislation, and no widely reported action by Crist has been shown to uniquely benefit Duke Energy in the manner asserted. Without a specific bill, year, or mechanism, the causal claim is unsupported.

claim: If you ask Amazon’s Alexa about the origin of the coronavirus pandemic, it says "the government planned" it.
rationale: There is no evidence that Amazon programmed Alexa to assert ‘the government planned’ the coronavirus pandemic; fact-checkers traced viral clips to manipulated devices or user-created custom skills/routines rather than an official Alexa response. Amazon’s assistant typically answers by citing scientific uncertainty or mainstream reporting, and the company has denied any built-in conspiracy responses.

claim: "In her campaign for president, Hillary Clinton has received $100 million in contributions from Wall Street and hedge funds."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton personally received $100 million from "Wall Street and hedge funds" for her presidential campaign. Federal campaign finance records and contemporary fact-checks show much smaller direct contributions from the finance sector; while wealthy Wall Street donors and hedge-fund managers gave substantial amounts to Clinton, combining direct donations, bundling, and independent expenditures still does not clearly total $100 million attributable solely to her campaign.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: The claim is presented as a categorical fact but cannot be verified as stated because the November election and specific Proposition 2 are not identified. Texas constitutional amendments and propositions commonly have fiscal notes and can create direct or indirect state costs or revenue impacts; absent identification of the year and review of the official legislative fiscal analysis, it is incorrect to assert with certainty that it "does not cost state taxpayers any money." Therefore the absolute claim is likely false or at least unsubstantiated.

claim: The Red Sox waited "87 long years" to win the World Series.
rationale: The Boston Red Sox last won the World Series in 1918 and then again in 2004. The interval from 1918 to 2004 is 86 years, so saying they waited 87 years is off by one year.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on an assault weapons ban.
rationale: Romney has made inconsistent public statements about bans on assault-style weapons over time. Records show he previously supported or tolerated stricter assault-weapon restrictions linked to Massachusetts policy and at other times, particularly while running for national office, he opposed a federal assault-weapons ban, which constitutes a change in position. The label “flip-flop” is reasonable though details depend on which specific statement or time period is cited.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: The statement refers to U.S. terror watch/no‑fly lists which can bar people from boarding aircraft but are not automatically synced to firearm background‑check prohibitions. Multiple reputable investigations and congressional reporting around 2015 found roughly 2,000+ names on the government watchlist were matched to federal firearms background checks and resulted in sales. Thus the broad claim — that people who can’t fly have nevertheless been able to buy guns — is supported by contemporaneous reporting.

claim: John McCain refuses to support a new bipartisan energy bill "because it would take away tax breaks from oil companies like Exxon Mobil."
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that John McCain publicly refused to support a specific bipartisan energy bill citing protection of oil-company tax breaks such as those for Exxon Mobil. McCain’s public statements and voting record show mixed positions on energy and taxes, but the claim assigns a specific motive and firm refusal without verifiable sourcing. Given the lack of documented statements tying his opposition to protecting Exxon-style tax breaks, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Debt has almost doubled in Austin under Gov. Perry."
rationale: The claim is misleading: a Texas governor does not directly set City of Austin borrowing and available budget records do not support that Austin's municipal debt nearly doubled over Rick Perry's tenure. While some public-sector liabilities changed during 2000–2015, municipal debt decisions are made by city officials and any increases were modest rather than an almost 100% rise attributable to the governor.

claim: Says "Harry Reid, when asked about the Republican field, said the Republican he likes the best is Donald Trump, and he said, because I can work with him. He'll cut deals."
rationale: There is no credible record of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid praising Donald Trump as the Republican he liked best and saying Trump would be easy to work with and cut deals. Reid publicly criticized Trump on many occasions, and the quoted language is inconsistent with his known statements and media coverage. The line appears to be a misattribution or fabricated quote circulated online.

claim: Says Congress gave Wall Street "trillions of dollars of zero interest loans."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Congress authorized bailout and support programs (e.g., TARP, CARES Act) and the Federal Reserve provided large emergency liquidity, but these were not simply "trillions of dollars of zero-interest loans" directly handed by Congress to Wall Street; many supports were Fed loans or Treasury-backed facilities, carried interest, collateral, or were guarantees, and much TARP money was repaid with interest. Calling them "zero-interest loans" and attributing them directly to Congress misstates who lent the funds and the terms.

claim: DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz "denied unemployment went up under Obama."
rationale: This is false. Unemployment did rise in the early months of Obama's presidency (peaking near 10% in 2009), and public statements from Democrats including DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz generally acknowledged the rise while attributing it to the 2008 financial crisis and policies preceding Obama, rather than flatly denying that unemployment increased.

claim: Israel has seen a "90 percent reduction in terrorist attacks" that it attributes to building a 500-mile fence.
rationale: This statement is misleading. While Israeli officials and some studies have reported roughly a ~90% drop in suicide bombings and other attacks after the early-2000s security measures, the decline occurred due to a mix of policies (barrier segments, checkpoints, intelligence operations, closures, and Palestinian security cooperation) rather than solely because of a single 500‑mile fence; the barrier itself was not a single contiguous 500‑mile structure and was never the only measure implemented. Presenting a 90% reduction as entirely attributable to a 500‑mile fence overstates the causal claim.

claim: "In 1992, the Democratic Party had in their platform provisions that said that illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing."
rationale: I am unaware of any passage in the 1992 Democratic Party platform that verbatim claims illegal entrants repeatedly commit felonies, are deported, and immediately return; the quoted wording appears to be a paraphrase or political characterization rather than a direct platform provision. While the 1992 platform did address immigration and enforcement, party platforms typically use more measured, policy-focused language and do not include such blunt assertions about criminal recidivism at the border. Without an exact citation to the platform text, the claim that the platform contained that specific statement is not supported.

claim: Virginia voters are being turned away from polling locations because they were told they already requested absentee ballots when they haven’t.
rationale: There are documented reports from recent Virginia elections of some voters being turned away or given provisional ballots after poll workers said records showed an absentee ballot request they denied making. State and local election officials acknowledged isolated errors and reiterated that voters who have not returned an absentee ballot should be allowed to cast an in-person ballot.

claim: Sherrod Brown "failed to pay his own taxes three separate times."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Senator Sherrod Brown “failed to pay his own taxes three separate times.” Contemporary fact-checks and public records do not substantiate a pattern of three distinct tax non-payments; at most isolated, old disputes or late payments have been reported and have been presented misleadingly in some attacks. The broad claim therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the record.

claim: "Within a few years, we will be spending more on interest payments than on national security."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by available budget projections as of mid-2024. Current federal defense/national-security outlays remain larger than net interest outlays, and CBO-style projections show interest rising sharply but typically predict any crossover later in the decade under baseline assumptions, not necessarily “within a few years.” Timelines vary by assumptions about growth, interest rates, and spending choices, so the specific short-term prediction is not reliably true.

claim: "DirecTV cancels OAN after Joe Biden orders media outlets and tech giants to banish voices that deviate from the regime’s official narrative."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Biden issued any order directing media outlets or technology companies to 'banish' dissenting voices, and the U.S. president does not have direct authority to command private broadcasters like DirecTV to drop channels. While distributors sometimes remove channels for contractual, business, or legal reasons, attributing such an action to a presidential order is unsupported. The claim mixes a likely corporate carriage decision with an unfounded allegation of government coercion.

claim: Says Marshall Tuck "is backed by Donald Trump’s education advisor" pictured as Betsy DeVos.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Betsy DeVos personally backed Marshall Tuck. Tuck’s campaigns were widely reported to be supported by pro‑charter and Democratic donors and local education reform backers, and DeVos (Trump’s education nominee/secretary) was not publicly recorded as endorsing or funding him. The claim appears to conflate DeVos’s national profile on school‑choice with direct support for Tuck.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "shows up in Broward County" and had a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Hillary Clinton traveled to Broward County to hold a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes. Fact-checking organizations and public records of schedules and news coverage around the relevant period found no documentation of such a meeting; the claim appears to have originated on social media without verification. Given the absence of records and reliable reporting, the assertion is not supported.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: There is no credible reporting that Stephen Curry split with Nike over a Nike ban on Bible scriptures in his shoes. Curry signed a major deal with Under Armour in 2013 and has been publicly open about his Christian faith, but reputable sources do not support the claim that Nike refused scripture and that this prompted any split. The claim appears to be a rumor or misattribution.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The core points are accurate: in the 2016 presidential election Trump carried West Virginia by about 42 percentage points (commonly reported as roughly "almost 43"). West Virginia was among — and by 2016 vote share often cited as — his strongest-performing state. State-level approval polls during his term regularly showed his approval in West Virginia near the high 50s to around 60 percent, so the "close to 60 percent" claim is plausible.

claim: Says Joe Biden took a knee during the national anthem.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden has taken a knee while the U.S. national anthem was playing at a public, documented event. Photographs and videos that show Biden kneeling are from other contexts (comforting individuals, talking with children, or prayer), and official footage of ceremonies shows him standing for the anthem.

claim: Bryan County, Ga., has "corrupted voter rolls."
rationale: There is no credible, public evidence or official finding that Bryan County, Georgia, had “corrupted voter rolls.” State election officials and post‑election audits of Georgia have not documented systemic corruption of Bryan County voter rolls; allegations appear to be unverified or based on rumor. Without specific incidents, dates, or authoritative reports, the claim is not supported.

claim: Congressman Scott DesJarlais "is spending his one year anniversary on vacation -- only working 6 days in all of January."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous (no year specified or what counts as “working”), and I find no reliable reporting or public record indicating Rep. Scott DesJarlais spent a January on vacation having worked only six days. Congressional schedules, roll-call votes and public calendars are public and would normally document such minimal presence; absent corroborating evidence, the assertion appears false. Without a specific year or source this reads like an unfounded social-media claim.

claim: "We don’t allow filming inside of the City Hall unless there is a specific reason."
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal rule but cannot be verified without specifying which City Hall and the jurisdiction involved. Policies on filming in municipal buildings vary: some city halls allow filming in public areas or during public meetings (often under open-records or open-meetings laws), while others require permits or have restrictions for security or privacy reasons. Therefore the blanket statement is not reliably true as written.

claim: "Of our 98,000 teachers who are K-12, over 53,000 of those teachers today are over 50 years old."
rationale: The claim gives precise counts but provides no jurisdiction, date, or source, so it cannot be verified. Teacher workforce sizes and age distributions vary by district and state; without specific HR or state education data confirming 98,000 K–12 teachers and that over 53,000 are over 50, the statement is unsubstantiated and therefore treated as false.

claim: Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now," so they should address election social distancing concerns.
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Wisconsin's governor (Tony Evers) is a Democrat, the state legislature is controlled by Republicans and election administration is largely local and overseen by a bipartisan state elections commission. That means Wisconsin is not uniformly "run by Democrats," so assigning sole responsibility to Democrats to address social-distancing at elections is inaccurate.

claim: Germany "is crime-riddled right now" because of migration to Europe.
rationale: This claim overstates and misattributes current crime trends in Germany. Official statistics in recent years show overall crime levels have been stable or declining rather than a country being "crime-riddled," and while some offense categories and isolated high-profile incidents increased at times, migrants are not shown to be the sole or primary cause of broad crime trends. Causal links between migration and crime are complex and vary by offense type, location, and time period, so the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "Republicans are attempting to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s Presidential Ballot in 2012."
rationale: While there were isolated ballot-eligibility challenges in 2012 by fringe 'birther' activists (some of whom identified as Republicans), there was no coordinated effort by the Republican Party of Georgia or mainstream Republican officials to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s 2012 presidential ballot. Georgia election officials certified Obama’s place on the ballot and courts rejected the eligibility lawsuits.

claim: "Kim Jong Un dead: North Koreans calling Trump an assassin"
rationale: This claim is false. Widely circulated rumors that Kim Jong Un had died were debunked when he subsequently made public appearances and North Korean state media did not report his death. There is no credible evidence that North Koreans broadly called Donald Trump an "assassin," and such a notable accusation would have been documented by reliable international reporting and official DPRK statements. The assertion appears to be a conflation of unverified rumors and social-media claims.

claim: "Most of the people that work in finance make $70,000, $80,000 a year."
rationale: The finance sector includes a wide range of jobs (tellers, clerks, loan officers, accountants, analysts, traders, managers) with a broad pay distribution, so it is incorrect to say a majority earn specifically $70,000–$80,000. Labor statistics and industry compensation data show many frontline finance roles earn well below that range while many professional and senior roles earn well above it, so fewer than half of finance workers fall into that narrow band.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no specific time, place, or named individuals and there are no corroborating reports from credible news or official sources. Without such identifying details or independent confirmation, the allegation cannot be substantiated and should be treated as false.

claim: Says "Canada has one-tenth of our population—yet it issues far more high-skilled visas (more than 150,000) yearly than we do (65,000)."
rationale: The claim mixes different categories and is therefore misleading. While Canada (population ~1/9–1/10 of the U.S.) does admit well over 100,000 economic/skill-based entrants in many recent years, the U.S. 65,000 figure is the annual H‑1B statutory cap for a temporary nonimmigrant category; the two figures are not directly comparable. Thus the numeric contrast is true in some years but the comparison as stated is misleading.

claim: Columbia, Mo., is "one of the fastest growing cities in the region, the only city in the state to grow jobs faster than the nation as a whole."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute statement without a timeframe or data source, and such blanket assertions about being the only Missouri city to outpace national job growth are unlikely to be true across all periods. Job-growth rankings vary by year and by the specific metrics and geographic definitions used, and other Missouri metros (e.g., Kansas City or Springfield in certain years) have at times grown jobs faster than national averages. Because the claim lacks context and is plausibly contradicted by available labor-market data for some periods, I judge it false as stated.

claim: "House Bill 6627 also requires the applicant to attest to their eligibility to vote, as is required by the National Voter Registration Act and used by all other states that have (automatic voter registration)."
rationale: The claim bundles three points but is not fully supportable as stated. While the National Voter Registration Act does require a signed attestation on federal registration forms and most automatic voter registration (AVR) implementations include an attestation step, the text of “House Bill 6627” is unspecified here and cannot be verified as containing that requirement; moreover, not every AVR program is identical. Because the bill’s jurisdiction and language aren’t provided and the blanket “all other states” wording is overbroad, the claim is not reliably true.

claim: In comparing mass shootings, "France had a higher casualty rate in one year than the entire two administrations of Barack Obama."
rationale: The claim is false under the ordinary reading. France’s worst single-year terrorist/mass-shooting tolls (for example the 2015 attacks with roughly 130–150 killed in Paris plus earlier incidents) do not exceed the total number of U.S. mass-shooting fatalities over Barack Obama’s two terms; the U.S. saw more mass-shooting and firearm deaths cumulatively from 2009–2016. The statement also mixes poorly defined terms ("casualty rate," what counts as a mass shooting, per-capita vs absolute), which weakens its accuracy.

claim: Americans "bought into climate change" in 2004-06, but then most "began wandering away from this issue."
rationale: This claim overstates the downward trend. National polls (e.g., Gallup, Pew) show that public belief in and concern about climate change rose into the mid-2000s (helped by events like the 2006 documentary and scientific coverage), and although concern and prioritization have fluctuated afterward and become more partisan, there was not a sustained collapse where “most” Americans abandoned the issue. Instead the data show variability by year and subgroup rather than a broad exodus from climate concern.

claim: Video shows helicopters in Ukraine "being picked off in ambush - Short range air-to-air missile"
rationale: The claim attributes the footage to helicopters being downed by a short‑range air‑to‑air missile launched in an ambush. Short‑range air‑to‑air missiles are typically air‑launched from other fixed‑wing or rotary aircraft, whereas ground ambushes commonly use MANPADS, larger surface‑to‑air systems, or guns; social media posts often mislabel the munition or launch platform. Without verifiable metadata or corroborating evidence that an aircraft fired an A2A missile, the specific attribution is unlikely and thus assessed as false.

claim: Missouri "is the state with the lowest paid workers."
rationale: This claim is false: Missouri is not the state with the lowest-paid workers. Federal data (e.g., Census median household income and BLS average/median wage tables) consistently place states such as Mississippi, West Virginia, Arkansas and Louisiana below Missouri in typical wage and income measures; Missouri generally ranks near the national median rather than last.

claim: "You (Hillary Clinton) get a subpoena, and after getting the subpoena you delete 33,000 emails."
rationale: This claim is false: Hillary Clinton's roughly 30,000+ personal emails were deleted in 2014 by her team after sorting her private server, but that deletion occurred before any FBI or Justice Department subpoena related to the emails. The FBI didn’t open its investigation and issue subpoenas until 2015, and Clinton’s team has said the deleted messages were deemed personal and not work-related before turning over work emails to State.

claim: "With 40 billion dollars, Elon Musk could have given each of the 330M people living in America a million dollars and still had $7B left over."
rationale: The claim is false. 330 million people × $1,000,000 each equals about $330,000,000,000,000 (≈$330 trillion), which is vastly larger than $40 billion, so $40 billion could not pay $1 million to each person and still leave $7 billion. The numbers are off by many orders of magnitude.

claim: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security warned that the SAVE "database is not a foolproof means of verifying (citizenship on) the voter rolls."
rationale: This is accurate. DHS/USCIS has told states and officials that the SAVE system is intended to verify immigration or benefit eligibility and is not designed to definitively determine U.S. citizenship for voter registration purposes, warning it can produce incomplete or inconclusive results and therefore is not a foolproof way to verify citizenship on voter rolls. That guidance was made explicit in correspondence and agency guidance communicated to states around 2017–2018.

claim: Says Republican-approved changes to "make it more difficult to participate in Ohio elections include reducing in-person early voting from 35 days to six."
rationale: The claim as stated is inaccurate. While Ohio Republican lawmakers have passed voting-law changes that reduced or constrained some forms of early and weekend in-person voting, there is no clear, verifiable change that universally cut Ohio’s in-person early voting window from 35 days to a uniform six days statewide. Reporting and legislative text describe narrower alterations (limits on weekend/extended hours or specific county procedures) rather than a straight 35→6 day reduction across the state.

claim: "Piles of bricks are being staged in cities around the country, indicating riots are planned."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that piles of bricks in multiple cities are part of a coordinated nationwide effort to incite riots. Many viral photos and reports have been traced to routine construction, landscaping, sidewalk repairs, or local municipal work, and fact-checkers have not found proof of organized staging for violent unrest. The claim generalizes isolated images and misinterprets common urban activities as a coordinated threat.

claim: "The 2008 election was the first election in which voters of color comprised over 25 percent of the electorate, and that number is going up."
rationale: Reliable exit-poll and Census analyses show that the 2008 U.S. electorate included a record share of voters of color (around the mid-20s percentage points), surpassing the 25% threshold for the first time, largely driven by higher Black and Hispanic turnout for that election. Subsequent elections have continued the upward trend in the nonwhite share of the electorate, so the statement that the number is going up is supported by later data.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The claim is uncheckable as written because it refers to an unnamed "he" and gives no state, time period, or evidence; without specific identity or budget data I cannot verify that someone legitimately reined in spending. Per instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain, I mark it FALSE while noting the lack of verifiable detail. If a specific governor, state, and years are provided the claim could be evaluated against budget and audit records.

claim: Says remdesivir is responsible for killing patients hospitalized with COVID-19.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that remdesivir is responsible for killing patients hospitalized with COVID-19. Large randomized trials and regulatory reviews have not shown a signal that remdesivir causes increased mortality; while rare serious adverse effects (e.g., renal or hepatic injury) have been reported, they do not support the blanket claim that the drug is killing hospitalized patients.

claim: Milwaukee’s problems include "52 percent black male unemployment."
rationale: This specific phrasing is misleading: official labor statistics do not record a 52% unemployment rate for Black men citywide in Milwaukee. The 52% figure often cited is a misinterpretation or conflation of different measures (for example, percent not employed, out of the labor force, or rates for a narrow age cohort or neighborhood) rather than the official unemployment rate for all Black males in the city.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: Multiple contemporaneous fact-checks and archival footage show McCain at earlier points endorsing private personal retirement accounts or supporting partial privatization of Social Security, while during his 2008 campaign he at times denied having supported privatization. The existence of on-record video statements by McCain advocating private accounts contradicts later blanket denials, so the claim that he said he never supported privatization despite video showing he did is accurate.

claim: There are "approximately 20,000 annual gun purchases in Rhode Island."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented and is likely incorrect. Publicly reported indicators (like FBI NICS background checks) are commonly used as proxies for gun sales and vary substantially by year, and they are not identical to completed purchases; without a specific year or definition of “purchases,” the flat figure of “approximately 20,000” cannot be confirmed and is misleading for Rhode Island’s small population.

claim: "I was the most bipartisan senator in the United States Senate."
rationale: The claim is a self-superlative with no named speaker, timeframe, or metric, so it cannot be verified as true. Bipartisanship is quantified by different measures (e.g., cross-party voting rates, Bipartisan Index), and without evidence showing this person ranked highest by a specific measure and period, the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: Under David Dewhurst’s leadership, the Texas "Senate passed an expansion of in-state tuition and free health care to illegal immigrants."
rationale: This is inaccurate. Texas’ law allowing certain undocumented students to pay in-state tuition (HB 1403) was enacted in 2001, before David Dewhurst became lieutenant governor, and the Texas Legislature has not passed a law granting blanket “free health care” to undocumented immigrants; Medicaid and most public benefits remain restricted to citizens and qualified immigrants. While there have been occasional local programs and legislative proposals, the specific claim that the Senate (under Dewhurst) passed expansions of both in-state tuition and free health care to illegal immigrants is misleading.

claim: "In many instances, (people's) health care costs are more than their mortgage costs or their rent, which, by the way, is a first in American history."
rationale: Available US data show housing (mortgage or rent) is the single largest regular household expense for most Americans, while out-of-pocket health care spending is typically much smaller. Although some individuals or families with very high medical bills can face health costs exceeding housing, that is not the common or new pattern implied by the claim, nor is it clearly a unique first in US history.

claim: "It isn't me cutting the budget. It's the Congress' decision on sequestration. So it isn't secretary of defense or the president doing this."
rationale: Sequestration as an automatic cut mechanism was created by Congress via statute (e.g., the Budget Control Act), so Congress set the trigger. However, the President signs laws and the executive branch — including the Secretary of Defense for DoD budgets — is responsible for implementing and distributing those cuts. Saying it is not the president or secretary of defense ‘doing this’ is therefore inaccurate because they execute and manage the enforced reductions constrained by law.

claim: "This is the first time since Roe was decided in 1973 that a court has granted personhood status to the preborn."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because courts and legislatures have recognized fetal or preborn 'personhood' in various limited legal contexts since 1973, particularly through state fetal-homicide and wrongful-death laws and related judicial decisions. Those rulings and statutes have treated a fetus as a legal victim or person for specific purposes, so a recent court action would not be the first time any court has granted such status since Roe. The truth depends on the narrowness of the claim (e.g., constitutional personhood vs. statutory/criminal recognition), but broadly it is false.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: The claim that "most black children" in 1960 were raised in two‑parent households is broadly correct, but the assertion that today only 20% are raised in two‑parent, monogamous families is incorrect. Contemporary U.S. Census and research data show a substantial decline in two‑parent households since 1960, but the share of Black children living with two parents is far higher than 20% (estimates vary by definition, generally well above one‑third and often around half or more depending on whether stepfamilies are counted).

claim: "Every day in the United States, we are losing 15 factories."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the U.S. is losing 15 factories every single day; that rate would imply roughly 5,500 factory closures per year, which is inconsistent with public data on manufacturing establishments and employment trends. Official sources (Census/BLS) report much smaller net changes and the numbers vary by year and by how “factory” or “closure” is defined. The claim is therefore misleading and not supported as a general daily fact.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: The claim is framed with charged language and does not identify a specific bill or vote; there is no clear record that Sen. Sherrod Brown cast a vote specifically to keep an explicitly described “extreme, job-killing IRS paperwork mandate.” While Brown has supported increased IRS enforcement and funding and has backed some reporting provisions, he has also backed exemptions and protections for small businesses in related debates. Given the vagueness of the allegation and lack of a precise roll-call tying Brown to an identified mandate described that way, the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Since 2009, "after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and is not supported as presented: it does not specify the country, population (households vs individuals), whether figures are inflation‑adjusted, or the end year. Different official series (CBO after‑tax/after‑transfer income, Census or BEA measures, median vs mean) show varying growth rates since 2009, and many commonly cited measures report smaller gains than 'nearly 14%'. Without a clearly identified dataset and definition, the blanket claim is not reliably true.

claim: "The federal government is now on track" for the second-largest budget deficit "in 65 years."
rationale: The statement is too ambiguous and likely inaccurate as presented. Publicly reported U.S. federal deficits in recent years (notably 2020) were described as the largest since World War II, and whether a given year is the “second-largest in 65 years” depends on the missing reference year and whether deficits are measured in nominal dollars or as a share of GDP. Without a clear timeframe and metric the claim cannot be verified and is misleading as stated.

claim: "New York, for all of their complaining, Gov. Cuomo's complaining, has only had a 1.5% decrease in revenue" due to the coronavirus pandemic.
rationale: The claim that New York experienced only a 1.5% revenue decline from the coronavirus is inconsistent with widely reported budget projections and tax receipt data showing multi‑billion dollar shortfalls. During 2020–2021 the state projected and reported steep drops in income, sales, and business tax collections far larger than 1.5%, prompting emergency budget actions and requests for federal aid. The 1.5% figure appears to understate the actual revenue impact.

claim: "Kids are less likely to get it (COVID-19). You know, they’re less likely to spread. So I think there’s some pretty good data out there that will help alleviate some of the concerns."
rationale: The statement is an oversimplification and can be misleading. Early in the pandemic children often had lower reported infection and symptomatic rates, but they can and do become infected and transmit SARS-CoV-2, and transmission risk has changed with later variants (e.g., Delta, Omicron). Saying they are simply “less likely to get it” and “less likely to spread” without temporal or variant context is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Roy Blunt "voted to raise his own pay 12 times" while in Congress.
rationale: The claim is misleading: independent fact-checkers have found that whether Blunt "voted to raise his own pay 12 times" depends on how you count votes (direct pay-raise votes vs. broader bills or automatic adjustments). Public analyses during his campaigns showed fewer clear, standalone votes to directly increase congressional pay and noted many votes were on larger bills or routine cost-of-living adjustments, so the flat claim of 12 unambiguous votes is inaccurate.

claim: Greg Abbott "has campaigned with a sexual predator who has bragged about having sex with underage girls."
rationale: The claim provides no named individual or incident and I find no credible, widely reported evidence that Texas Gov. Greg Abbott campaigned with a person who publicly bragged about having sex with underage girls. Abbott has appeared with many Republican figures, but major news outlets and public records do not substantiate the specific allegation as stated. Given the lack of a identified person or verifiable reporting, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Cannabis reform "is supported by the majority of the residents of our state, including a majority of Republicans."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because no state, timeframe, or definition of “cannabis reform” is provided. While national polls show a majority of U.S. adults favor legalization, Republican support is uneven and often below a clear majority depending on state and poll wording, so the blanket statement cannot be confirmed. Without recent, state-specific, party‑breakdown polling on the exact reform measure, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Wayne Powell has a "stated position of having no objection to taking `In God We Trust" off of U.S. currency."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that a person named Wayne Powell publicly stated he had no objection to removing 'In God We Trust' from U.S. currency. The name matches multiple private individuals and minor public figures, but there is no reliable record or media report attributing that exact position to a specific Wayne Powell. Without a clear identity, time, or citation, the claim is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the FBI physically lost Hunter Biden’s laptop. Public reporting indicates the device originally came from a Delaware repair shop and copies were circulated to private actors and the media; the FBI later obtained copies and used files in investigations, but mainstream sources do not report the bureau misplacing the laptop itself. Questions have been raised about chain-of-custody and how copies were handled, but that is not the same as the FBI having lost the laptop.

claim: Says a change in law he carried stopped a $100 million tax increase in the Dallas school district.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “he” is, which specific law was changed, or when, and I find no corroborating evidence tying a named lawmaker’s change in law directly to preventing a $100 million Dallas school district tax increase. School tax outcomes typically depend on multiple factors (state statute, local tax rates, property appraisals, and school board actions), so a single unnamed lawmaker’s claim cannot be confirmed without specific documentation. Pending those specifics, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate would make it a federal felony to "leave town for more than seven days, and leave someone else at home with your firearms."
rationale: There is no known Senate gun bill that criminalizes simply leaving town for more than seven days and leaving someone else in your home with your firearms. Federal firearm proposals focus on background checks, prohibited persons, transfers, and in some cases safe-storage or negligent storage rules, but none impose a temporal felony based on being away from home and leaving household members with guns. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation of other proposals or state rules.

claim: Says Matt Rosendale "consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana."
rationale: The claim overstates the record. While Matt Rosendale is a property developer by profession and has supported property‑rights and development‑friendly positions at times, there is not clear, consistent evidence that he systematically backed land‑use rules designed to benefit developers and harm Montana farmers. Available records show mixed votes and policy positions on land use and regulation rather than a uniform, targeted pattern described in the claim.

claim: The Postal Service’s financial losses result from "a 2006 law that drains $5 billion a year from post office revenue, while the Postal Service is forced to overpay billions more into federal accounts."
rationale: The 2006 Postal Accountability and Enhancement Act did impose a roughly $5–5.8 billion-per-year prefunding requirement for retiree health benefits, which materially increased reported USPS losses. However, saying the Postal Service’s financial losses “result from” that law ignores major other causes (long-term declines in mail volume, economic downturns, pricing and operational issues). The second clause about being “forced to overpay billions more into federal accounts” is vague and not clearly supported as a separate, equivalent mandated outflow.

claim: California’s Central Valley and Inland Empire "are experiencing tremendous job growth."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and misleading. While parts of the Inland Empire have seen notable job gains in logistics and construction in past years, the Central Valley’s job growth has been uneven, often trailing state averages and accompanied by higher unemployment and lower wages; neither region uniformly shows sustained “tremendous” growth across counties and sectors. Without a specific timeframe or metric the statement is not supportable as a general fact.

claim: COVID-19 is a synthetic version of "snake venom" that evil forces are spreading through remdesivir, the COVID-19 vaccines and drinking water to "make you a hybrid of Satan."
rationale: There is no scientific evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 is a synthetic form of snake venom or that remdesivir, COVID‑19 vaccines, or municipal drinking water are being used to spread such a substance. Genomic analyses show SARS‑CoV‑2 is a coronavirus related to animal coronaviruses, not a venom construct; remdesivir is an antiviral drug and vaccines contain viral antigens or genetic instructions to provoke immunity, not toxins. The claim that these exposures would make someone a “hybrid of Satan” is supernatural and unsupported by biology or medicine.

claim: "More college graduates are living at home than in decades."
rationale: U.S. survey and Census data show the share of young adults living with parents rose substantially during and after the COVID-19 recession, and this increase includes those with college degrees—reaching levels not seen in several decades. Economic shocks, high housing costs and student debt contributed to more college-educated young adults returning to or remaining in the parental household.

claim: The departments of Commerce, Education and Energy and the EPA saw their spending increase by between 130 percent and 219 percent between 2008 and 2010.
rationale: This claim is not supported by available budget data. While the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act did boost funding for Commerce, Education, Energy and EPA programs, none of those entire departments’ total spending roughly doubled to tripled (130–219%) between 2008 and 2010; increases were much smaller at the department-wide level. The statement likely conflates specific stimulus program increases with overall departmental budgets, producing a misleading impression.

claim: "For more than 80 years, there has not been a nomination and confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice in a presidential election year. This is simply not the time to break with decades of bipartisan practice."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. In 2020 (a presidential election year) President Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett in late October and the Senate confirmed her that same month, so a nomination and confirmation did occur within an election year. While there is debate about norms for confirming justices near elections, the statement that this hadn’t happened for more than 80 years is factually wrong.

claim: Gov. Lincoln Chafee has imposed "a mandatory abortion fee" on all Rhode Islanders who buy health insurance through the state’s Obamacare exchange.
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Governor Chafee did not impose a blanket mandatory ‘‘abortion fee’’ on all buyers on Rhode Island’s exchange; state rules around that time required insurers to offer abortion coverage as a separately priced option and to keep funds segregated per federal requirements, not to force every enrollee to pay for abortion coverage. Those who declined abortion coverage would not have been charged a separate abortion premium.

claim: Says CNN and other news organizations tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters.
rationale: There is no verifiable record that CNN and other major news organizations tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters. While unverified social-media claims have occasionally circulated about attacks on journalists in Afghanistan, major outlets did not publish or stand by a tweeted claim of an execution in Kabul without attribution or evidence. Given the lack of corroborating reporting, the specific assertion that CNN and others tweeted this is not supported.

claim: Says "Ammar Campa-Najjar is working to infiltrate Congress" and "is being supported by CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Ammar Campa‑Najjar is attempting to “infiltrate” Congress; he ran for office as a normal political candidate, which is not the same as a secretive infiltration effort. Similarly, reliable records do not show CAIR or the transnational Muslim Brotherhood funding or directing his campaigns — allegations tying him to those groups have been promoted as attack ads and conspiratorial smears without corroborating documentation.

claim: "People are less likely to just vote for party now. … They’re looking at the personalities."
rationale: The claim states voters are generally less likely to vote by party and instead focus on personalities. Broad empirical evidence—especially in the U.S. and several other democracies—shows rising partisan polarization and stronger party-line voting in recent decades, though personality can matter in particular races. Therefore the sweeping generalization is not supported as a universal trend.

claim: "There's no negative advertising in my campaign at all."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that is practically unverifiable without a comprehensive audit of all campaign messaging and independent spending. In modern campaigns negative advertising is common and can come from the campaign itself or independent outside groups; saying there is 'no negative advertising... at all' is therefore unlikely to be true. Without precise definitions and a full media record, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Nationwide tuition at public universities is up almost 300 percent ... in the last 20 years."
rationale: This claim is not supported by national data. Federal and College Board statistics show average published in‑state tuition and fees at public four‑year institutions rose substantially over the past 20 years but by roughly 150–200% in nominal terms (and far less after adjusting for inflation), not “almost 300%.” Some subsets (out‑of‑state rates, individual schools, or longer time spans) may show larger changes, but the nationwide average does not approach 300%.

claim: Letting the Bush tax cuts expire would raise taxes on small businesses.
rationale: Most small businesses are organized as pass-through entities (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S-corporations, LLCs) whose income is taxed on owners' individual returns; the Bush-era tax cuts lowered individual income and capital gains rates, so letting those cuts expire would generally raise the individual tax rates paid by those owners and thus their business taxes. Corporations taxed at the corporate level would not be directly affected, so the effect depends on business structure and owner income.

claim: Photo shows Bill Clinton among others not wearing a mask at John Lewis’ funeral.
rationale: Contemporaneous news photos and reporting from John Lewis' memorial services do not support the claim that a verified photo shows Bill Clinton unmasked among others at the funeral; published images from the event show attendees following mask guidance and no credible source has produced an authenticated image of Clinton maskless at that service. The viral claim appears to be a misidentification or an alteration.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous: it gives no country, time interval end year, or profit measure. Insurance industry profitability varies by subsector and year (affected by events like 9/11, the 2008 crisis, investment returns), and while some firms or segments have seen large percentage gains in certain periods, aggregated industry profits do not uniformly show a >400% increase since 2001. Without a clear metric and source the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: The Murray-Ryan deal "is the first divided-government budget agreement since 1986."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: there have been several bipartisan budget/debt agreements after 1986. Notable examples include the 1990 deficit-reduction deal under President George H.W. Bush, the 1997 balanced-budget legislation negotiated under President Clinton with a Republican Congress, and the 2011 Budget Control Act reached during President Obama’s term with a Republican House. These show the Murray-Ryan deal was not the first such agreement since 1986.

claim: "Gavin Newsom reportedly intervened at the request of Nancy Pelosi and directly ordered the California Highway Patrol to drop all charges" against Paul Pelosi for his DUI arrest.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or evidence that Governor Gavin Newsom personally intervened at Nancy Pelosi’s request to order the CHP to drop charges against Paul Pelosi. Prosecutorial decisions to file or drop charges are made by district attorneys, not the governor, and law-enforcement agencies like the CHP do not take lawful charging orders from the governor. Multiple contemporary news accounts and the institutional separation of powers contradict the claim.

claim: Says "I’ve been proven right" about "Hillary Clinton's radical call for open borders, meaning anyone in the world can enter the United States without any limit at all."
rationale: The characterization is false: Hillary Clinton has not called for "open borders" allowing anyone to enter the U.S. without limit. Her public positions and campaign platforms supported comprehensive immigration reform including border security and enforcement and a pathway to citizenship, not unrestricted, unlimited entry. The statement misrepresents her stated policies and comments.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I cannot verify a credible, widely cited economic impact study that precisely reports a $1 → $1.79 payoff as 'total spending within the state' for Pennsylvania pre-K. Many studies report a range of short‑term economic multipliers or longer‑term social returns for pre‑K, but the claim appears to conflate different measures (immediate in‑state spending vs. long‑term benefit/cost ratios) and lacks a cited source. Because the precise wording and context matter for such estimates, the claim as stated is not substantiated.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad claim that is not consistently supported by available crime data. Since Scott Walker took office in January 2011, Wisconsin violent-crime measures have fluctuated — there were periods of decline in the 2010s and notable increases around 2020–21 — so it is incorrect to say the data uniformly show the state has become less safe without specifying a timeframe or metric. The claim generalizes year-to-year variation into a single sustained trend that the data do not unambiguously demonstrate.

claim: "42 percent of (Walmart’s) associates are black."
rationale: Publicly reported Walmart U.S. workforce demographic data show the share of Black associates is substantially lower (generally in the mid-teens percentage range), not 42%. A 42% figure is inconsistent with Walmart’s diversity disclosures and with U.S. demographic context, so the claim is incorrect unless it refers to a very specific subset or locale.

claim: Says Christopher Little has "a history of working against environmental protection by defending the worst types of corporate polluters"
rationale: I cannot verify the assertion as stated. There is no clear, verifiable public record tying a specific Christopher Little to a documented, ongoing pattern of defending “the worst types of corporate polluters,” and the name matches multiple individuals; the claim provides no concrete examples, cases, clients, or time frame to substantiate it. Because key identifying details and supporting evidence are missing, the claim is not supported by available knowledge.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot verify the precise claim; while Portland did run a year-long curbside composting pilot involving roughly 2,000 households, I do not have authoritative evidence that 87% of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system. Without the original pilot report or a reliable secondary source giving that exact percentage, the specific numeric claim is unconfirmed and thus judged false for lack of verification.

claim: Says that Minnesota Democratic congressional candidate Dean Phillips doesn’t offer health insurance for his employees.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Dean Phillips universally refused to offer health insurance to all of his employees. Criticisms that circulated during campaigns typically referenced part-time or seasonal workers not qualifying for employer-sponsored plans or alleged lapses in specific periods, not a blanket policy of providing no insurance to any employee. The absolute wording of the claim is unsupported by available reporting.

claim: "Too many dead people voted" in Michigan
rationale: Post-election investigations, audits, recounts, and court reviews of Michigan's recent high-profile elections (notably 2020) found no evidence of widespread voting by deceased people; only a tiny number of isolated or clerical errors were identified and investigated. State certification and multiple audits upheld the results and prosecutions related to ballot fraud were limited to very small-scale cases, far short of the implication that "too many" dead people voted.

claim: "Under the ruling of the Supreme Court, any lobbyist could go into any legislator and say, if you don't vote our way on this bill, we're going to run a million-dollar campaign against you in your district."
rationale: Supreme Court rulings like Citizens United permit unlimited independent expenditures by outside groups but do not authorize direct coordination with or bribery/extortion of legislators. A lobbyist directly threatening a legislator to change a vote would likely be illegal (coordination, solicitation of a bribe, or criminal extortion) and is not permitted by those rulings. While outside groups can spend large sums independently, the decision does not grant a license to make such direct threats.

claim: Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and his wife Ginni posted a photo of themselves enjoying a $5,135 bottle of wine "as American women despair about abortion rights being taken away from them."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Justice Clarence Thomas and his wife Ginni publicly posted a photo of themselves enjoying a bottle of wine priced at $5,135 tied to abortion-related despair. Reporting and fact-checking around viral posts found misattributions and inflated price claims rather than a verified, contemporaneous post showing that specific price and context.

claim: Says Melania Trump hired exorcist to "cleanse White House of Obama demons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump hired an exorcist to 'cleanse the White House of Obama demons.' Major fact‑checking organizations and mainstream news outlets examined the viral claim and found it originated from tabloids/satire and unverified social posts rather than reliable reporting. No reputable source documented an exorcism or that Melania characterized former residents as 'demons.'

claim: Says taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel jumped $100 million in closed-door sessions
rationale: I cannot find credible evidence that a taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel increased by $100 million as a result of closed‑door sessions. Reporting and publicly filed documents about the project through mid‑2024 show negotiation of subsidies and incentives but do not document a discrete $100 million upward jump attributable to private meetings; final subsidy figures have been disclosed in public records. Without a verifiable source for this specific claim, it appears unsupported.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The specific quantitative claim that “a rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months” is not supported by verifiable statewide data and reads as an oversimplification. While rural hospital closures have occurred and lack of Medicaid expansion (prior to 2021) likely worsened financial strain on some providers, Missouri voters approved Medicaid expansion in 2020 and it was implemented thereafter, so attributing ongoing closures solely to a legislative failure is inaccurate and time-dependent. The statement mixes an unverified fixed closure rate with a broad causal claim without specifying timeframe or evidence.

claim: A "majority of our students are trapped in" underperforming schools.
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it lacks any jurisdiction, time frame, or definition of “underperforming.” Without specifying which students (e.g., a particular district, state, or country) and using a measurable performance standard, the claim cannot be supported. Given the ambiguity and absence of data, the default assessment is that the claim is not factually established.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that exactly 20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance as a direct result of the Affordable Care Act. While the ACA prompted some non‑compliant individual market plans to be cancelled nationally and people received cancellation notices, state‑level tallies do not substantiate that precise figure and 'lost' can mean different things (cancellation notice vs. net loss of coverage). The claim appears to conflate disparate metrics and lacks a verifiable source for Kansas specifically.

claim: "As a 27 year old staff attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate investigation, Hillary Rodham was fired by her supervisor, lifelong Democrat Jerry Zeifman. When asked why Hillary Rodham was fired, Zeifman said in an interview, ‘Because she was a liar. She was an unethical, dishonest lawyer, she conspired to violate the Constitution, the rules of the House, the rules of the Committee, and the rules of confidentiality.’"
rationale: While Jerry Zeifman did publicly criticize Hillary Rodham in 2007 and is quoted using harsh language and saying he “fired” her, contemporaneous committee records and other officials indicate Rodham left the House Judiciary Committee in 1974 rather than being formally fired, and Zeifman was not her direct supervisor in the clear-cut way the claim asserts. Major fact-checks and historical accounts treat Zeifman’s recollection and characterization as disputed and not definitive proof that she was fired for the reasons he stated.

claim: Says Sen. Chuck Schumer in 2014 "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" and now opposes Trump's $5 billion request for a border wall "just because he's a Republican." ​
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Schumer did not "help put together and sign a $25 billion deal" in 2014 to fund a border wall; his Senate work around 2013–2014 involved a broad immigration bill with various border-security provisions, not a $25 billion wall agreement. The statement that he now opposes Trump's $5 billion request "just because he's a Republican" asserts a motive that cannot be substantiated from the record.

claim: "All" University of Texas "student-athletes get an iPad."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement and is not supported by available information: while some University of Texas athletic programs or departments may provide iPads or other devices to certain teams or athletes for academic or recruiting purposes, there is no evidence that every student‑athlete at UT universally receives an iPad. Distribution of devices varies by program, funding source (school vs. booster), and time period, so the blanket "all" assertion is inaccurate.

claim: Health care premiums for consumers have doubled since 2001.
rationale: The statement is overly broad and inaccurate for the typical U.S. context. Historical data for employer-sponsored and individual-market plans show premiums rose substantially more than a simple doubling since 2001 (many commonly used measures rose well in excess of twofold), so the claim as stated is misleading. Without specifying country, type of plan, or end year the claim cannot be verified and is likely false in common usages.

claim: Says "Scott Walker says he would ban stem cell research"
rationale: The claim as stated implies Scott Walker said he would ban all stem cell research, which is inaccurate. Walker has voiced opposition to embryonic stem cell research and to use of fetal tissue or human cloning, but has supported adult (non-embryonic) stem cell research and made nuanced distinctions in his statements. Thus saying he broadly said he would ban 'stem cell research' is misleading.

claim: In one year, the United Nations "did 24 resolutions and 20 of them were against Israel."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: it does not specify which year or which UN body (General Assembly, Security Council, Human Rights Council, etc.). Typical UN bodies issue many resolutions annually and while some bodies have adopted multiple resolutions concerning Israel in particular years, there is no clear evidence that in any single year the UN passed exactly 24 resolutions with 20 directed at Israel. Without a precise year and body the statement is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: The statement is misleading. While the Treasury may report large receipts or temporary cash balances (sometimes on the order of trillions over a period), having "$3 trillion in cash flow" is vague and does not eliminate default risk because the debt ceiling can bar issuance of new debt and timing of receipts can leave shortfalls; Treasury could exhaust cash and extraordinary measures and be unable to pay all obligations if the limit isn’t raised.

claim: Says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Tammy Baldwin ranks "as the most liberal member of the House."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it presents an absolute ranking without specifying a metric or timeframe. Tammy Baldwin was consistently among the most liberal House members by several measures, but different indexes (DW-NOMINATE, ADA scores, party unity measures) and different years name different individuals as the single "most liberal," so she was not definitively the most liberal member overall.

claim: Abortion services are "well over 90 percent of what Planned Parenthood does."
rationale: This is false: abortion services are a small fraction of Planned Parenthood’s clinical services, not well over 90%. Planned Parenthood’s own annual statistics and independent fact-checks indicate abortions are roughly around 2–4% of total services in recent years, while the majority of care consists of contraception, STI testing/treatment, cancer screenings and other reproductive-health services.

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: The claim is not reliably supported because official counts of "state government employees" depend on definition (payroll headcount vs. full‑time equivalents, inclusion of authorities and local school staff) and the unspecified word "today" makes the comparison ambiguous. Independent fact‑checkers and state reports have found similar assertions misleading — some measures show reductions while others do not — and the statement that it was done "without any layoffs" is contradicted by agency‑level actions (furloughs, reorganizations and some separations) in relevant periods. Given those uncertainties and mixed data, the claim as stated is not verifiable as true.

claim: "Barack Obama has consistently voted against tougher penalties for criminals."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and inaccurate. Obama’s record on criminal penalties is mixed: at times (especially earlier in his political career) he supported tougher sentences or crime-fighting measures, while at other times he opposed sentencing enhancements and as president pursued clemency and reform efforts. Therefore he did not “consistently” vote against tougher penalties.

claim: Says Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has these offshore accounts" like Mitt Romney.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting showing Debbie Wasserman Schultz holds offshore bank accounts like those often cited in reporting about Mitt Romney. Public congressional financial disclosures and major fact-checks do not document offshore accounts for Wasserman Schultz, while Romney's investments and tax filings have been reported to include offshore holdings.

claim: Austin’s Pease Elementary "is a school that was created as part of the Texas Constitution."
rationale: State constitutions (including the Texas Constitution) establish the public school system and funding rules but do not create individual elementary schools. Individual schools such as Pease Elementary are created and run by local school districts or boards and are typically named by those districts, not authored as specific institutions in the state constitution.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official audit showing a 68% error rate in Michigan voting machines; independent post‑election audits, recounts and certification processes have not produced results anywhere near that magnitude. The 68% figure appears to be a misinterpretation or misuse of some other statistic rather than a measured machine tabulation error rate. Election equipment is federally and state certified and routinely subject to logic-and-accuracy tests and audits that are intended to keep error rates very low.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: The claim misrepresents the nominee (Saule Omarova) and her proposals. Omarova proposed restricting how commercial banks use customer deposits and treating core banking functions more like utilities, but she did not call for eliminating private bank accounts; she and fact-checkers have noted her proposals target banks’ business models and risky activities, not individuals’ deposit accounts. The phrase is a misleading extrapolation of her academic writings and testimony.

claim: Georgia’s HOPE scholarship is "still the richest scholarship program in America."
rationale: The HOPE Scholarship was historically one of the most generous state merit programs, but it has been scaled back over time and does not currently stand out as the single richest scholarship program in the U.S. Other state and federal programs (and some state scholarships) now provide comparable or larger awards and budgets, so the blanket claim that HOPE is "still the richest" nationwide is inaccurate. The statement also fails to define how "richest" is measured or the time reference.

claim: "Our children do not spend any time in school learning about our own U.S. Constitution."
rationale: The claim is an absolute that no children spend any time learning the U.S. Constitution; this is incorrect. U.S. K–12 curricula routinely include U.S. history and civics/government courses that cover the Constitution (Preamble, Bill of Rights, branches of government), and many states explicitly require constitutional instruction. While coverage varies by grade and district, it is not true that children receive zero instruction nationwide.

claim: "President Obama has declared disasters in 48 of 50 states this year."
rationale: This is false. Presidential disaster declarations are issued for specific incidents and counties, not whole states, and official FEMA records and prior fact-checking have shown no single year in which President Obama declared disasters in 48 of 50 states. The claim likely misinterprets cumulative or county-level actions or is simply incorrect.

claim: "666,000 teachers have been laid off already since March."
