rationale: The VA does negotiate and contract for prescription drug prices for its pharmacy benefit, and it typically pays lower rates. While Medicare was long unable to directly set national drug prices, the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act gave Medicare authority to directly negotiate prices for selected high‑cost Part B and Part D drugs, with a phased implementation—so the blanket claim that Medicare doesn't negotiate is no longer accurate.

claim: "The committee that advises @GovEvers and his department tasked with leading during this pandemic is recommending allowing prisoners to receive the vaccine before 65 year old grandma?"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the advisory committee to Governor Evers officially recommended vaccinating incarcerated people ahead of all adults aged 65+. Most pandemic vaccine prioritization frameworks, including federal and state advisory bodies, placed healthcare workers, long‑term care residents, and older adults (65+) at the front of early allocation. While some guidance allowed vaccination in congregate settings or placed incarcerated people in similar phases, that is not the same as a recommendation to put prisoners before 65‑year‑olds statewide.

claim: "China owns about 29% of (the U.S.) debt."
rationale: This is false. China holds roughly $800 billion–$1.1 trillion in U.S. Treasury securities, which represents only about 3–4% of total U.S. federal debt (and well under 29%). Even measured as a share of foreign-held Treasuries, China’s portion has historically been well below one-third.

claim: The Tampa Bay Rays' "prices have been judged the most affordable in all of professional sports."
rationale: This claim is an overbroad assertion not supported by a clear, authoritative source. While the Tampa Bay Rays have frequently been listed among the cheapest teams for average ticket prices in MLB and sometimes among the least expensive in major North American pro sports, there is no consistent, widely accepted ranking that declares them definitively "the most affordable in all of professional sports." The statement omits timeframe, metric (tickets vs. overall cost), and source.

claim: Obama's budget plan would "take national debt up to about 80 percent of gross national product. ... Historically, it's been about 40 percent."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and depends on definitions and timeframes. Some CBO projections under certain assumptions showed federal debt (debt held by the public) rising toward roughly 70–90% of GDP over the following decade, but that was scenario- and measure-dependent; the administration and CBO used different baselines and often reported debt relative to GDP (not GNP). The statement’s round 80% figure and the blanket historical “about 40%” ignore these distinctions and the WWII-era spike that skews long-term averages.

claim: Rubio's "got more experience than Obama had."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not supported as a blanket statement: whether Rubio had “more experience” than Obama depends on which point in time and which kinds of experience are counted. Obama had U.S. Senate service (2005–2008), Illinois state senate service, a law degree, and years of community organizing and teaching; Rubio’s résumé includes Florida state legislative service and U.S. Senate service beginning in 2011. On most straightforward comparisons of national/federal experience before a presidential run, Rubio does not clearly have more experience than Obama did, so the broad claim is false without further context.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The claim is vague and implausible: unemployment rate lows are well-documented (for example the U.S. 3.5% low in early 2020) and attributing such a result to having spent no taxpayer money is unsupported. Economic outcomes reflect many policies (tax policy, federal spending, and central bank actions) and routine government programs and tax cuts are financed by taxpayers, so the statement that the low unemployment occurred “without using taxpayers money” is misleading or false. Without specifying country and precise date the absolute "lowest in history" part is also unverifiable.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: State-level baby-name data for recent years (Social Security Administration records) show names like Liam, Noah, and Mateo topping Texas rankings; Jose has not been the No. 1 name statewide in the modern SSA annual lists. Name popularity varies by year and local subpopulations, so the blanket claim that the top male baby name in Texas is Jose is incorrect for the typical recent reporting period.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported by clear evidence: while Nathan Deal voted for and at times supported stricter immigration enforcement, he was not broadly recognized as a leading national figure on U.S. border security while serving in Congress. His congressional work focused more on judiciary/criminal justice and other issues, and he did not author or lead the major, high-profile border-security initiatives typically associated with a "leader" on the topic.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted to deport" young people known as Dreamers.
rationale: There is no clear roll-call showing Marco Rubio formally "voted to deport" DACA recipients as a category; that phrasing overstates the public record. Rubio has a mixed immigration record—he co‑sponsored the 2013 comprehensive reform offering legalization and has also supported measures to end or restrict DACA and increase enforcement—but he did not cast a single, explicit congressional vote that directly ordered the deportation of Dreamers. The claim therefore mischaracterizes his voting record.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Sen. Sherrod Brown promised the very first federal stimulus bill would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. He has repeatedly advocated for federal investment in the bridge, but the initial major stimulus measures (e.g., early COVID relief or earlier ARRA provisions) did not contain a specific, guaranteed funding promise for that bridge and news reporting does not show him making such a categorical pledge.

claim: The U.S. government spends less on energy innovation "than the pet food industry invests in its own products."
rationale: This is false. Annual U.S. federal spending on energy research and development (DOE programs, ARPA‑E, EERE and related RD&D) totals multiple billions of dollars per year, while pet food companies’ own product R&D is a small share of industry revenue and totals only a few hundred million annually. Using those typical magnitudes, the government spends more on energy innovation than the pet food industry spends on product investment.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: The statement mixes a debatable factual claim with an unsupported causal claim. While NFL TV ratings and some metrics have dipped or fluctuated in recent years, attendance and viewership remain high by historical and sports-industry standards and are not uniformly “WAY DOWN.” There is no credible evidence that a large share of fans are avoiding games primarily “because they love our country”; motives for viewership changes are mixed and unproven.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy "smoked cannabis in the White House, while president, because he suffered from severe back pain and Addison's disease."
rationale: There is no credible historical or medical evidence that John F. Kennedy smoked cannabis in the White House. Declassified medical records and authoritative biographies document extensive prescription treatments for severe back pain (opioids, amphetamines, cortisone injections) and show no reliable documentation of marijuana use; an Addison's disease diagnosis is not supported by mainstream medical records either.

claim: Banks paid Hillary Clinton "over $1 million and are contributing millions more to elect her."
rationale: Public reporting and campaign finance records show that Wall Street and major banks (and their employees/PACs) paid the Clintons sizable sums in speaking fees and donations that exceed $1 million collectively, and employees/PACs tied to banks gave millions more to Hillary Clinton’s campaign and allied groups. While exact totals vary by source, the broad claim that banks paid over $1M and contributed millions more toward her election is supported by available records and news coverage.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: The attribution is misleading. During the 2015 Scott County HIV outbreak in Indiana, Governor Mike Pence's administration was widely criticized for not acting immediately and for initially opposing syringe-exchange programs; state approval of an emergency needle-exchange and broader mobilization of health resources came only after mounting cases and external pressure. Saying he declared “we immediately deployed health resources” misstates the timing and responsiveness of the official response.

claim: President Barack Obama’s policies "have resulted in gas prices being reduced from $3.07 per gallon when he was sworn in in 2009 to $2.30 today."
rationale: The numeric assertion is incorrect and the causal claim is misleading. National average retail gasoline prices at the time of Obama’s Jan 20, 2009 inauguration were substantially lower than $3.07/gal (around the mid-$1.80s to low-$1.90s by common historical averages), and prices since then have moved mainly with global crude oil markets, demand, and the recession rather than solely because of White House policy.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The factual claim is incorrect: the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (the state’s consumer advocate) does not employ 74 lawyers — state consumer‑advocate offices typically have modest legal staffs and public information shows OCC’s legal team is far smaller. The follow‑on statement that funding them is "wasteful duplication" is a normative judgment not established by the factual record and depends on policy perspective and context.

claim: One Wisconsin school district "is so worried about losing state funding that it has stopped giving milk to elementary school kids during snack time."
rationale: I could not corroborate the specific claim that a Wisconsin district stopped giving elementary students milk specifically because it feared losing state funding. Reports about school milk changes exist but are typically tied to budget cuts, program changes, or short-term logistical issues; the claim as stated is anecdotal and lacks identifying details or independent verification. Given the lack of a named district, time frame, or reliable sourcing, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Lauren Boebert received a PPP loan for her restaurant."
rationale: Public Small Business Administration PPP recipient data and contemporaneous news reporting show that Boebert’s restaurant received a Paycheck Protection Program loan in 2020. Reporting indicated the loan was made to the restaurant business associated with Lauren Boebert and was in the publicly disclosed range rather than a single exact figure.

claim: "Some of the wealthiest Americans are African-American now."
rationale: The statement is true: several African‑American individuals appear on contemporary lists of the wealthiest Americans. High‑net‑worth African‑American figures such as Robert F. Smith, Oprah Winfrey, Michael Jordan and Jay‑Z have been listed as billionaires or among the richest Americans in recent years, so the claim that some of the wealthiest Americans are African‑American is accurate.

claim: "Politicians and their corporate lobbyists are trying to take away my right to spend my paycheck how I want."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While politicians and corporate lobbyists sometimes push laws, regulations, taxes, or corporate policies that limit or influence certain purchases or financial flows, there is no widespread, universal campaign to entirely eliminate individuals’ basic ability to spend their paychecks as they choose. Specific proposals may restrict particular transactions (e.g., illegal goods, sanctions, age-restricted items) but that is not the same as a blanket removal of spending rights.

claim: "Since I took office, Michigan has added more than 25,000 auto jobs."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about the speaker’s start date and what counts as “auto jobs” (OEM assembly only vs. suppliers and broader auto-related employment). Public labor data (state BLS series for motor vehicle manufacturing and related sectors) show large pandemic-era losses and a recovery, but do not clearly support a net increase of more than 25,000 pure auto-manufacturing jobs since early 2019; any larger-sounding totals typically rely on broader definitions or shorter time windows. Given the ambiguity and lack of clear corroborating statewide counts showing +25,000 in the core auto sector, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Hepatitis outbreak in kids may be related to Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence linking the pediatric acute hepatitis outbreak to the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. Investigations by public health agencies found most affected children were too young to have received COVID-19 vaccines and epidemiology points toward adenovirus (not COVID-19 vaccination) or other infectious/immune causes. Ongoing surveillance has not identified a causal connection to J&J vaccination.

claim: In the past three years, state legislatures have "enacted more of these restrictions (on abortion) than in the previous 10 years combined."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because credible trackers of state abortion laws (e.g., research groups and policy monitors) show a large surge in restrictions after 2021–2022 but do not uniformly report that three recent years produced more restrictions than the prior ten years combined. Whether the statement could be true depends on how one defines and counts “restrictions,” the exact three-year window, and which prior ten-year period is used; available aggregate counts do not clearly substantiate the blanket claim.

claim: Undocumented immigrants "pay $12 billion a year into Social Security."
rationale: Multiple estimates from the Social Security Administration actuary and independent researchers find that unauthorized/undocumented workers contribute on the order of $10–13 billion per year in payroll taxes, commonly summarized as about $12 billion. Those payments are made through payroll withholding or taxes paid under invalid or borrowed Social Security numbers, and undocumented workers generally cannot collect benefits. The figure is therefore consistent with reputable estimates, though exact totals vary by year and method.

claim: Due to U.S. Senate rules, Democrats need "more than a majority ... to codify Roe vs. Wade."
rationale: Under current Senate practice the filibuster means most legislation requires 60 votes to invoke cloture and proceed to final passage, so a simple 51-vote majority typically is insufficient to "codify" Roe v. Wade by statute. While the majority could try to change or eliminate the filibuster by a separate majority vote (the "nuclear option"), that is a distinct and politically difficult step, so the claim is accurate in ordinary Senate practice.

claim: "National Guard doctors find hospitals empty of COVID patients."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. While a few National Guard medical teams in specific locations and at particular times reported lighter-than-expected patient loads, nationwide and state hospital data during COVID showed large numbers of inpatients and many hospitals operating at or over capacity. Therefore the blanket claim that National Guard doctors found hospitals empty of COVID patients is false.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is a specific, verifiable numeric claim about 20 individuals and payment history but no evidence, documentation, or corroboration is provided. Without independent records (the letters, transaction histories, or named individuals) the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unverified/false.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: The claim is almost certainly false: congressional districts are political boundaries and electricity generation is reported by plant, utility service area, county, state, and regional grids, not by House districts. Even in coal-dominated regions, generation is mixed with natural gas, renewables, imports/exports on the regional grid, so it is implausible that any modern U.S. congressional district obtains 100% of its electric generation from coal. No authoritative energy data source reports 100% coal generation for an entire congressional district.

claim: "In South Dakota, I’m putting prayer back in our schools."
rationale: The statement implies the speaker can reinstate official, school‑led prayer statewide. U.S. Supreme Court rulings prohibit school‑sponsored prayer in public schools, so a state cannot constitutionally mandate or lead prayer; at most schools can permit voluntary, student‑led prayer or moments of silence. Without evidence of a lawful policy change that respects constitutional limits, the claim that prayer is being "put back" as an official practice is inaccurate.

claim: In the United States, we’ve had "12 years in a row of wages declining."
rationale: U.S. wage series do not show a contiguous 12-year decline. Official data (e.g., BLS real average hourly earnings and Census median household income) show multiple years with increases and only shorter stretches of real declines; there is no documented 12-year consecutive drop across broad national wage measures. Whether wages fall depends on the specific measure (nominal vs. real) and timeframe, but the blanket statement is incorrect as written.

claim: Paul Ryan’s budget "keeps the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare, but then cuts all of the benefits."
rationale: This characterization is misleading. Paul Ryan’s budgets proposed repealing the Affordable Care Act’s coverage expansions (individual mandate, subsidies and Medicaid expansion) while also altering or proposing alternative offsets; they did not simply keep all of the ACA’s taxes and spending cuts intact and then eliminate all benefits. Independent analyses note Ryan aimed to preserve some Medicare payment changes or broader entitlement savings while eliminating ACA coverage, but he also sought to repeal or replace many specific ACA tax provisions, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim gives precise totals and share breakdowns but fails to specify the exact two‑year period and no source is provided; super PAC fundraising totals and donor breakdowns vary substantially by election cycle. While it is true that a small number of very wealthy donors often account for a large share of super PAC money and corporations can and do contribute, the specific figures (>$180 million, about half from fewer than 200 people, ~20% from corporations) cannot be confirmed as a general statement without a cited timeframe and source and are likely inaccurate for many recent two‑year periods.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is false. The statement both ambiguously refers to "America" and asserts 50% fully vaccinated is the highest of any country; many individual countries (e.g., UAE, Portugal, Chile, Spain, the UK and others at various points) have had higher shares of their populations fully vaccinated than the United States. Without a clear date or definition of "fully vaccinated" or "America," the claim is unsupported by broad global vaccination data.

claim: Florida students take "an array of standardized high stakes tests which eat up as much as 45 school days per year."
rationale: This overstates reality. Florida's statewide required assessments (FSA, end‑of‑course exams and other mandated tests) amount to a number of testing hours that translate to a few school days for most students, not 45 full school days. Claims of 45 days typically conflate mandated test administration with separate local benchmark tests, preparatory activities, and make‑ups rather than official statewide testing time.

claim: "We know mask mandates work. There’s enough evidence out there between counties that have done it and counties that haven’t."
rationale: Multiple observational studies comparing jurisdictions with and without mask mandates have found reductions in COVID-19 case growth after mandates, and randomized and quasi-experimental studies (including a cluster RCT of mask promotion and multiple natural experiments at county/state level) support a protective effect. While effect size varies with compliance, mask type, and other measures in place, the preponderance of evidence indicates mandates reduce transmission at the population level.

claim: The Orlando shooter used "a weapon of war."
rationale: Investigations of the 2016 Orlando (Pulse) shooting found the attacker used a semi-automatic rifle and a handgun — civilian firearms (reports named an AR-style/Sig MCX-type rifle and a Glock-style pistol). He did not use a fully automatic or military-grade weapon; calling it a "weapon of war" is a rhetorical characterization rather than a factual description of the firearms' operation or classification.

claim: California Republican gubernatorial hopeful Meg Whitman "contributed to, and campaigned, for" Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer.
rationale: While Meg Whitman has given small donations to Democratic candidates in the past (records show contributions to some Democrats, including Barbara Boxer), there is no clear evidence she actively campaigned as a surrogate for Boxer. Contemporary reporting and campaign records distinguish isolated donations from overt campaigning, so the claim overstates her role.

claim: "Over the past 10 years, the number of people living in Lower Manhattan has nearly doubled. In fact, Lower Manhattan has added more people over the last 10 years than Atlanta, Dallas and Philadelphia combined."
rationale: This claim is inconsistent with U.S. Census and city population data. Lower Manhattan did see substantial residential growth in recent decades but did not nearly double in a single recent 10-year span, nor did its net population gain exceed the combined gains of large cities such as Atlanta and Dallas (and Philadelphia) over comparable 10-year periods. Census counts and municipal estimates show the three named cities added tens to hundreds of thousands of residents collectively, far more than the net increase in the smaller Lower Manhattan neighborhood.

claim: "A family of four can make up to $88,000 a year and still get a subsidy for health insurance" under the new federal health care law.
rationale: This statement is misleading. Premium tax credits under the Affordable Care Act are based on household income as a percentage of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL) and that FPL is updated annually and varies by household size and state; there is no single fixed $88,000 cutoff that universally determines subsidy eligibility.

claim: Says swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is a "safe, easy way" to remove them from skin.
rationale: Public-health guidance does not endorse swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball as a safe removal method. Agencies recommend using fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin and pull upward steadily because smothering or irritating a tick (with soap, petroleum, heat, etc.) can cause it to regurgitate and increase the risk of pathogen transmission.

claim: Says no elections protest was filed, McCready conceded and "every" county board certified its results from the Mark Harris, Dan McCready race.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. After the 2018 NC-9 race there was a formal state investigation into absentee-ballot fraud (centered on operative McCrae Dowless), the North Carolina State Board of Elections declined to certify the result and in February 2019 ordered a new election. While many county boards initially certified local tallies, the State Board’s action and the public investigation show the race was contested and not simply conceded without protest by McCready.

claim: Says George Patton said, "Politicians are the lowest form of life on earth. Liberal Democrats are the lower form of politicians."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence that General George S. Patton ever said that line; it does not appear in his published speeches, letters, or vetted quote compilations and resembles a partisan joke frequently misattributed online. Quote researchers and historians have not verified this attribution, so the claim is unsupported.

claim: The debt ceiling deal will result in "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."
rationale: This is misleading. The debt-ceiling deal limits future growth in spending but does not cut annual domestic outlays back to the absolute or inflation-adjusted levels seen under President Dwight Eisenhower (1953–1961). Federal domestic spending today — including large entitlement programs created after the 1950s — is substantially higher in real terms and as a share of the economy, and independent analyses said the deal trims growth rather than reverting spending to mid‑20th century levels.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We’ll never have to worry about China attacking us! They are 12 hours ahead, so we’ll have plenty of time to shoot down their missiles!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ever made this remark; the line appears to be a satirical or fabricated quote circulating online. The substance is also technically incorrect: time-zone differences do not provide a 12-hour early warning for missile attacks, and missile detection/response depends on flight times and sensors measured in minutes to hours, not civilian clock offsets.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: This claim is false. The EPA does not have any proposal or plan to hire 230,000 new government regulators for $21 billion; the agency’s workforce is on the order of tens of thousands (roughly ~14,000 employees) and its annual budget is far smaller than the implied one-time hiring cost. The 230,000/$21 billion figures often stem from misreading regulatory analyses that estimate compliance costs, affected private‑sector labor or aggregated economic impacts, not a plan to add hundreds of thousands of federal regulator positions.

claim: "Thousands of Westerners and Americans" are fighting with extremists in eastern Syria and Iraq.
rationale: While at the peak of the Syrian/Iraq conflicts tens of thousands of foreign fighters overall traveled to join extremist groups and several thousand came from Western European countries, the number of US citizens was in the low hundreds, not thousands. Moreover, after ISIS’s territorial defeat many foreign fighters were killed, captured, detained in camps, or returned, so the claim that "thousands of Westerners and Americans are fighting" currently is inaccurate without a specific historical timeframe.

claim: Says "every school will be negatively impacted" if Education Stability Fund is not tapped.
rationale: The claim is an absolute claim that every school would be negatively impacted if the Education Stability Fund is not tapped; that is unlikely. School funding mixes federal, state, and local revenue and varies widely, so some schools could avoid harm via reserves, alternate funding, or state responses while others might be affected. Whether and how schools are harmed depends on the specific fund, jurisdiction, timing, and budget choices.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme: it is a statutory, pay‑as‑you‑go social insurance program funded by payroll taxes with legally mandated benefit formulas and a trust fund invested in Treasury securities. A Ponzi scheme is a fraudulent investment scam that pays earlier investors with money from later investors and depends on concealment and deception; Social Security operates openly under law and has actuarial projections and policy levers rather than criminal fraud. While the program faces long‑term funding challenges, that fiscal risk does not make it a Ponzi scheme.

claim: "CDC Director Robert Redfield says healthy people should NOT wear masks."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Early in the COVID‑19 pandemic (Feb–Mar 2020) CDC guidance and Director Robert Redfield emphasized masks for symptomatic people and healthcare workers and said healthy people did not need masks, but by mid‑2020 both Redfield and the CDC were publicly endorsing widespread public mask use. Stating flatly that Redfield "says healthy people should NOT wear masks" without a timeframe is inaccurate given his later reversal and evolving guidance.

claim: "After California taxes, Trey Lance's $34.1M rookie deal becomes just $16M."
rationale: The statement is an oversimplification and misleading. While federal and California state taxes plus payroll taxes can take a large share of high NFL earnings, whether a $34.1M rookie contract reduces to about $16M depends on payment timing, signing-bonus treatment, residency, multi-state taxation from away games, agent fees and deductions—not a blanket California-only haircut. Therefore claiming the deal “becomes just $16M” after California taxes is inaccurate without those details.

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as a blanket statement. Official labor statistics during Chris Christie’s tenure (2010–2017) show net job gains in the state and a decline in the unemployment rate, so it is not correct to say that jobs were not being created at all. That said, growth was uneven across sectors and regions, which explains some criticism.

claim: The climate-change agreement between the United States and China "requires the Chinese to do nothing at all for 16 years."
rationale: The 2014 U.S.–China climate announcement did not instruct China to “do nothing for 16 years.” China pledged to peak CO2 emissions around 2030 while also increasing the share of non‑fossil energy to about 20% by 2030, expanding forest carbon sinks, and pursuing emissions‑intensity reductions and other domestic measures. Those are active commitments and policy directions, not a requirement to take no action.

claim: "When Rachel Zenzinger was on the Arvada City Council, she voted to spend taxpayer funds for a junket to China."
rationale: I can find no clear evidence that Zenzinger explicitly voted to spend municipal taxpayer funds on a personal “junket” to China. Reporting about her time on Arvada’s council mentions participation in a sister‑city/cultural exchange trip and routine council travel approvals, with funding described as a mix of nonprofit or program support rather than a council‑authorized personal taxpayer junket. Given limited public records and the pejorative nature of “junket,” the specific claim as stated is not substantiated.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: This quotation is a widely shared social-media meme misattributed to Keanu Reeves; thorough searches of interviews, speeches and credible reporting find no record, video, or reliable source showing Reeves saying these words. Established fact-checkers have traced the line to anonymous online posts rather than any verified public remark by Reeves. Because no primary evidence supports the attribution, the claim is false.

claim: Says "former Democrat Kelli Ward attacked President Trump's plans to crack down on illegal immigration, saying Trump was making a mistake."
rationale: Kelli Ward is a Republican (former Arizona GOP chair and two-time Republican Senate candidate) and has generally supported tougher immigration enforcement; there is no reliable record of her attacking President Trump’s immigration crackdown or publicly saying his policy was a mistake. The claim appears to misattribute criticism to Ward or confuse her with another figure. Given her partisan history and public statements, the assertion is inconsistent with known reporting.

claim: Says Donald Trump warned outgoing Ghana President against last-minute job appointments.
rationale: I find no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Donald Trump publicly warned an outgoing Ghanaian president against making last‑minute job appointments. Major news outlets and Trump's public statements through my knowledge cutoff (June 2024) do not record such a remark, and it appears to be unreported and unverified. Without a reliable source, the claim is likely false or at least unproven.

claim: "We are within the margin of error."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it gives no data, poll, estimate, or numerical margin to check. Saying "we are within the margin of error" is a statistical claim that requires the specific estimate, margin value, sample size and confidence level; without those details it cannot be confirmed. Because the assertion is ambiguous and could be true or false depending on missing information, I rate it false in this context.

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: There is no clear congressional vote in Schrader’s record that directly authorized a $500 billion cut to Medicare; the claim appears to conflate or mischaracterize budget/healthcare votes and campaign ads. Public roll-call records and contemporaneous fact-checking do not show Schrader voting for a specific measure that cut Medicare by that exact amount.

claim: An all-female construction company built the Florida bridge that collapsed.
rationale: This is false. The widely reported Florida pedestrian bridge collapse (FIU, 2018) was built by Munilla Construction Management with design by FIGG—companies not described as an all‑female firm—and investigations pointed to design and construction failures rather than being attributable to an all‑female crew. No credible reports identify an all‑female construction company as having built the collapsed bridge.

claim: Says Jill McCabe "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jill McCabe said "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable." That phrasing echoes lines from undercover videos involving Planned Parenthood personnel in 2015, not statements by Jill McCabe, and the claim appears to be a misattribution or fabrication. Fact-checking sources and public records do not document McCabe making those remarks or endorsing such language.

claim: "Withheld union dues fund half of Dem (Democratic) campaigns in Florida."
rationale: There is no evidence that 'withheld union dues' finance half of Democratic campaigns in Florida. Campaign finance disclosures show Democratic campaigns are funded by a mix of individual donors, party committees, PACs, out-of-state donors, and some union contributions, but not a single source supplying 50% statewide. The phrase 'withheld union dues' is also ambiguous and does not match how political contributions from unions are typically collected or reported.

claim: The IRS is going to be "in charge" of "a huge national database" on health care that will include Americans’ "personal, intimate, most close-to-the-vest-secrets."
rationale: This claim is false. While the IRS does receive limited tax-related information about health coverage and subsidies (e.g., ACA reporting), it does not operate a ‘‘huge national database’’ of individuals’ medical records or their ‘‘most intimate’’ personal health secrets. Enrollment data and medical records are primarily held by insurers, providers, and HHS/CMS, and HIPAA and other rules restrict disclosure of detailed medical information to the IRS.

claim: "All of the records, as far as I know, about what we did with health care, those are already available."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify and unlikely to be strictly true as stated. Whether "all of the records" about actions on health care are publicly available depends on which records, which actors, and where they would be stored; many documents can remain private, redacted, or classified. Without specific references or evidence, the blanket assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or video evidence that Barack Obama used John Lewis’s funeral to tell attendees that "rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote." News coverage of Lewis’s memorials and Obama’s public statements in 2020 do show he supported safe voting methods broadly, but the specific claim about that line being said at the funeral is unsubstantiated and appears to conflate separate events or statements.

claim: Democratic U.S. House candidate Julie Lassa pushed for a "Canadian-style government takeover of health care."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Julie Lassa explicitly called for a ‘Canadian-style government takeover of health care.’ Her known campaign positions emphasized protecting the Affordable Care Act, Medicaid expansion, and lowering prescription drug costs rather than advocating wholesale nationalization or a single-payer Canadian model. The phrasing appears to be a political opponent’s characterization rather than a direct policy proposal from Lassa.

claim: "We need to also recognize that we just had two of the coldest years, biggest drop in global temperatures that we have had since the 1980s, the biggest in the last 100 years. We don't talk about that."
rationale: Global temperature datasets show the recent years are among the warmest on record, not the coldest; there is no evidence of "two of the coldest years" or the largest drop in global temperatures since the 1980s or in the last 100 years. Year-to-year variability occurs but the long-term trend is warming, and any short-term declines have been small compared with century-scale changes.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: State tax data and independent analyses consistently show that roughly 70% of New York State personal income tax receipts are generated in New York City together with Westchester, Nassau and Suffolk counties. The exact share varies by year, but published breakdowns commonly report about seven-tenths of PIT collections coming from that downstate region.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad, unsubstantiated generalization. While some recent surveys and reports show a decline in business confidence toward China and renewed interest in the U.S., there is no single, global declaration by ’business leaders around the world’ abandoning China as the top investment destination for the first time in over a decade; FDI flows and sentiment polls are mixed and have varied by year and sector. Historical FDI data also show the U.S. has been a top recipient in multiple recent years, and China remains a major investment destination, so the absolute statement does not hold.

claim: "The CBO says if we raise the minimum wage the way Charlie (Crist) wants to do it, it would lose 500,000 jobs."
rationale: The Congressional Budget Office’s 2014 analysis estimated that raising the federal minimum wage to $10.10 by 2016 would reduce employment by about 500,000 workers (it reported a central estimate around 500,000 and a wide uncertainty range). The statement is accurate if Crist’s proposal matched that $10.10 federal increase; differences in timing, level, or applying it at the state level could change the applicability of the CBO number.

claim: A photo shows Joe Namath and Al Woodall kneeling on the sideline of a football field during the national anthem.
rationale: A widely circulated photo of Joe Namath and Al Woodall kneeling on the sideline has been miscaptioned. Contemporary reporting and fact-checkers traced the image to Jets-era sideline/warmup/game moments and found no reliable evidence it was taken while the national anthem was being played or as an anthem protest.

claim: Members of Congress "have not reduced their salaries ... since the Great Depression," meaning they've gone "eight decades without a pay cut."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Since the 1930s Congress has periodically frozen or canceled pay increases (for example cancelling automatic cost-of-living adjustments and instituting pay freezes in recent decades) and congressional compensation has been adjusted many times, so it is not accurate to say members have gone eight decades without any pay reduction. The statement also fails to specify whether it means nominal dollars or inflation-adjusted pay, which changes the conclusion.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted himself health care for life."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Members of Congress participate in the Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) program and, like other federal employees, may keep coverage into retirement if they meet standard vesting/age-and-service rules — this is a longstanding federal benefit, not a special “vote” by Rep. Steve Southerland to give himself lifetime health care. There is no evidence Southerland cast a standalone vote that unilaterally granted himself lifetime health care beyond the existing federal benefits system.

claim: Says law enforcement officials alerted the public to check the caps of bottled water for tampering because someone is injecting poison into them, and that a "few people already died in the Richmond area" as a result.
rationale: There is no evidence that law enforcement in the Richmond area issued an official alert warning that people were injecting poison into bottled water or that a few people had died as a result. Local police and public-health authorities have repeatedly debunked similar viral social-media claims and reported no confirmed incidents or fatalities tied to tampered bottled water. The story matches a recurring hoax pattern rather than documented, verifiable events.

claim: A man was arrested "for wearing a T-shirt that says ‘We The People’ and has a picture of the ‘Statue of Liberty.’"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting that a person was arrested solely for wearing a T‑shirt reading “We The People” with a Statue of Liberty image. Viral social‑media claims about arrests for political shirts are frequently mischaracterized or omit context (other alleged conduct or private‑property rules) and I found no reliable account confirming this specific arrest. U.S. law and news coverage make purely expressive arrests uncommon and well‑documented when they do occur, which is not the case here.

claim: President Barack Obama "had the legal authority" to strike Syria without a vote from Congress.
rationale: Whether President Obama “had the legal authority” to unilaterally strike Syria is contested, not settled as a fact. The President can claim commander-in-chief powers for limited uses of force, but the War Powers Resolution and constitutional separation of powers mean Congress’s authorization is generally required for prolonged hostilities, and legal scholars and courts have disagreed; the absence of a definitive judicial ruling means the claim that he unequivocally had authority is false. Obama’s administration sought congressional approval in 2013, reflecting the legal uncertainty.

claim: Says Ted Strickland admits his record on jobs and taxes is "mixed and spotty."
rationale: I am not aware of any reliable instance where Ted Strickland himself described his record on jobs and taxes as “mixed and spotty.” Public statements and campaign materials from Strickland typically defend his economic record rather than use that self-critical phrasing, so the claim appears to be a misquote or opponent characterization. Without a primary source showing he made that admission, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official roster showing 89 U.S. members of Congress hold Israeli citizenship; fact‑checking organizations and public records do not support such a large number. Dual Israeli‑U.S. citizenship among members would be a notable, verifiable status and only a very small handful of members (if any) have been reported to hold Israeli citizenship. The claim appears to be a recycled social‑media rumor without substantiation.

claim: Says Burisma admitted in a Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000.
rationale: This claim is false. There is no credible court record or verified reporting that Burisma admitted paying Joe Biden $900,000; reputable fact-checkers and public court documents show no such admission, and both Burisma and Biden have denied payments to Joe Biden. While Hunter Biden served on Burisma's board and received payments, that is distinct from any verified payment to Joe Biden.

claim: The employer mandate "affects only 5 percent of businesses in this country."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While only a small share of firms by count (often cited around 4–6%) have 50 or more employees, the ACA employer mandate is based on employee counts and therefore applies to employers that account for a large share of private‑sector employment and payroll. Saying it "affects only 5 percent of businesses" ignores that those businesses employ a disproportionate number of workers and that definitions (firm vs. establishment vs. employer) change the percentage.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The claim that someone personally warned President Trump in January that the pandemic was coming cannot be verified from the public record as stated. Public timelines show key briefings to the administration from intelligence and health agencies occurred in late January and February, and many lawmakers publicly raised concerns in February and March; there is no clear, documented instance confirming the speaker privately warned the president in January. Without a named speaker or supporting evidence, the statement is not substantiated.

claim: Under the North American Free Trade Agreement, "we lost millions of jobs."
rationale: While the U.S. experienced millions of manufacturing job losses over the 1990s and afterward, most academic and government analyses conclude that only a minority of those losses can be directly attributed to NAFTA. Other factors—automation, productivity gains, and trade with non-NAFTA countries (especially China)—explain much of the decline, and credible estimates of NAFTA-specific job losses are generally in the hundreds of thousands rather than multiple millions.

claim: "New evidence ties COVID-19 creation to research funded by Fauci"
rationale: No credible, verifiable evidence ties Anthony Fauci to funding the deliberate creation of SARS-CoV-2. While NIH grants (administered through EcoHealth Alliance) supported coronavirus surveillance and limited collaborative work with Wuhan researchers, multiple investigations and official statements have found no evidence those funds were used to create the virus or that Fauci directed such activity. The claim conflates routine research funding with intentional virus creation without substantiation.

claim: Under Republican-backed state budget, the state education agency estimates expansion of Wisconsin’s school voucher program "could cost nearly $2 billion annually"
rationale: This matches reporting from Wisconsin education officials and state analyses: the Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction and related fiscal analyses warned that a Republican-backed budget proposal to broaden voucher eligibility could cost on the order of $1.8–$2.0 billion per year, which is commonly described as "nearly $2 billion annually." The estimate is presented as a projected maximum dependent on enrollment and policy details rather than a guaranteed fixed outlay.

claim: Wisconsin's Lincoln Hills youth prison has a "66 percent recidivism rate," while "states like Missouri, that have more of a regional model -- 8 percent."
rationale: The two percentages are misleadingly presented as directly comparable. While Lincoln Hills has been reported to have relatively high post‑release re‑offending on some measures and Missouri’s Department of Youth Services has reported unusually low recidivism on others, the 66% vs 8% figures come from different definitions, timeframes, and outcome measures (e.g., rearrest vs. re‑incarceration/re‑adjudication). Comparing them without clarifying metric and follow‑up period misstates the situation.

claim: Says El Chapo testified in court that he paid off Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open for drug cartels.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or court transcript in which Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán testified that he paid Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open. El Chapo’s U.S. trial and reporting from major outlets did not include any such allegation, and Pelosi has never been credibly accused or charged in connection with payments from Guzmán. The claim appears to be a baseless rumor or disinformation.

claim: Says China and Singapore impose the death penalty on drug dealers.
rationale: Both China and Singapore retain capital punishment provisions that apply to serious drug trafficking and dealing offenses. China routinely sentences major traffickers to death under its criminal law, and Singapore historically imposed a mandatory death penalty for trafficking specified quantities of drugs (though limited judicial discretion was introduced in reforms). The statement is broadly accurate though application depends on offense severity and other factors.

claim: "Phoenix is already one of the kidnapping capitals of the world."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or internationally recognized ranking that places Phoenix among the world’s top cities for kidnappings. While Phoenix, like many large U.S. cities, has incidents of abduction and violent crime, global kidnapping hotspots are typically in regions with organized crime, insurgency, or weak state control, and the U.S. overall has far lower kidnapping rates than those areas. The claim is an unsupported hyperbole rather than a verifiable fact.

claim: "We bailed out" Johnson Controls when "we saved the auto industry" and "now they want to avoid paying taxes."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate as phrased. The 2008–09 U.S. auto rescue explicitly targeted automakers (notably GM and Chrysler); while some suppliers received limited support or benefits indirectly through government programs, Johnson Controls was not a primary recipient of a direct federal “bailout” in the way the claim implies. Separately, Johnson Controls has used corporate reorganizations and transactions that critics say reduced its tax burden, but that is a distinct issue and does not prove a prior government bailout of the company.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: There is no evidence that the Icelandic government or legal system has declared "all religions" to be mental disorders. Freedom of religion is protected in Icelandic law and psychiatric classifications of mental disorders are governed by medical authorities (e.g., WHO ICD), not by blanket governmental declarations labeling religions as disorders. The claim appears to be false or a mischaracterization/misreading of some other statement.

claim: The Republicans' alternative health care plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages."
rationale: The specific claim that a Republican alternative health plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages" is not supported by authoritative analyses. CBO, Kaiser Family Foundation and other independent studies of various GOP repeal-and-replace proposals showed differing premium impacts for different groups and states, but none produced a single, general finding that premiums would rise four times faster than wages across the board; the claim appears to be an exaggeration or an out-of-context summary.

claim: President Obama was "raised Muslim."
rationale: This is false. Although Obama’s father was Muslim and Obama spent part of his childhood in predominantly Muslim Indonesia, biographical sources and Obama’s own statements say he was not raised as a Muslim; he was largely raised by his mother and grandparents, who were nonreligious or Christian, and he later became a Christian as an adult.

claim: "We are imprisoning or giving jail sentences to young people who are smoking marijuana."
rationale: The claim is overly broad. While some jurisdictions still arrest and in rare cases incarcerate young people for smoking or possessing marijuana, many states and countries have decriminalized or legalized recreational use or use diversion programs and fines rather than jail, so it is not true as a blanket statement.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: I cannot verify this specific national-ranking figure and such totals are typically self-reported by state parties using varying definitions of a “contact.” Given larger GOP organizations in more populous states (e.g., Texas, Florida) and the absence of an authoritative, standardized nationwide tally, the claim that Ohio alone made nearly 6.6 million contacts and more than any other state since 2009 is not reliably supported. Without a verifiable independent source, the claim should be treated as unproven and likely false.

claim: Video shows Joe Biden saying "we can only re-elect Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden ever said 'we can only re-elect Donald Trump.' The viral clip appears to be edited or manipulated (audio splice or AI/deepfake) and the original remarks from the speech use different wording, so the claim misrepresents what Biden actually said.

claim: "New Jersey taxpayers … will now face the highest tolls in the country."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad, unsupported statement. While New Jersey has recently raised tolls and is among states with substantial toll revenues, it is not clearly established that New Jersey now has the single highest tolls in the country — toll levels vary widely by crossing, metric (per-trip, per-mile, annual burden), and jurisdiction, and several New York and California facilities and express lanes charge higher absolute rates.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely false. Individual senators (including Bill Nelson) cannot unilaterally "pass a budget," and Senate budget resolutions and appropriations require action by the whole Senate and the House and are tracked with specific dates — there is no clear, verifiable event showing that Nelson and Senate Democrats last "passed a budget" exactly 750 days ago. Additionally Bill Nelson left the Senate in January 2019, so attributing a current Senate budget passage to him is incorrect without a specific timeframe.

claim: Norway decided "that (the coronavirus) should be treated like other respiratory diseases, such as the flu or cold, because… it is no more dangerous than those mentioned."
rationale: Norway did move toward treating COVID-19 as an endemic respiratory infection and lifted many legal restrictions, but Norwegian health authorities did not state that coronavirus is "no more dangerous" than the flu or a cold. Officials and public-health experts continued to warn that COVID-19 carries higher risks for severe illness, death in vulnerable groups, and long-COVID, so equating its danger level with a common cold is inaccurate.

claim: "U.S. agricultural & food exports are expected to increase more than $2 billion annually under #USMCA"
rationale: The claim overstates a consensus projection. While U.S. officials and USMCA proponents did cite figures around $2 billion in potential annual gains for agricultural exports, independent analyses and the U.S. International Trade Commission found only modest and model-dependent effects, and estimates vary widely rather than clearly showing >$2 billion annually. Thus the statement as an unequivocal expectation is misleading.

claim: "People have actually broken down the transcripts for oral arguments and (Antonin Scalia) told more jokes and got more laughs than any of the other justices."
rationale: There is no widely accepted, comprehensive quantitative study showing Antonin Scalia definitively told more jokes and drew more laughs than every other justice. Scalia had a well‑known reputation for wit and many commentators and some informal transcript reviews note frequent humorous remarks, but available analyses are limited, vary in methods, and do not establish a clear across‑the‑board numerical lead over all other justices. Because the claim asserts a definitive empirical ranking, it overstates the evidence.

claim: "Since 1999, firearm deaths in Ohio have risen 58 percent."
rationale: The statement as written is not verifiable and is likely incorrect because it gives no end year or whether it refers to counts or rates (and whether it includes suicides, homicides, accidents). Federal vital-statistics (CDC/NCHS) data show Ohio firearm deaths have fluctuated since 1999 and the percent change depends on the chosen end year and whether one uses raw counts or age-adjusted rates; none of the commonly used endpoints unambiguously support a 58% rise. Without a specified endpoint and definition, the claim is misleading.

claim: Says "72% of refugees admitted into U.S. (2/3 -2/11) during COURT BREAKDOWN are from 7 countries: SYRIA, IRAQ, SOMALIA, IRAN, SUDAN, LIBYA & YEMEN."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no year or clear meaning for “COURT BREAKDOWN” and cites a narrow date window (2/3–2/11) without a source. U.S. refugee admissions are published by date and nationality by the State Department/ORR and percentages this precise require a cited dataset; without that, the assertion that 72% came from those seven countries is unsubstantiated and unlikely for an arbitrary multi-day window. Given the ambiguity and lack of evidence, the claim is treated as false.

claim: "I said two years ago that the Fannie and Freddie thing was a very serious problem and we had to work on it."
rationale: The statement as given is unverifiable because it does not identify who “I” is or the exact date meant by “two years ago.” Without a named speaker and timestamp, there is no way to confirm that this person actually said those words; therefore I judge the claim false for lack of evidence. If a specific speaker and date are provided, the claim could be checked against public records or transcripts.

claim: "Pfizer and Moderna could share their design with dozens of other pharma companies who stand ready to produce their vaccines and end the pandemic."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While Pfizer and Moderna can technically share vaccine designs, producing mRNA vaccines at scale requires specialized lipid-nanoparticle manufacturing, validated processes, trained personnel, supply-chain inputs and regulatory approvals, so dozens of unrelated companies are not immediately “ready” to produce and release safe, effective doses that would instantly end the pandemic. Legal, trade‑secret/IP issues and fill-and-finish and distribution constraints also limit how quickly broad production could be expanded.

claim: The U.S. Justice Department "conservatively estimated that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The Department of Justice did not publish a canonical "conservative" estimate of 1.5 million defensive gun uses per year; that large figure is more closely associated with academic survey estimates (e.g., Kleck & Gertz) and has often been misattributed to DOJ. DOJ's large national survey programs (like the NCVS) produce much lower estimates, and official DOJ publications do not endorse a 1.5 million/year conservative count.

claim: "We're the only system of federalism in the world."
rationale: The claim is false. Numerous other countries operate under federal systems — for example Germany, Canada, Australia, India, Brazil, Switzerland, Mexico, Nigeria and others — so the United States is not the only federal system in the world. The statement would only be true under a highly idiosyncratic and unsupported definition of 'federalism.'

claim: Says Austin trains are "full" at rush hour and "packed" for special events.
rationale: The claim is overly broad. While Austin’s commuter rail and event service can become crowded—especially during major events (e.g., music festivals, UT game-day service)—the city’s rail system does not consistently run “full” at every rush hour and most regular service sees moderate capacity. Without a specific route, time period, or data, the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker is making voting more difficult by closing Department of Motor Vehicles offices where "low-income voters" live.
rationale: This claim mixes two different facts into an assertion of targeted voter suppression. The Walker administration did reduce and consolidate some DMV/DMV service locations and opponents argued those changes disproportionately burdened urban and low-income residents trying to obtain photo IDs; however, there is no clear evidence that offices were closed specifically with the intent to target "low-income voters" or as an explicit policy to make voting harder. The factual part (closures/criticisms) is true, but the implication of deliberate targeting to suppress votes is not supported by clear evidence.

claim: "In North Carolina, they used stimulus money to hire one new state worker. His job, apply for more stimulus funds from the taxpayers by the way of the federal government."
rationale: The claim is misleading: there is no evidence that North Carolina used stimulus money to hire exactly one new state worker whose sole job was to apply for more federal stimulus funds. Fact‑checking and reporting around ARRA showed states did use stimulus dollars for some administrative/grant‑management positions, but those roles were part of broader duties (compliance, reporting, managing programs) and not a single hire dedicated exclusively to 'applying for more stimulus.'

claim: "President Biden says he wants to ban handguns."
rationale: President Biden has publicly advocated for tighter gun regulations (e.g., reinstating an assault-weapons ban, banning high-capacity magazines, universal background checks, and limits on 'ghost guns'), but he has not said he wants to ban handguns outright. Public statements and his policy proposals focus on assault-style weapons and other specific measures rather than a broad prohibition on handguns.

claim: "If Joe Manchin had his way, Judge Gorsuch never would have been able to get a vote."
rationale: This is false. Joe Manchin publicly supported giving Neil Gorsuch a floor vote and ultimately voted to confirm Gorsuch to the Supreme Court; he did not try to prevent Gorsuch from getting a vote. The Senate’s change to confirmation rules was driven by Republican leadership, not by Manchin.

claim: Obamacare has led to fewer health insurance options for millions of Americans.
rationale: After the Affordable Care Act's major coverage reforms began in 2014, many insurers withdrew from some individual marketplaces and plan choices were reduced in numerous counties, leaving millions of people with fewer carrier options. While outcomes varied by state and year and some areas later saw restored or increased options, the immediate and measurable effect for large numbers of Americans was a net reduction in marketplace choices.

claim: "Suntrust Bank cancels account because company sells guns."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general fact but lacks specifics and there is no well-documented, public policy or widely reported incident showing SunTrust systematically cancels accounts solely because a company sells firearms. Banks sometimes close individual accounts for legal, compliance or reputational reasons, but that is not the same as a confirmed blanket policy by SunTrust. Given the ambiguity and absence of corroborating reports, the assertion as stated is not supported.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which election, jurisdiction, date, or metric (vote margin, electoral votes, turnout) is being referenced. Whether an election is "unusually close" requires comparison to historical baselines and specific numeric margins; without that context the assertion is unsupported. Therefore I judge the claim false due to lack of necessary detail to confirm it.

claim: Quotes actor Will Smith as saying: "I’m not afraid to say that Trump and his supporters are ba…"
rationale: The claim presents a truncated, unattributed quote and there is no verifiable record up to mid‑2024 of Will Smith saying the displayed wording about Trump and his supporters. Major news outlets, interviews, and Smith’s verified social media accounts do not contain that quote, and no reliable fact‑checks or transcripts support it. Without a full sourced citation this appears to be an unverified or misattributed statement.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum is running "from the FBI."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Andrew Gillum has been physically fleeing or actively evading the FBI. While Gillum has been the subject of federal scrutiny and media reports about investigations and executed search warrants, reputable reporting does not describe him as “running from the FBI.”

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: The U.S. Chamber did publicly warn that proposed carbon rules would cause job losses and raise household costs, but the commonly cited job figure from their materials was 224,000 (not 244,000) and the $1,200/year household cost estimate is model-dependent and has been challenged by other analyses. In short, the claim misstates (or at least overprecisely repeats) contested figures and omits that the numbers depend heavily on assumptions and methodology.

claim: "Alabama’s Crimson Tide was disqualified from national championship."
rationale: There are no credible records or major news reports indicating that the University of Alabama’s Crimson Tide were disqualified from a national championship. While Alabama programs have faced NCAA investigations and penalties at times, those sanctions did not include an official disqualification or stripping of a national title in the widely reported historical record. If a specific sport or year is meant, that would need to be specified to check a narrow case.

claim: Says the Obama administration plans to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration planned to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens via international treaties. The Obama team supported measures like the Arms Trade Treaty (ATT) to regulate international arms transfers, but such treaties address state-to-state trade and trafficking, not a blanket domestic ban on civilian ownership; treaty commitments also require Senate ratification and cannot directly override the Constitution. Claims that Obama sought a universal disarmament of U.S. citizens mischaracterize treaty text and U.S. law.

claim: "When Nancy Nusbaum was Brown County executive, spending went up nearly 50 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Public fact‑checks and budget reviews show the “nearly 50%” figure came from comparing non‑comparable budget totals/years and including one‑time items and pass‑throughs; core county operating expenditures and the county levy rose far less than 50% during Nusbaum’s tenure. When measured on a consistent basis (annual operating budget or levy, adjusted for timing), the increase is substantially smaller.

claim: Text from someone "connected" to Raleigh police: "antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs."
rationale: The message appears to be an unverified rumor with no corroboration from Raleigh police or other credible sources. There is no public evidence that an organized 'antifa' operation was planning to target wealthy neighborhoods that night; 'antifa' is a decentralized label and such specific operational claims require credible verification. Because the claim rests on a vague attribution (“someone connected”) and lacks official or independent confirmation, it should be treated as false until proven otherwise.

claim: Says the CEO of Camping World told Trump supporters "Frankly, don’t shop at my business."
rationale: I could not verify that the CEO of Camping World publicly said the exact line “Frankly, don’t shop at my business.” While Camping World’s well-known CEO Marcus Lemonis has criticized political figures and expressed strong views on social media, I found no reliable record of him making that precise quoted statement. Without a contemporaneous, attributable source for the quote, the claim as stated is unverified and likely false or misattributed.

claim: Says Texas voters are being asked to act this November on a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes.
rationale: Statewide constitutional amendments in Texas are placed on the ballot only after the Legislature proposes them and are typically voted on in even‑year November general elections. As of the current timeframe, there is no clear evidence that Texas voters are being asked this November (an odd‑numbered year) to decide a statewide constitutional amendment specifically affecting property taxes. The claim is therefore likely incorrect without further date context.

claim: The United States paid for a 274-mile wall between Jordan and Syria, "approved by the Dems in the house and senate," in order "to keep ISIS out."
rationale: There is no evidence the United States paid for a continuous 274-mile wall along the Jordan–Syria border. Jordan built fences, berms and other fortifications beginning around 2016 to block infiltration (including from ISIS), and the U.S. provided some security assistance to Jordan, but that assistance did not constitute paying for a single 274‑mile wall specifically "approved by the Dems in the house and senate." The claim conflates Jordanian construction, limited U.S. aid, and a partisan congressional approval that is not supported by records.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes DOJ practice and statements. While some officials in certain administrations (notably the Trump-era DOJ) expressed skepticism about consent decrees, the Department historically has used and defended consent decrees as a tool to reform police departments; there is no DOJ-wide finding that they “don’t work” or routinely cause immediate crime increases. Empirical evidence on crime trends after consent decrees is mixed and context-dependent, so the blanket assertion is inaccurate.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: This mixes a partly-true technical fact with an unsupported conclusion. State officials did say the Antrim problem was due to a reporting/configuration issue and that the same reporting software was used in several other Michigan jurisdictions, but multiple audits, hand counts and reviews found no evidence that votes were fraudulently switched statewide. The leap from shared software to ‘potentially fraudulent’ votes in the state is not supported by the available investigations and evidence.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: There is no documented instance in major news coverage or speech transcripts showing Sarah Palin repeating Abraham Lincoln’s words while discussing the Iraq war. Palin has used general patriotic phrasing and occasionally invoked historical figures, but reporters and transcript archives do not record her directly quoting Lincoln in an Iraq-related remark. Given the lack of corroborating primary-source evidence, the claim is unsupported.

claim: After merging with Tim Hortons of Canada, Burger King is "not moving. … Our headquarters will remain in Miami" and "(we) will continue to pay all of our federal, state and local U.S. taxes."
rationale: Following the 2014 merger that created Restaurant Brands International, Burger King executives publicly stated the company would keep its operational headquarters in Miami and said it would continue to pay U.S. federal, state and local taxes. Those assurances were made even though the merged parent was legally domiciled in Canada, which changed the company’s federal corporate tax treatment on non‑U.S. income.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified reporting that human meat was found in any McDonald’s meat factory. Claims like this have circulated as social-media hoaxes in the past, while investigations and routine food-safety audits of fast-food supply chains have found no substantiation. Given the absence of reliable sources and the implausibility given regulatory oversight, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Even today part of Romney’s fortune is invested in China."
rationale: There is no public, verifiable evidence that Mitt Romney currently holds direct investments specifically in China. His wealth largely derived from Bain Capital, which historically invested in companies that did business in China, and some diversified funds can have global exposure, but those facts do not prove the specific claim that part of his fortune is invested in China today. Without current, specific disclosure of direct Chinese holdings the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "99 percent of all new income today (is) going to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad, context-free assertion. Empirical studies of U.S. income distribution (e.g., work by Piketty/Saez and IRS data) show that the top 1% captured a very large share of income gains in some specific recovery years, but not a persistent or universal 99% of all new income “today.” Whether the top 1% captured near-total gains depends strongly on the precise timeframe, definition of “new income” (income growth vs. national income vs. wealth), and country, so the flat 99% statement is misleading.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott is "spending a quarter of a million of our tax dollars to robocall people."
rationale: The claim presents a specific dollar amount and accuses Gov. Rick Scott of spending $250,000 of taxpayer money on robocalls, but there is no well-documented, verifiable evidence tying Scott personally or his administration to that exact expenditure for robocalls. Government agencies do sometimes pay for automated outreach (e.g., emergency alerts or public-service campaigns), but the claim as phrased asserts a precise misuse of funds without substantiation. Given the lack of corroborating reporting or budget records showing this specific $250,000 robocall charge to Scott, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Due to the recent downturn in steel production, more than 13,600 Americans have been laid off and the steel industry is facing billions in losses."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion that a recent downturn led to more than 13,600 American layoffs; public reporting on steel job losses in recent years tends to document plant- or company-level layoffs in the hundreds to low thousands, not a single verified nationwide total of 13,600 linked to one downturn. The claim that the industry is "facing billions in losses" is vague and unsubstantiated without a defined timeframe or accounting basis, so the overall statement is not supported by corroborated evidence.

claim: Says the government has "gotten the TARP money back plus a profit."
rationale: By the time Treasury finished winding down most TARP activity, official reports showed total repayments, dividends, interest and asset sales exceeded the amounts disbursed, yielding a small net gain to taxpayers overall. However, that overall profit reflected gains in some programs and losses in others (results vary by program and by date of reporting).

claim: "One of the most troubling aspects of the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill was that it gave President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees, including Syrian refugees, without mandating any background checks whatsoever."
rationale: The 2013 'Gang of Eight' bill (S.744) was a comprehensive immigration reform proposal focused on legalization, border security, and visa system changes; it did not give the president blanket authority to admit refugees nor did it eliminate refugee vetting. Refugee admissions are governed separately by the Immigration and Nationality Act and processed through an interagency refugee vetting system that includes biometric checks, FBI name/fingerprint checks and other security screening. The claim misstates the bill's contents and the existing refugee-screening procedures.

claim: "The EPA has tried to define a puddle or a drainage ditch on your farm to be navigable waters and thus subject to massive environmental regulations."
