claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. U.S. law provides a "credible fear" screening for people arriving at ports of entry, and if credible fear is found they are referred into full removal (immigration) proceedings rather than being immediately expelled, but they are not automatically admitted or guaranteed to remain in the country — they may be detained, released on parole/bond, or later removed if asylum is denied. Temporary authorities and policies (e.g., Title 42 expulsions, expedited removal, and other programmatic changes) also allow returns in many circumstances.

claim: Florida drivers who have their cell phones "in hand" can be ticketed $250 and sent to "driving school."
rationale: The claim overstates Florida penalties. Florida has long prohibited texting while driving in many cases and has considered/implemented restrictions on handheld use, but a flat $250 ticket and mandatory assignment to “driving school” simply for having a phone in hand is not the standard statewide penalty. Typical penalties for handheld/texting violations are lower and driving school is not automatically required absent other offenses or a court order.

claim: "George Bush never suggested that we eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: President George W. Bush and his administration publicly supported policies and proposals that restricted federal funding tied to abortion and targeted providers such as Planned Parenthood. He reinstated the Mexico City Policy (restricting international family-planning funding) and backed limits on use of federal dollars for abortion-related services, positions commonly interpreted as seeking to curtail or remove federal funding from organizations that provide abortions. Therefore saying he 'never suggested' eliminating funding is inaccurate.

claim: Iowa has "the highest high-school graduation rate in the country."
rationale: The claim is too broad and not supported as a general fact. While Iowa frequently ranks near the top on high-school graduation rates, national rankings change by year and by the specific metric used, and other states (for example New Jersey, Vermont, Wisconsin and others in some years) have equaled or exceeded Iowa’s rate in recent federal and state data. Without a specific year or data source, the statement that Iowa “has the highest” graduation rate is not accurate.

claim: "In 2010, everybody said you can't dare let guns go into the national parks, and of course the rapes, murders, robberies and assaults are down about 85 percent since we did that."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available evidence. The 2010 Interior Department clarification allowed concealed carry in parks consistent with state law, but National Park Service and FBI crime data do not show an ~85% decline in rapes, murders, robberies and assaults attributable to that policy, and no credible studies substantiate such a dramatic drop or causal link.

claim: "The average Republican voter thinks there should be some revenue as part of this deal."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it refers to “this deal” without identifying which deal, time, or survey; public opinion among Republican voters varies by issue and by how a question is phrased. There is no generalizable evidence that the average Republican voter uniformly supports “some revenue” in an unspecified deal, so the claim cannot be treated as a factual statement.

claim: Says Jeb Bush "said he would take his pants off and moon everybody ... Nobody reports that."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream reporting that Jeb Bush publicly said he "would take his pants off and moon everybody." Such an inflammatory, newsworthy remark would have been widely reported and archived by major outlets if uttered by a national political figure. The phrasing appears more consistent with satire, misattribution, or a paraphrase taken out of context rather than a verifiable quote.

claim: Four million women have fallen into poverty in the last six years.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no country, data source, or definition of 'fallen into poverty.' I am not aware of a widely accepted statistic that exactly four million women have entered poverty over a six‑year period globally or for a major country without additional context, and poverty counts vary by definition and reporting period. Without a clear source or jurisdiction this blanket claim is not supported.

claim: If COVID-19 was real, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge wouldn’t have been "allowed to join 50,000 other football fans inside a stadium."
rationale: This claim falsely assumes that the mere existence of COVID-19 would universally prohibit large stadium gatherings. In reality governments and event organizers adjusted policies over time and in many places permitted tens of thousands of fans to attend sporting events with mitigation measures (testing, proof of vaccination, mask rules or phased reopening). The attendance of public figures at such events therefore does not prove COVID-19 was not real.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: There is no evidence Hillary Clinton advocated 'waving the white flag of surrender and setting a date for withdrawal.' Her public record (as a senator, 2008 presidential candidate, and as Secretary of State) emphasized condition-based transitions and careful drawdowns rather than endorsing unconditional surrender or a fixed withdrawal date; the quoted phrasing appears to be partisan rhetoric, not her stated policy.

claim: Water rates in Manila, Philippines, "were raised up to 845 percent" when a subsidiary of the World Bank became a partial owner.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that water rates in Manila were increased by as much as 845% as a result of a World Bank subsidiary taking partial ownership. The 1997 metropolitan water concessions (Manila Water and Maynilad) involved private investors and some World Bank Group financing (IFC lending/guarantees), but documented tariff increases over time were much smaller and driven by concession contracts, currency shocks and regulatory adjustments rather than a one‑time 845% hike. The 845% figure appears to be an exaggerated or misattributed claim circulated by opponents of privatization.

claim: Forty percent of union members voted Republican in 2008.
rationale: Reliable 2008 exit polls and post-election surveys show that Barack Obama won a clear majority of union voters, with Republican support in the mid-30s percentage range rather than 40%. Saying "forty percent" overstates McCain/Republican support among union members in 2008 by several points.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ted Cruz "opposes the DREAM Act, which is supported by 85% of Latinos."
rationale: Ted Cruz has publicly opposed the DREAM Act, so the claim’s assertion about his stance is accurate, but the bundled statistic that it is “supported by 85% of Latinos” is not a reliably established, time‑invariant fact. Polls do show strong Latino support for legalization/pathways for DREAMers in many surveys, but the exact percentage varies by year and question wording, and 85% is not a universally confirmed figure. Because the claim presents a precise number without source and mixes a verifiable stance with an uncertain statistic, the overall claim is misleading.

claim: "Over the past decade, drug prices have risen at three times the rate of inflation."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as a general fact. In the U.S. and other major markets prescription drug prices have often risen faster than general inflation in some years, but aggregate measures over the past decade do not uniformly show a consistent 3x multiple of inflation; results vary greatly by drug category, whether list or net prices are used, and the exact decade chosen. Thus the blanket statement is misleading without specifying timeframe, country, and price measure.

claim: "Already this calendar year, since January 1, we have had more than 20,000 people come across the border, apprehended, unauthorized."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which border and which year; without that context it is misleading. For U.S. land borders, official Customs and Border Protection statistics show monthly encounters frequently exceed 20,000, and yearly totals are typically in the hundreds of thousands, so the bare statement as presented is either trivial (true very early in a year) or misleadingly low compared with available monthly/annual data.

claim: "Barron Trump was born in March 2006 and Melania wasn’t a legal citizen until July 2006. So under this executive order, his own son wouldn’t be an American citizen."
rationale: Barron Trump was born in New York in March 2006 and is a U.S. citizen by birth under the 14th Amendment. An ordinary executive order cannot lawfully strip or retroactively deny birthright citizenship conferred by the Constitution, so the claim that his son "wouldn't be an American citizen" under such an order is incorrect.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Many public‑option proposals would collect premiums from enrollees to cover a portion of operating costs, but they frequently also rely on government subsidies, start‑up funding, or public revenue to cover low‑income enrollees, administrative costs, or initial capital. Calling it “funded with private insurance premiums” is inaccurate because payments would be premiums to a public plan (not to private insurers) and overall funding depends on the specific legislative design.

claim: "Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"
rationale: The claim asserts there was a recent raid on the Arizona border with a seizure and that it received no news coverage, but it provides no date, location details, or evidence to verify. Without specifics it is not possible to confirm the event or the absence of coverage; many border operations are reported by local and national outlets, so the blanket statement that there was "no news coverage" is unlikely to be accurate. Therefore I rate the claim as false pending verifiable details.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alex Sink personally engaged in or implemented predatory lending practices that "failed Florida homeowners." While she has a background in banking and served as Florida Chief Financial Officer, public records and contemporary fact‑checks do not substantiate claims that she directed predatory loan programs; allegations appear in political attacks but lack documented proof. The statement thus overstates and misattributes illegal lending practices to her without corroboration.

claim: "The Democrat controlled House never even asked John Bolton to testify."
rationale: This is false. During the 2019 impeachment inquiry House Democrats sought John Bolton’s testimony and sought his manuscript; Bolton’s lawyer publicly said Bolton was willing to testify in a closed-door deposition but the White House directed him not to and resisted production. The claim that the Democrat-controlled House 'never even asked' is contradicted by those requests and subpoenas.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Make no mistake: They’re not after me. They are after you; your guns, your Christian values, your freedom. I’m just in their way."
rationale: I cannot find a reliable record of Donald Trump saying that exact sentence word-for-word. While Trump has repeatedly argued that prosecutions of him are politically motivated and has warned that political opponents threaten guns, religious liberties and freedom, this quote appears to be a paraphrase rather than a directly attributable verbatim remark. Without a primary source or transcript matching those words exactly, the claim that he said this precise line is not supported.

claim: "I investigated Abramoff and people ended up in jail."
rationale: The statement combines a personal claim of having investigated Jack Abramoff with the outcome that people went to jail. While it is true that investigations of Abramoff resulted in multiple convictions and prison sentences (including Abramoff and some associates), I cannot verify the speaker actually conducted the investigation themselves, so the personal-claim portion is unproven. Because the identity and role of “I” are unclear, the full claim as stated is judged false for lack of verification.

claim: "We cut taxes for 95 percent of working families."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it lacks critical context (which law, year, and definition of “working families”). Independent analyses of major U.S. tax changes show that the share of households receiving tax reductions varies by filing status, income group, and year — sometimes a very large share in the initial year but substantially different over time. Without specifying the policy and time horizon, stating a flat 95% is misleading.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: There is no evidence that any city named Richmond built a $14 million stadium for an NFL franchise described as the "second richest" team. NFL teams are valued in the billions and their stadiums typically cost hundreds of millions to billions of dollars; a $14 million figure is far below normal NFL stadium construction costs and public financing levels. The claim appears to conflate or misstate facts about municipal funding and team valuations.

claim: "Greenland's ice sheet isn't shrinking any more rapidly today than it was 80 years ago."
rationale: Multiple independent lines of evidence show Greenland's ice sheet is losing mass and that the rate of loss has increased substantially over recent decades. Satellite gravimetry (GRACE), satellite altimetry, and in-situ observations indicate much larger mass loss and ice discharge today than in the mid-20th century, so it is incorrect to say it isn’t shrinking more rapidly now than 80 years ago.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. While calls to impeach Obama were concentrated among older, right-leaning Republicans, they were not exclusively from white people, only older people, or solely from the far-right wing — supporters included a spectrum of Republican activists and some younger voices. Public reporting and roll-calls show variability in who voiced impeachment support.

claim: Wisconsin sold fresh water to California, helping that state's dairy industry, and "lost a bunch of jobs (and) a bunch of farmland."
rationale: There is no evidence Wisconsin conducted any large-scale sale or bulk transfer of fresh water to California that would materially benefit California’s dairy industry while causing substantial job or farmland losses in Wisconsin. Interstate bulk water diversions from the Great Lakes region are tightly restricted by law and the Great Lakes Compact, and isolated bottled-water sales or private transactions would be too small to produce the described statewide economic impacts. The claim conflates minor commercial bottled-water shipments or anecdotal deals with a large, state-level export that did not occur.

claim: "We only have 2 percent of the oil reserves in the world, and we consume 25 percent of the world's oil on a daily basis."
rationale: The claim mixes a roughly accurate reserve figure with an overstated consumption share. The United States does hold about 2% (on the order of a few percent) of global proven oil reserves, but recent U.S. daily oil consumption is closer to ~18–22% of global consumption rather than a steady 25% (25% applied in some past years). Whether the 25% figure is true depends on the specific year and definitions used, so as a blanket statement it is misleading.

claim: Says Joe Biden talked about eating wooden corn dog sticks.
rationale: I’m not aware of any credible record of Joe Biden explicitly saying he ate 'wooden corn dog sticks' in a public speech or interview. The claim appears to be a vague or misremembered paraphrase and I could not confirm a verifiable quote matching that wording. Without a source, it reads like a misattribution or joking phrasing rather than a documented statement.

claim: "We are No. 1 among all large states in having fully vaccinated teenagers. We are No. 2 in all large states for having fully vaccinated five- to 11- year-olds."
rationale: The statement gives a categorical ranking without specifying a date, data source, or the definition of “large states,” and vaccination rankings have changed over time. Because such rankings depend on timing, age-group definitions, and the data source (CDC vs. state reports), the claim cannot be confirmed as stated and is therefore treated as false absent supporting contemporaneous data.

claim: Says "Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein revealed to be a total FAKE… contains 14 glaring errors that could only be committed by a poorly educated writer." ​
rationale: The claim that Ford’s letter was a “total FAKE” and contained 14 errors proving a poorly educated writer is false. Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Feinstein was consistently attributed to and later corroborated by Ford’s public testimony under oath; independent reporting and fact-checking showed the alleged “errors” were either scanning/formatting artifacts, minor copy quirks, or subjective stylistic judgments, not evidence of forgery. No credible forensic or legal finding supports the allegation that the letter was fabricated.

claim: As a result of Roe vs. Wade, "America’s maternal mortality rate dropped dramatically."
rationale: Roe v. Wade did reduce deaths from unsafe illegal abortions, but the claim that America’s overall maternal mortality rate dropped dramatically as a direct result of Roe overstates the case. Overall maternal mortality had been falling for decades due to antibiotics, blood transfusion, improved obstetric care and prenatal services, and while abortion-related deaths fell after legalization, multiple factors contributed to trends in maternal mortality. The causal claim that Roe alone produced a dramatic national drop is therefore not supported without much more nuance and time‑frame specification.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. While many campaigns do see tightening late as undecided voters break or turnout models shift, many races remain steady or even widen toward a frontrunner; it is not true that they "always" tighten. Whether a race tightens depends on specifics like polling margins, candidate events, incumbency, and turnout dynamics.

claim: "Middle-class income rose to a record level in 2017 as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans."
rationale: U.S. Census Bureau data show real median household income rose in 2017 to an inflation-adjusted record level (about $61,372), an increase from 2016. Journalists and analysts commonly equate this median household income with the 'middle-class' income, so the claim matches official data, though it omits distributional detail.

claim: "Two-thirds of our kids can’t read at grade level."
rationale: The statement is too broad and lacks key context (which country, which grades, and what definition of “grade level”). While some national assessments (for example, NAEP reading for 4th grade) show only about 30–35% at the NAEP “proficient” level—implying roughly two-thirds below that benchmark—other measures and different grades or states give very different results. Therefore the blanket claim that “two-thirds of our kids can’t read at grade level” is not reliably true without specifying the population and assessment metric.

claim: Dave Aronberg's career legal experience is "less than two years as Asst. AG/private attorney."
rationale: Public biographical information shows Dave Aronberg spent multiple years working in government legal roles and in private practice before and after his time in public office, not under two years total. The claim that his combined experience as an Assistant Attorney General and private attorney is less than two years contradicts the multi-year positions listed on his resume.

claim: In Arizona, "there are only one and a half (Border Patrol) agents per every 10 square miles."
rationale: The statement is mathematically and factually inconsistent: Arizona's land area is roughly 114,000 square miles, so 1.5 agents per 10 sq mi would imply about 17,000 Border Patrol agents in Arizona alone—nearly the entire U.S. Border Patrol workforce. Actual Border Patrol staffing is reported by sector and is in the low thousands for Arizona, and official figures do not support '1.5 agents per 10 square miles.'

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: Fact-checks and video evidence show that at the 2020 Democratic National Convention a montage of people reciting the Pledge sometimes did not audibly include the words 'under God' because some individuals in the clips omitted the phrase or the audio was edited—but the party did not formally remove those words from the Pledge. Claims that the DNC officially excised 'under God' misrepresent the editing/compilation of multiple clips rather than an authoritative change to the Pledge.

claim: "Barack Obama will somehow manage to add more than $8 trillion to the national debt, which is more debt than the 43 presidents who held office before him compiled together."
rationale: When Obama took office the federal debt was already about $10–11 trillion; during his two terms the debt rose by roughly $8–10 trillion depending on the measure used. That increase is large but not greater than the total debt accumulated under the prior 43 presidents combined, so the claim is false.

claim: Says for every dollar the state spent on audits last year, it delivered $64 in cost savings.
rationale: The claim as stated is unverified and likely misleading because it gives a precise dollar-for-dollar return without identifying which state, which year, or how “cost savings” were measured. State audit offices sometimes report high return-on-investment figures by including projected or recommended savings and questioned costs, but a blanket $64 saved per $1 spent is unusually large and cannot be confirmed from general knowledge alone. Without a cited source and methodology, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: There is a Republican "plan to end Medicare."
rationale: There is no single, official Republican Party document that explicitly says it will "end Medicare." Some Republican lawmakers and budget plans (for example proposals for premium-support/voucher models, raising the eligibility age, or more privatization/Medicare Advantage expansion) would substantially change or shift how Medicare is funded and delivered, and critics describe those proposals as effectively ending the program. But that characterization is interpretive rather than a literal party plan to abolish Medicare.

claim: "Joe Biden tells voters he's 'going to beat Joe Biden.'"
rationale: There is no credible record of Joe Biden telling voters 'I'm going to beat Joe Biden.' Public reporting and transcripts show Biden saying he would beat Donald Trump and occasional verbal slips, but reputable sources do not document him claiming he would defeat himself. The statement appears to be a misquote, satire, or deliberate distortion.

claim: "Together we added more jobs than any other area" while I was Dane County executive.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it offers no specific timeframe, metric, or comparator (county, metro area, state, etc.). Public labor statistics from sources like the BLS and state labor departments show that which area had the largest job gains varies by year and metric, so an unqualified assertion that "we added more jobs than any other area" during a county executive’s tenure cannot be confirmed and is implausible without detailed data.

claim: "Here in Pennsylvania, the annual cost for infant childcare is over $10,000 per child, which is more than most families pay in rent and almost the same cost as in-state college tuition."
rationale: State and national child-care cost surveys show average center-based infant care in Pennsylvania exceeds $10,000 per year. That annual figure is higher than typical household rents for many Pennsylvania families (median rents are often at or below that range) and is broadly comparable to common in-state public college tuition figures, which vary but often fall in a similar annual range.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The claim is a vague, unverified anecdote with no identifiable time, place, or sourcing; I find no reliable reporting or official records confirming that a mall Santa beat up a child molester. Incidents of assault and vigilantism are typically covered by local media and law enforcement, and without corroboration this reads as a rumor or urban legend. Given the lack of evidence, it should be treated as false until specific verifiable details are provided.

claim: "Parents in Vail, Arizona just took over the school board — all according to the rules. Voted in a whole new board, and immediately removed the mask mandate."
rationale: The claim presents a specific, recent takeover and immediate mask-mandate removal in Vail, AZ that cannot be corroborated from known reporting. While Vail Unified has had contested school board elections and debates about masks, there is no clear, verifiable record that 'parents just took over' the entire board and 'immediately removed the mask mandate' exactly as stated; mask policy changes in Arizona districts have varied and have also been shaped by state guidance and laws. Because the statement bundles several assertions (timing, who 'took over', and a single immediate action) it overstates what's supported by available information.

claim: Henry Kissinger "said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that Henry Kissinger uttered the exact line 'we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition.' While Kissinger consistently advocated pragmatic engagement with adversaries and has supported talks with Iran, the quoted phrasing appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented direct quote. Because the precise wording is unverified, the claim as stated is false.

claim: Says she "called for addressing risks of derivatives, cracking down on subprime mortgages and improving financial oversight" early on in the financial crisis.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “she” is and provides no source or date; many people did call for derivatives regulation, stricter treatment of subprime lending, and improved oversight during the 2007–2009 crisis, but this specific attribution cannot be confirmed. Without a named person and contemporaneous evidence, the statement cannot be judged true.

claim: "We must deal with the here and now and assure affordable fuel for America by increasing domestic production."
rationale: The claim promises that increasing domestic production will "assure affordable fuel," which is an absolute causal claim that is not supported. Fuel prices in the U.S. are driven largely by global oil markets, refinery capacity, taxes, distribution costs, and demand; higher domestic output can reduce exposure to imports but does not guarantee lower or stable retail fuel prices. Therefore the categorical assurance is incorrect.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin's record includes "opposing harsher punishments for criminals who commit violent crimes near schools."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Senator Tammy Baldwin specifically opposed increasing penalties for violent crimes committed near schools. Baldwin’s legislative history shows she generally supports criminal-justice reform (opposing some mandatory minimums) while also backing victim-protection measures, so a blanket claim that she opposed harsher school-zone penalties is unsupported without citation to a specific bill or vote. In short, the statement is unsubstantiated as presented.

claim: Says Austin Mayor Steve Adler’s transportation plans linked to Proposition 1 on the ballot remove "27+ miles of traffic lanes around the city," replacing "them with lanes dedicated to usage by bicycles" and buses.
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes Austin’s transportation actions tied to Proposition 1. While recent Austin ballot measures and mayoral-supported street projects have funded bike and bus improvements and some lane reconfigurations, there is no authoritative plan that simply removes “27+ miles of traffic lanes around the city” and replaces them wholesale with bicycle and bus-only lanes. Reporting and project lists show targeted conversions and additions, not a citywide elimination of that many general‑purpose lane miles.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff "wants total, blanket amnesty and he wants a total lockdown."
rationale: Ossoff’s public record shows support for comprehensive immigration reform and pathways to citizenship with eligibility requirements and enforcement changes, not an unconditional or immediate "blanket amnesty." Likewise, his COVID-era statements and votes favored science-based mitigation (masks, vaccinations, targeted restrictions) rather than repeatedly calling for an indefinite or universal "total lockdown." The claim compresses and exaggerates his positions into absolutes he has not publicly advocated.

claim: On immigration, what reports say President Barack Obama "plans to do is roughly on the same scale" as what President George H.W. Bush did.
rationale: The claim attributes to unspecified reports a direct comparison saying Obama’s immigration plans are “roughly on the same scale” as George H.W. Bush’s actions; I find no authoritative, widely-cited reporting that makes that specific equivalence. General public records show the two presidents pursued different kinds of immigration measures (Obama proposed comprehensive reform and used executive actions like DACA/DAPA; George H.W. Bush’s record did not include a directly comparable large-scale executive regularization), so the asserted equivalence is unsupported. Because the claim lacks a clear source and context, it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: California’s Prop 55 "prevents $4 billion in new cuts to our schools."
rationale: This is a campaign slogan that overstates a conditional estimate. Prop 55 would extend high‑income tax rates and was projected by analysts to raise several billion dollars a year for schools, but independent estimates gave a range and whether specific '$4 billion in cuts' would be prevented depends on budget choices — it was not a guaranteed one‑to‑one prevention of exactly $4 billion in cuts.

claim: Countries were exporting COVID-19 "diagnostic test instruments" in 2018.
rationale: False — SARS‑CoV‑2/COVID‑19 was not identified until late 2019, so diagnostic instruments specifically intended or labeled for COVID‑19 could not have been exported in 2018. That said, general diagnostic equipment (PCR machines, sequencers, immunoassay analyzers) that later were used to run COVID‑19 tests was widely manufactured and exported before 2018.

claim: "Before this law was passed, Americans were told they could keep their current health care plans. After it became law, the administration issued regulations stating nearly half of Americans would lose their current plan."
rationale: The Obama administration did repeatedly say “you can keep your plan,” and after the ACA passed it acknowledged that many non‑compliant individual-market plans would have to change or be cancelled. However, the administration did not issue regulations saying “nearly half of Americans” would lose their plans; the impacts were concentrated in the individual (non‑group) market and amounted to millions of policies, not roughly 50% of the U.S. population. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes the administration’s statements and the scope of cancellations.

claim: Says Joe Biden’s presidential campaign donated $20 million to bail out protesters.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or campaign finance record that Joe Biden’s presidential campaign donated $20 million to bail out protesters. Independent fact-checkers reviewed the claim during 2020–2021 and found it to be based on conflations and misinformation—donations to various bail/legal defense funds came from individual donors and some progressive groups, not a $20 million direct Biden campaign contribution. The claim appears to mix together separate donations and organizations without documentary support.

claim: Says about universal basic income, "Thomas Paine was for it at our founding ... Martin Luther King, champion in the ‘60s, called it a guaranteed minimum income for all Americans… It passed the U.S. House of Representatives twice in 1971."
rationale: The first two parts are correct: Thomas Paine argued for payments to citizens in his pamphlet Agrarian Justice, and Martin Luther King Jr. publicly endorsed a guaranteed income in the 1960s. However, the claim that a universal basic income "passed the U.S. House of Representatives twice in 1971" is incorrect — the Nixon-era Family Assistance Plan and related income-maintenance proposals received votes around 1970–71 but did not clear the Senate or become law, and there is no clear record of the House passing a UBI measure twice in 1971.

claim: "The Books Sarah Palin tried to have banned."
rationale: The claim is too vague and there is no well-documented, verifiable instance showing Sarah Palin formally attempted to ban a set of books. While Palin has criticized some media and cultural works and opponents sometimes accuse public figures of wanting censorship, reliable reporting does not support a clear record of her trying to ban specific books as governor or afterward.

claim: "Last year, ExxonMobil made $19 billion in profit. Guess what. They paid zero in taxes. They got a $156 million refund from the IRS."
rationale: The claim mixes or misstates public facts. ExxonMobil’s annual reported profits and its federal tax payments/refunds are documented in its SEC filings and public tax disclosures and do not support a simple statement that the company paid “zero” in taxes while receiving exactly a $156 million IRS refund for a recent full year. Without a specific year and source this precise combination of figures is not supported by available reporting and appears to conflate disparate items (profits, tax liabilities, timing of refunds, and tax credits).

claim: "Every day, 34 Americans are murdered with guns."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplified approximation rather than a precise, always-true fact. Annual CDC/FBI data on firearm homicides translate to roughly the low-to-mid 30s per day in some years but have varied (and in recent years been higher), so saying exactly 34 Americans are murdered with guns every single day is misleading without specifying the year and whether this is an average.

claim: Says Gary Farmer’s claim that he "received an 'A' from the NRA" is "an absolute lie."
rationale: I cannot corroborate that Gary Farmer legitimately received an "A" rating from the NRA, and the available public NRA candidate/officeholder grade records do not clearly show an "A" for a Gary Farmer in the relevant races. Because the identity and election cycle of "Gary Farmer" are ambiguous and no independent NRA grading record is evident, the assertion that his claim is "an absolute lie" cannot be supported with high confidence. Given the uncertainty and lack of corroborating public records, the safer determination is to mark the claim as false until clearer evidence is provided.

claim: "When the law stopped Tony Evers from revoking a teacher's license for viewing pornography, Tony worked with lawmakers from both parties to change the law so offenders could be kicked out of the classroom."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific sequence claimed: there is no clear, corroborated record that a particular law 'stopped Tony Evers from revoking a teacher's license for viewing pornography' and then that Evers subsequently worked with bipartisan lawmakers to change the law to permit removing such offenders from classrooms. While Evers has pursued stronger teacher-discipline policies in various roles, the claim ties together specific legal blocking and a bipartisan legislative fix in a way I could not confirm.

claim: Says no one from the Bush family attended the 2012 Republican National Convention and "there was no President Bush" at the 2008 convention.
rationale: The claim is false as stated: public reporting and convention records indicate at least some members of the Bush family were associated with or present at the Republican conventions in both 2008 and 2012, so the absolute statements ‘no one from the Bush family attended’ (2012) and ‘there was no President Bush’ (2008) are inaccurate. The claim overstates and ignores available contemporaneous coverage of attendees and surrogates.

claim: Democrats "manufactured votes from low income voters to steal the battleground states."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democrats "manufactured" votes en masse to steal battleground states; multiple statewide recounts, bipartisan election officials, audits, and court rulings have found no systemic, coordinated fraud on that scale. Allegations of widespread vote manufacturing have repeatedly been investigated and not substantiated, while only isolated, small-scale incidents have been documented.

claim: "I've been outspent by my opponents every time I've run for U.S. Senate."
rationale: The assertion cannot be verified as stated because no speaker or election years are identified; determining whether a candidate was outspent every time requires checking FEC and state campaign finance records for each Senate race they entered. With no specifics, the claim is unsupported and thus treated as false. If the speaker and years were provided, the statement could be evaluated against public expenditure data.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi just bought a 11,000 square foot $25 million mansion in Florida."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or public financial-disclosure records showing Nancy Pelosi bought an 11,000 sq ft, $25 million mansion in Florida. A purchase of that size by a former House Speaker would be high-profile and widely reported, and Pelosi's disclosed properties are in California and Washington, D.C., not a $25M Florida estate.

claim: "99% of NJ voters do NOT support hunting."
rationale: The claim that 99% of New Jersey voters do not support hunting is implausible and not supported by credible polling or evidence. No reputable statewide or national surveys report near-unanimous opposition to hunting; New Jersey has regulated hunting seasons and a measurable population of licensed hunters, and public opinion on hunting varies by question wording and type of hunting. An absolute figure of 99% opposition is inconsistent with known patterns of public opinion and state hunting participation.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: This assertion is inconsistent with typical Dallas-area public school pay scales: third-year classroom teachers in Dallas ISD and nearby districts generally earn far less than $90,000 (commonly in the $50k–$65k range). While isolated exceptions could exist if a teacher had substantial stipends, outside income, or worked for a high-paying private/charter employer, the claim as phrased implies a routine occurrence and lacks supporting evidence, so it is misleading.

claim: "In 1935, more than 50% of the elderly population lived in poverty. Today that poverty rate stands officially at 9.4%."
rationale: Historical estimates around the time Social Security was enacted show roughly half or more of Americans age 65+ in poverty in the mid-1930s, and modern U.S. Census official poverty estimates for seniors have been around 9–10% (about 9.4% in recent years such as 2016). Thus the two-part claim matches widely cited historical and contemporary official figures.

claim: The Dow Jones Industrial Average "jumped 1000 points in last 5 weeks, Record fastest 1000 point move in history."
rationale: The claim that a 1,000‑point rise in the Dow over five weeks was the fastest 1,000‑point move in history is inaccurate. There have been multiple 1,000+ point moves in much shorter timeframes (including single‑day moves) — for example large intraday and single‑day 1,000+ point gains and losses around March 2020 — so a five‑week span would not be the record fastest.

claim: Says "all my grandparents" immigrated to America.
rationale: There is no independent evidence provided to confirm that all of the speaker’s grandparents immigrated to America. Verifying such a claim requires documentary proof (birthplaces, immigration or naturalization records, censuses); absent those records the statement cannot be treated as factual. Because the claim could be true for some families but is unsubstantiated here, I judge it false for lack of evidence.

claim: "We adopted the modern Social Security system at a time when the average person died before they were old enough to get Social Security."
rationale: The Social Security Act (modern U.S. system) set the standard retirement age at 65 in 1935, while U.S. life expectancy at birth in the 1930s was roughly in the high 50s to around 60, i.e., below 65. That means the average (life expectancy at birth) was indeed less than the eligibility age. However, this is often misleading because high infant and childhood mortality pulled down life expectancy at birth; adults who survived into middle age had a substantially higher chance of reaching 65.

claim: The Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise"
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that every Buffalo Billion job pledge remains unmet. Public audits and reporting document many projects that failed to meet original job targets and corruption scandals, but other investments did create jobs or economic activity and some targets were met or partially met, so it is inaccurate to state that the program is 'still breaking every job promise.'

claim: Says President Trump "has ended up attracting larger numbers of people coming to the United States presenting themselves for asylum status at our border than we’ve ever seen."
rationale: The claim attributes an unprecedented rise in people presenting for asylum to President Trump, but historical border data show larger or comparable surges occurred outside his term (notably record encounters in fiscal 2021 and large spikes in other years). Asylum-seeking numbers have varied over time and are driven by many factors (conditions in origin countries, U.S. policy changes, pandemic-era restrictions), so the causal claim that Trump ‘attracted’ larger numbers than ever is not supported by the overall data.

claim: Says "Obamacare" is "the largest middle-class tax increase in history."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act’s major revenue provisions largely targeted higher-income households (for example, the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% additional Medicare payroll tax above high-income thresholds) and excise taxes on insurers/employers; it did not constitute the single largest tax increase on the middle class in U.S. history. Analyses by the CBO and Treasury showed most ACA tax increases fell on higher earners or employers, while many middle-income households received subsidies or faced cost changes through premiums rather than a sweeping direct middle-class tax increase.

claim: New food safety legislation will regulate backyard gardening.
rationale: The claim is overly broad and unsupported as stated: there is no known, widely applicable "new food safety legislation" that specifically regulates backyard gardening. Most food-safety laws target commercial production, processing and distribution; backyard gardens are generally governed, if at all, by local zoning, public-health or HOA rules. Without a named jurisdiction or bill the statement cannot be verified.

claim: "Right now, we are about 4% behind the (census) response rate where we were in 2010. But for Black and Latino and Native American communities, they’re behind by 10%."
rationale: The claim gives precise percentage gaps without specifying a date; Census self-response rates did lag 2010 levels during parts of the 2020 operation and minority groups showed larger shortfalls, but the exact gaps varied by date and measure. Public reporting from the Census Bureau and independent analyses show overall lags of a few percentage points and larger, but not consistently a 4% overall and a uniform 10% deficit for Black, Latino and Native American communities at a single verified point in time. Because the claim is specific and lacks a clear timestamp, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Says Marco Rubio believes the earth is 9,000 years old and that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction; says  Rand Paul believes the earth is 10,000 years old and God removed dinosaurs "to make space for humans."
rationale: The specific attributions in the claim are not supported by the public record. Marco Rubio has not publicly stated a 9,000‑year age for Earth or that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction; he has expressed personal uncertainty about evolution but avoided citing a specific young‑Earth age. Rand Paul has made remarks consistent with Christian creationist views in interviews, but there is no reliable evidence he asserted the Earth is 10,000 years old or that God removed dinosaurs “to make space for humans” in those exact terms.

claim: Under the new Arizona immigration law, police can't stop someone to check their immigration status unless they think they see something illegal.
rationale: Arizona's well-known immigration statute (SB 1070) allows officers to inquire about immigration status during a lawful stop, detention or arrest only if they have reasonable suspicion the person is unlawfully present. The U.S. Supreme Court in 2012 upheld that provision while striking down other parts of the law, so officers may not legally stop someone solely to check immigration status absent reasonable suspicion.

claim: Says Donald Trump "just promised that if he wins reelection, he’ll gut Social Security and Medicare."
rationale: There is no verifiable public statement in which Donald Trump explicitly “just promised” to “gut Social Security and Medicare.” In fact, Trump has repeatedly said he would protect those programs during campaign cycles; while some proposals from allies or budget documents suggest changes to entitlement programs, that is not the same as a direct pledge to eliminate or “gut” them.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: This claim overstates and generalizes: there is no authoritative public-health or regulatory determination that Bath & Body Works products as a whole are suspected of damaging fertility or unborn children. While some fragranced personal-care products can contain chemicals (e.g., certain phthalates or preservatives) that some studies associate with reproductive risks, formulations vary and health agencies have not issued a blanket warning specifically against Bath & Body Works products. Individuals concerned about pregnancy should check ingredient lists and consult a clinician.

claim: "920 women lose their unborn babies after getting vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is misleading and lacks necessary context (which vaccine, timeframe, and source). Passive reports (for example to VAERS) have included hundreds of spontaneous abortion reports but these are unverified and do not establish causation; controlled studies of COVID-19 vaccination have not shown an increased risk of fetal loss. Therefore stating categorically that “920 women lose their unborn babies after getting vaccinated” is not supported as a factual causal statement.

claim: In the infrastructure bill that just passed the House, "only 10% is actual infrastructure."
rationale: The bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that the House passed contains roughly $550 billion in new federal spending targeted to traditional infrastructure (roads, bridges, transit, rail, broadband, water, power), which is far more than 10% of the package. Even against the bill's $1.2 trillion headline figure, the infrastructure-directed share is well above 10%, so the claim substantially understates the infrastructure component.

claim: "We’re the seventh highest taxed state in America. And that’s not just state, it’s local as well."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which state or which tax measure (e.g., total state+local tax burden per capita, percentage of personal income, marginal rates) or time period is being referenced. Rankings of "highest taxed" states vary by metric and year — different sources (Tax Foundation, Census Bureau, etc.) produce different orderings — so the blanket statement cannot be confirmed without those specifics.

claim: A bill to eliminate Delta Air Lines’ jet fuel tax breaks "violates federal law and puts the state at risk of losing critical funding from the Federal Aviation Administration."
rationale: There is no clear federal statute that automatically forbids a state from eliminating a jet fuel tax exemption or that would by itself force the FAA to withdraw airport funding. FAA grant assurances bar discriminatory or impermissible practices at federally funded airports, but removing a tax break that is applied uniformly to all carriers generally would not violate those assurances or trigger loss of federal funding. Claims that a neutral repeal of an exemption "violates federal law" or "puts the state at risk" are therefore overstated without evidence the bill singled out Delta or breached specific grant terms.

claim: This year’s state budget and my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016 represent an infusion of more than $1 billion in additional money for K-12 education.
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated because it lacks the identity of the state and specific budget line items; without those details there is no basis to confirm an aggregate “more than $1 billion” increase for K–12. Budget claims often hinge on definitions (one‑time vs ongoing, included pension or federal funds, baseline year) and those are not specified here, so the statement cannot be substantiated. Given the missing context, I mark it false pending corroborating budget documents.

claim: Says a photo of a young girl crying alongside an ISIS member is a Christian being forced into sexual slavery as a child bride.
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence tying that specific photo to a named Christian child forced into sexual slavery; similar images have been widely miscaptioned and circulated without provenance. Reliable fact-checkers have repeatedly found such photos lack corroborating metadata or independent confirmation of the girl's identity, religion, or the circumstances shown, so the specific claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "You may not have stayed in a hotel in the past year, but illegals arriving since Biden’s inauguration, they get to stay free of charge."
rationale: The claim asserts a blanket policy that all undocumented immigrants arriving since Biden's inauguration are given free hotel stays. There is no federal policy that universally provides free hotel lodging to all arriving undocumented migrants; some cities, states, and agencies have in limited circumstances contracted hotels or provided temporary shelter funded by local, state, federal, or nonprofit sources, but those are case‑specific and not a universal entitlement.

claim: The Biden administration’s American Jobs Plan will be "the biggest non-defense investment in research and development in the history of our country."
rationale: The claim is an overstatement that isn’t clearly supported. The American Jobs Plan proposed a large increase in non-defense R&D funding (roughly in the low hundreds of billions over multiple years), but the U.S. has previously committed very large civilian R&D sums (for example NIH budgets of tens of billions per year and sizable past civilian science and stimulus investments). Without a precise definition (single bill vs. annual or cumulative spending, proposed vs. enacted), the assertion that it is the "biggest non-defense investment in R&D in history" is not demonstrably true.

claim: ABC News recently banned reporters from wearing American flag lapel pins on air.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that ABC News issued a recent ban on reporters wearing American flag lapel pins on air. Similar claims have circulated on social media and been debunked by independent fact-checkers; while news organizations often discourage overt political messaging to maintain neutrality, an explicit network-wide prohibition on U.S. flag pins has not been substantiated.

claim: "Forty-five percent of those who've been unemployed, they've been unemployed for six months or longer."
rationale: The statement is presented as a general fact without time or place, but the share of unemployed people who are long‑term unemployed (27+ weeks) varies month to month and is not universally 45%. While the long‑term unemployment share did approach or briefly exceed roughly 40–45% during the Great Recession/post‑2009 period, it is not a standing, always‑true figure and often is much lower in other periods.

claim: "The (ARC Tunnel) project was originally estimated to be $8.7 billion, and New Jersey alone was on the hook for all overruns."
rationale: The ARC project was widely reported with an initial estimated cost around $8.7 billion, but the claim that New Jersey alone would be liable for all cost overruns is incorrect. Funding and liability were complex — the project involved cost-sharing arrangements among New Jersey, New York, the Port Authority and federal programs, and responsibility for overruns was disputed rather than legally assigned solely to New Jersey.

claim: Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint against him alleging he used county workers for campaign work, which is an indictable offense.
rationale: I cannot verify that a specific ethics complaint exists against a person named Jeff Mann alleging he used county workers for campaign work, nor can I confirm that such an allegation has led to an indictable offense. The claim mixes an alleged complaint (which I cannot corroborate against any identified public official named Jeff Mann) with a legal conclusion: whether misuse of county staff is an indictable offense depends on local law and facts. Because I have no reliable, specific evidence tying this complaint and criminality to a named individual, I judge the composite claim false pending verification.

claim: A lawyer demanded "several Houston pastors hand over to the city government many of their private papers, including their sermons."
rationale: There is no credible documentation that a lawyer broadly demanded several Houston pastors turn over their private papers and sermons to the city. Reporting about disputes between Houston officials and clergy has generally discussed subpoenas or requests tied to campaign or public communications, not a wholesale seizure of private sermons; such an action would also pose clear First Amendment concerns. The claim appears to be unsubstantiated or a mischaracterization of more limited legal requests.

claim: Says a leader of the Blackfeet Nation tribe designed the current Washington Redskins logo and once said it "made us all proud to have an Indian on a big-time team."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that a leader of the Blackfeet Nation designed the Washington Redskins’ long‑used logo or that such a leader is on record saying it “made us all proud to have an Indian on a big‑time team.” Historical reporting on the Redskins logo attributes its creation and modifications to team artists and designers and to team officials rather than to a Blackfeet leader, and the quoted endorsement does not appear in credible contemporary sources. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute statements and design credit.

claim: "President Obama will now own 60 percent of GM, and his union buddies will own almost 20 percent."
rationale: The statement is incorrect because the roughly 60% stake in the reorganized GM was owned by the U.S. government (Treasury), not personally by President Obama. The United Auto Workers’ retiree trust (VEBA) received about 17.5% of the new GM—close to but under 20%—and other stakeholders (including the Canadian government and creditors) held the remainder. The claim conflates government ownership with personal ownership and mischaracterizes the union’s role.

claim: "In 2011, (Debbie) Wasserman Schultz missed 62 congressional votes — one of the worst records of any member of Congress."
rationale: The claim mixes a true-looking number with a misleading evaluation. While fact-checks reported Wasserman Schultz missed dozens of votes in 2011, the characterization that it was “one of the worst records” is inaccurate — many members missed more votes and rankings vary by whether you count raw missed votes or percentage missed and which time window is used. Thus the numeric part is plausible but the evaluative claim is false or misleading.

claim: "We are not producing jobs. We created 80,000 jobs last month. We don't talk about the jobs that we lost. The net of it all is that we lost jobs."
rationale: The claim is internally inconsistent and unsupported as stated: reporting that 'we created 80,000 jobs last month' typically refers to the net monthly payroll change, which by definition is a net gain (not a net loss). Without specifying a different dataset or timeframe showing larger losses that outweigh the 80,000 gains, the assertion that the net of it all is a loss is unsubstantiated. Because no source, country, or month is given, the statement cannot be verified and is likely false as phrased.

claim: Says private-sector job growth in 2011 "places New Jersey in the top third among all of the states."
rationale: Contemporary labor‑market data and independent fact‑checks show New Jersey did not rank in the top third of states for private‑sector job growth in 2011; its growth was middling compared with other states. The claim appears to rely on a selective or different metric (such as a narrow timeframe or a particular subset), rather than the standard state‑by‑state comparisons used by BLS and reviewers at the time.

claim: A photo of a homeless camp on old railroad tracks is present-day Los Angeles.
rationale: There is no image, metadata, provenance, or corroborating evidence provided to verify that the photo depicts present-day Los Angeles. Similar scenes of homeless encampments on railroad tracks are common in many cities, so the claim is unsubstantiated. Without geolocation or reliable sourcing the assertion should not be accepted as fact.

claim: "Despite what you may have heard about Wisconsin’s finances, Wisconsin is on track to have a budget surplus this year."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it provides no fiscal year or source; whether Wisconsin is "on track" for a surplus depends on the official, contemporaneous revenue and spending projections from the state. Recent years have seen changing forecasts and both surpluses and deficits at different points in budget cycles, so without a specific year and an official projection the claim cannot be confirmed. Because the claim is broad and lacks context, I judge it false as stated.

claim: Says the Koch brothers want to "protect tax cuts for companies that ship our jobs overseas."
rationale: Koch-backed organizations and the Koch brothers have consistently advocated for broad corporate tax cuts and opposed policies that penalize or condition tax benefits on domestic job retention. Those positions would effectively preserve tax advantages for corporations that relocate jobs overseas, so the characterization that they want to protect such tax cuts is a fair summary of their policy stance. The claim is a paraphrase rather than a literal quote, which leaves some room for interpretation.

claim: Pennsylvania officials are "attempting to silence voters" by sending them letters that say they’ve been exposed to COVID-19 and "must remain quarantined and not vote in person on Election Day."
rationale: Health officials in Pennsylvania did notify people they may have been exposed and recommended quarantine, but there is no evidence state or county officials sent letters that legally barred people from voting in person or explicitly ordered them "not to vote in person on Election Day." Fact-checks found the notices were public-health exposure/quarantine guidance and at most encouraged avoiding public activities or using absentee/alternative voting, not an official attempt to prohibit voting.

claim: Says Craig Huey called Planned Parenthood a "murder mill."
rationale: I could not confirm in my available knowledge any reliable source or direct quotation showing Craig Huey used the term "murder mill" for Planned Parenthood. The phrase is commonly used by anti‑abortion activists, which can lead to misattribution, but without a cited source this specific attribution is unverified. Given the lack of corroborating evidence, I rate the claim as false/unsupported.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim gives a precise count without specifying a timeframe or country; public-health sources typically report prevalence as percentages and absolute counts depend on which population and year are used. Estimates of intimate-partner or domestic violence during pregnancy vary across studies and jurisdictions, so I cannot confirm 324,000 as a verified figure.

claim: Says of President Donald Trump’s actions on the coronavirus: "No. 1, he fired the pandemic team two years ago. No. 2, he's been defunding the Centers for Disease Control."
rationale: The first claim refers to the NSC’s global health/pandemic office being disbanded and staff reassigned in 2018 during an NSC reorganization — accurate in substance though described imprecisely as ‘fired.’ The second claim that Trump ‘has been defunding the CDC’ is misleading: his budgets repeatedly proposed cuts, but Congress largely rejected deep cuts and actual CDC appropriations were not eliminated, so portraying it as ongoing defunding is inaccurate.

claim: "The latest unemployment numbers have shown that nearly 315,000 Americans have simply given up hope when it comes to finding a job."
rationale: The claim presents a specific recent figure without a date or source and conflates 'unemployment numbers' with people who have stopped looking for work. The Bureau of Labor Statistics separately reports 'discouraged workers' and 'marginally attached' counts (which fluctuate month to month), and any statement that 'nearly 315,000 Americans have simply given up' is unsupported absent a specific month and citation and likely misstates how those categories are reported. Because the claim is ambiguous and probably mischaracterizes BLS categories, it cannot be accepted as true as presented.

claim: "If you are a hard-working law-abiding citizen who earns $80,000, you don’t get a stimulus check. But if you are a convicted murderer or rapist sitting in jail, you do."
rationale: The claim is a misleading oversimplification. Stimulus payments were based on adjusted gross income, filing status, and tax-return/benefit records with gradual phase-outs (so someone with $80,000 often still received at least a reduced payment depending on the specific program and filing status). Being incarcerated does not automatically guarantee a payment — eligibility for prisoners depends on the same income/filing rules and whether they are claimed as dependents, so it is false to assert all convicts in jail received checks while law‑abiding $80K earners did not.

claim: Getting the COVID-19 vaccine jeopardizes life insurance policies.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that receiving a COVID-19 vaccine voids or routinely jeopardizes life insurance policies. Insurers and regulators have indicated vaccines are not a disqualifying act; life policies are generally only voided for fraud, nonpayment, or specific contract exclusions. Rare adverse events would be handled like any other cause of death and could be subject to normal contestability or investigation periods.

claim: "Our last budget committed the highest level of need-based financial aid in state history."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks any identifying context (which state and which budget year) and would require comparing detailed budget appropriation data across multiple years. Without specific citations to the budget documents and a clear definition of what counts as "need-based financial aid" (recurring vs one-time, grants vs tax credits), the assertion is not supportable. Given the ambiguity, I judge the statement false pending evidence.

claim: Photo shows "Myrtle Beach 30 minutes ago."
rationale: There is no way to confirm a photo’s precise location and that it was taken '30 minutes ago' without the image, its metadata, or independent corroboration. Claims about time-and-place for images require EXIF timestamps, geolocation, or identifiable landmarks and contextual verification; absent that evidence the assertion cannot be substantiated. Therefore I treat the claim as false pending verifiable proof.

claim: "Unemployment insurance kept more than 620,000 children out of poverty in 2012."
rationale: Contemporary analyses (notably by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities drawing on Census poverty estimates) reported that unemployment insurance benefits reduced poverty in 2012 and kept more than 620,000 children out of poverty. That figure is cited in policy summaries that estimate UI lifted roughly 2+ million people, including about 620,000 children, above the poverty line that year.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Barack Obama and George Clooney were photographed together in a compromising situation with a child; such a sensational image involving two high-profile figures would have provoked widespread, verifiable coverage. Viral images of public figures are frequently doctored, miscaptioned, or deepfaked, so this claim is almost certainly false without original-source verification.

claim: "FDR was called a socialist and a communist."
rationale: Throughout the 1930s and 1940s many of Roosevelt’s opponents labeled his New Deal policies as “socialist,” and some critics even accused him of being a “communist” as a political smear. These were common pejorative attacks by conservatives, isolationists, and demagogues, though Roosevelt was not a member of socialist or communist parties.

claim: "The senior senator from Arizona (John McCain) said he couldn't support repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' because of the economy."
rationale: John McCain did oppose repealing 'don't ask, don't tell,' but his stated reasons centered on military readiness, unit cohesion, and the legislative process rather than the state of the economy. Contemporary reporting and his public statements from the repeal debates emphasize national security and timing concerns, not economic rationale for opposing repeal.

claim: Says he was "not part of transferring" any priests accused of sexual abuse.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous (no named individual, time, or jurisdiction) and cannot be verified as presented; historically, many similar denials by clerics were later contradicted by investigations and internal records showing transfers of accused priests. Given the lack of specific evidence supporting this particular denial, I treat the claim as false pending more context.

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence, indictments, or reporting linking Barack or Michelle Obama (or their daughters) to the Varsity Blues college admissions bribery scheme. The publicly charged individuals and documentation identify specific parents involved, and the Obama family has not been named, investigated, or charged in connection with that scandal. Claims asserting such a connection are unsubstantiated.

claim: "U.S. Department of Homeland Security has told banks -- in writing -- it may inspect safe deposit boxes without warrant and seize any gold, silver, guns or other valuables it finds inside those boxes!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security issued a written directive telling banks they may inspect safe-deposit boxes without warrants and seize valuables. Major fact-checkers and legal practice show banks generally require a court order or law-enforcement warrant/subpoena for access and seizure; DHS does not have blanket authority to bypass those legal protections.

claim: "So far, out of 175 arrested in Kenosha, 102 were not from Kenosha. Rioting has become its own industry."
rationale: The precise numeric claim cannot be verified as stated: counts reported about arrests during the Kenosha unrest varied by source and depend on how “not from Kenosha” is defined (city residents vs. county or state vs. out-of-state). The second sentence is a subjective characterization rather than a factual statement. Because of these ambiguities and lack of a single authoritative count matching the claim, the statement as presented is not reliably true.

claim: Says Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s "wealth has surged while in public office."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated — public financial disclosures for Sen. Jeanne Shaheen do show changes in reported assets over time, but there is no clear, widely documented evidence that her personal wealth has “surged” while in office. Without a defined timeframe, metric, or corroborating reporting of a large, rapid increase, the assertion is not substantiated. Routine investment gains or reporting variations do not by themselves prove a dramatic surge.

claim: Maj. Nidal Hasan, the man accused of the Fort Hood shootings, "was an ADVISOR to the Obama Administration."
rationale: There is no evidence Maj. Nidal Hasan held any formal advisory position to President Obama or the Obama Administration. Hasan was an Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood and the accused shooter in the 2009 Fort Hood attack; claims that he was an Obama adviser are misinformation or mischaracterizations of his military role.

claim: "Grandparents must pickup up all their grandchildren every weekend no matter what or they will be fined $5,000."
rationale: This statement is false as written. There is no general law that obligates all grandparents to pick up all their grandchildren every weekend under threat of a $5,000 fine; custody and visitation are determined case-by-case by family courts, and enforcement (if any) depends on individual court orders and local law rather than a blanket statutory fine. While a specific court order could impose obligations or sanctions, it would be individualized and not a universal rule applicable to all grandparents.

claim: "Jim Renacci cheated on his income taxes" and is a "deadbeat citizen."
rationale: There is no public record or credible reporting showing Jim Renacci was charged or convicted of deliberately cheating on his income taxes; allegations of unpaid taxes or business-related tax disputes (if referenced) do not by themselves prove criminal tax evasion. Calling someone a "deadbeat citizen" is a subjective, pejorative judgment rather than an established factual finding. Without documented legal findings of intentional tax fraud, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: 40 percent of illegal immigrants "had a visa and then became illegal," mostly because "they changed jobs."
rationale: While government and research estimates have put the share of unauthorized immigrants who initially entered on a visa (visa overstays) around 40–50%, the claim that this group became illegal mostly because they "changed jobs" is not supported. Most people who lose lawful status do so because their temporary visa expired or they overstayed a visit or student/work program; employer-tied visas can cause problems if jobs end, but job changes are not identified as the predominant cause.

claim: Says his barehanded catch posted on YouTube is real.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it lacks any identifying information about who “he” is or which YouTube video is meant. Without the specific video, uploader, date, or independent corroboration (e.g., eyewitnesses, expert analysis, or unedited footage), the claim that a barehanded catch is genuinely real is unprovable and thus treated as false. Many viral catch videos are staged, edited, or misleading, so asserting reality requires verification not provided here.

claim: "African-Americans are more likely to be arrested by police and sentenced to longer prison terms for doing the same thing that whites do."
rationale: Extensive empirical research and U.S. government reports document that Black Americans are arrested at higher rates than white Americans for many offenses (notably drug offenses despite similar usage rates) and on average receive harsher sentences. Analyses from the U.S. Sentencing Commission, Department of Justice, and peer‑reviewed studies find racial disparities in arrests, charging, plea bargains, and sentencing that persist after controlling for some legal factors. This supports the claim as a general statement about systemic disparities, though magnitudes vary by crime and jurisdiction.

claim: ISIS sends out "90,000 social (media) messages a day."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that ISIS consistently produces 90,000 distinct social‑media messages per day. Independent monitoring by researchers and platform takedown reports have shown much lower and highly variable volumes (and platforms actively suspend many accounts), and the quoted figure appears to be an exaggeration or misinterpretation of ephemeral peak activity or aggregated bot/amplification counts. The claim also fails to define timeframe, platforms, or what counts as a “message,” which makes the 90,000 number unreliable.

claim: Says Bill Nelson "skipped 45 percent of the hearings on national security."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Independent fact-checks found the 45% figure was derived from a selective counting method (specific public hearings over a chosen period) and does not reflect Nelson’s overall attendance at national security-related committee hearings and briefings, which were substantially better than the claimed 55% absence rate. The statement therefore overstates and misrepresents the attendance record.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Robert Hurt authored or publicly promoted a specific plan to cut "education" funding by 40 percent. While Hurt voted with Republican budget proposals that sought substantial reductions or caps in non-defense discretionary spending (which can affect some federal education programs), those votes are not the same as a named 40% across-the-board education cut he proposed. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes policy specifics.

claim: "About 47 percent of able-bodied people in the state of Maine don’t work."
rationale: The claim is not supported by labor-market data: Maine’s employment‑population ratios and labor‑force participation rates are far higher than implying 47% of able‑bodied people don’t work. The statement conflates undefined “able‑bodied” with non‑work and is likely a misreading of program participation statistics (e.g., SNAP or disability rolls), not the share of working‑age residents who are unemployed or out of the labor force.

claim: "Health care is the greatest contribution to spending increases in the state budget."
rationale: The claim is a blanket statement with no state or time period specified, so it cannot be verified as universally true. Budget drivers vary by state and year—Medicaid/health care is a leading contributor to spending growth in many states, but other factors (K–12/higher education, pension obligations, debt service) are the largest drivers in others. Without specific context the claim is not provably factual.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and misleading. While U.S. homicide counts did spike sharply around 2020 (with increases commonly reported in the ~20–30% range from 2019 to 2020), the claim gives no clear two-year window or data source and overgeneralizes a "30 years of decline" narrative that ignores fluctuations and the fact that declines were mainly from the early 1990s through the 2010s. Because the precise percent and period depend on the chosen years and dataset, the categorical phrasing is not supportable as stated.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: The claim is false as a blanket statement: a White House spokesman cannot unilaterally eliminate all rights to photograph a public official. While the White House or Secret Service can impose access restrictions in specific secure or private locations (e.g., restricted tarmacs, inside aircraft, or fenced areas) and set media credentialing rules, there is no general new legal prohibition barring everyone from photographing President Biden climbing stairs. Any temporary operational or press-pool restrictions would be narrow and situation-specific, not an absolute ban on all filming by all people.

claim: "Total deaths from COVID MUCH LOWER than reported."
rationale: The blanket claim that total COVID deaths are “MUCH LOWER than reported” is not supported by evidence. Global and national analyses of excess mortality show that in many places the true death toll is equal to or substantially higher than official COVID death counts, and early under-detection and reporting lags led to undercounts rather than large systematic overcounts. While individual cases and some locales have differences in attribution (deaths ‘with’ vs ‘from’ COVID), the overall pattern supports underreporting, not a much lower true total.

claim: There are "many unanswered and obvious questions" about the 2001 death of a staff member of Joe Scarborough.
