rationale: Official investigations concluded the 2001 death of Joe Scarborough’s staffer was an accidental death from a sudden cardiac arrhythmia leading to a fall and blunt head trauma, and investigators found no evidence of foul play. While online conspiracy theories claim unanswered questions, the medical examiner’s autopsy and law-enforcement reviews addressed the key facts of the case and found no criminal activity. Thus the claim that there are “many unanswered and obvious questions” is misleading.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The figure of 360,000 annual deaths attributable to swimming pools is not supported by available data. WHO reports roughly 236,000 global drowning deaths per year (all settings) and national agencies (e.g., CDC) report only a few thousand drownings per year in the U.S., with a minority occurring in pools—far below 360,000. The policy comparison about shutting down a country is a value judgment and does not make the numeric claim true.

claim: Says there’s no proven instance where hydraulic fracking has polluted groundwater.
rationale: This is false. Multiple investigations and studies have documented instances where activities associated with hydraulic fracturing—such as well-casing failures, faulty cementing, and surface spills—have led to groundwater contamination (examples include state and EPA investigations in places like Dimock, PA and Pavillion, WY, and peer-reviewed studies finding elevated methane in wells near shale gas operations). The U.S. EPA's assessment also identified specific cases of impacts even while noting limited evidence for widespread direct contamination from the fracturing process itself.

claim: "The job [of correctional officer] lowers your life expectancy . . . Metropolitan did a study in, I believe it was 1998, and the life expectancy was 58."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that correctional officers have a life expectancy as low as 58 or that a Metropolitan (e.g., MetLife) 1998 study reported that figure. Research does indicate correctional officers face elevated stress and some higher risks of disease and premature mortality relative to some groups, but not to the extent of an average life expectancy of 58 years. The specific claim appears to be a misremembered or exaggerated statistic rather than a supported actuarial finding.

claim: "One percent of the American people make over 21 percent of all the income in America. That wasn’t the way before George Bush became president."
rationale: The first part (that the top 1% receive over ~21% of U.S. income) is broadly consistent with widely cited income-share data for the mid-2000s, but the claim that this “wasn’t the way before George Bush became president” is inaccurate. Historical series (Saez/Piketty and others) show the top 1% share had already risen to around 20–21% by 2000, so high concentration was largely in place at the start of George W. Bush’s term and continued to rise thereafter. Therefore the absolute assertion that it was not true before his presidency is false.

claim: Says Wisconsin’s 2011-13 state budget contains "no fee increases"
rationale: False. The 2011–13 Wisconsin state budget enacted a variety of fee increases and measures that raised revenue through fees (examples include increases or new charges for parks/hunting and fishing licenses, motor vehicle/driver-related fees, court and licensing/permit fees, and provisions enabling higher university tuition). Contemporary budget summaries and news coverage documented these fee hikes, so the blanket claim of "no fee increases" is inaccurate.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I found no reliable evidence or contemporaneous reporting attributing that quote or position to a person named Gerald Daugherty. Public records and news coverage of debates over domestic-violence sentencing do discuss concerns about incarceration rates, but I could not verify that Daugherty explicitly advocated lowering penalties for strangulation with the quoted language. Without a credible source, the claim appears to be a misattribution or unverified assertion.

claim: "Since the president became the president, we have lost 3.3 million jobs in the private sector. But you know who's done OK and who's not complaining today? The public sector. We've gained 590,000 public sector jobs."
rationale: The claim gives absolute job-change numbers without specifying the president or exact start/end dates, so it cannot be verified as stated. Official BLS payroll data show private‑sector and government job changes vary greatly depending on the chosen timeframe (monthly/seasonally adjusted series around COVID and recovery periods produced very different net changes), and the specific figures 3.3 million lost private jobs and 590,000 gained public jobs do not match a single unambiguous BLS interval tied to a named president. Because the statement is underspecified and likely inaccurate as a standalone factual claim, it is judged false.

claim: "Trump’s daughter works at the White House. Her husband works at the White House. Rudy’s son works at the White House. Barr’s son-in-law works at the White House. Barr’s daughter works at Treasury. Trump’s sons do foreign business. Trump’s daughter is getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants."
rationale: The claim bundles several true, false, and unverified assertions. It is true that Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner served as White House senior advisers, and Andrew Giuliani (Rudy Giuliani’s son) held a White House staff role; however, specific claims that “Barr’s son‑in‑law works at the White House” and that “Barr’s daughter works at Treasury” are not supported by reliable public records. The statements about Trump’s sons broadly doing foreign business and Ivanka “getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants” are vague or misleading—there were reported foreign contacts and trademark filings, but the claim as written overstates and conflates facts. Because multiple specific parts are unsupported or inaccurate, the composite claim is false.

claim: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp "mandates restaurants reopen"
rationale: False. In spring 2020 Governor Kemp issued executive orders that allowed restaurants to resume dine-in service under capacity limits and safety rules and preempted some local restrictions, but he did not issue a blanket mandate forcing all restaurants to reopen — owners could keep their businesses closed. The claim misstates that restaurants were mandated to reopen.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because no speaker, time period, or supporting financial disclosures are provided. Without named individual/entity and access to tax records, disclosures, or corporate ownership documents, one cannot confirm the absence of direct or indirect financial interests in Saudi Arabia; therefore I default to FALSE due to lack of evidence.

claim: In "the past four or five" presidential elections, "people who poll high at the beginning are not the people who end up being the nominees."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While in some recent cycles early poll leaders (e.g., Rudy Giuliani in 2008, Jeb Bush in 2016) failed to win their party’s nomination, there are clear counterexamples where early high pollers did become the nominees (e.g., Mitt Romney in 2012 and Joe Biden and Donald Trump in the 2020 cycle for their respective parties). Because the outcome varies by year, party, and how you define “the beginning,” the claim as stated is not accurate.

claim: Says J. David Cox, "the boss" of the jail guards "who were supposed to keep" suspected sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein alive, is also "friends with Bill and Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The claim conflates roles and asserts a personal friendship without evidence. J. David Cox is the longtime president of the American Federation of Government Employees (a union), not the managerial “boss” of the Bureau of Prisons guards at MCC, and there are no credible sources showing he is personally “friends” with Bill and Hillary Clinton—while the union has had political ties to Democrats, that is not proof of a personal friendship.

claim: "Muslims offended that their kids have to recite national anthem."
rationale: The claim is a broad generalization without evidence; Muslims are a diverse group and there is no basis to say they are collectively offended that their children must recite a national anthem. While isolated individuals or families in particular countries have objected to pledges or anthems for religious or political reasons, these cases are exceptions rather than a universal or majority stance. The statement overstates and misattributes sentiment to an entire religious group.

claim: "Corrupt political bosses. Money laundering. Fraud. It’s just another day at the office for Vin Gopal."
rationale: There is no reliable public evidence that Vin Gopal routinely engages in corruption, money laundering, or fraud, and he has not been convicted of such crimes; mainstream reporting and official records do not substantiate the blanket criminal allegation. The statement reads as partisan rhetoric alleging criminality without documented proof.

claim: "All non-US citizens, illegal or not, will be provided with free health care services."
rationale: There is no US-wide policy that provides free health care to all non‑citizens, including undocumented immigrants. Federal programs (Medicaid, ACA subsidies) generally exclude many non‑citizens; undocumented people may receive emergency care and some states/localities offer limited or conditional coverage, but not universal free services for every non‑US citizen.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Federal spending as a share of GDP has varied over time (and recent years’ shares depend on how you measure spending and which year you pick), and saying it rose from 20% to 25% as a blanket historical fact is inaccurate. Moreover, even if government’s GDP share rises, that does not automatically mean the private sector has had exactly 5 percentage points of output “taken away” — GDP composition and causal effects involve taxes, borrowing, transfers, and cyclical changes.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine "want to shut down shale, and shut down natural gas."
rationale: Neither Hillary Clinton nor Tim Kaine advocated an explicit policy to "shut down shale" or to ban natural gas. Clinton's platform called for stricter regulation of fracking and a transition toward renewable energy while acknowledging natural gas's role as a bridge fuel; Kaine did not call for banning shale gas. The claim therefore misstates and exaggerates their stated positions.

claim: The "48, 49 percent" that supports President Barack Obama are "people who pay no income tax."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The “47/48/49 percent” line originated from a 2012 remark that conflated the share of households with no federal income tax liability with a presumed bloc that would automatically back Obama, but empirical data show Obama’s supporters included many people who did pay federal income tax and many non-payers still paid payroll or state taxes. The share of households owing no federal income tax (around mid‑40s percent in that period) is not identical to the share of Obama supporters, so the claim overstates and misattributes the relationship.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: The claim overstates and conflates prevalence and causation. While malnutrition or risk of malnutrition is common among hospitalized older adults (estimates vary widely by setting and assessment tool and often fall in the 20–60% range), robust evidence does not support that half of all hospitalized seniors have malnutrition so severe that it either caused their admission or definitively prevents recovery. Causation is complex and depends on definitions of “malnutrition” and “severe,” which the claim does not specify.

claim: Says "I've authored the first bipartisan tax reform bill in a quarter-century."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as true and is likely false: there have been bipartisan federal tax bills and bipartisan tax-related legislation within the past 25 years (for example bipartisan “tax extenders” packages and the 2015 PATH Act). The claim also lacks a speaker, date, and a clear definition of “tax reform,” making the absolute assertion of being the “first” in a quarter-century implausible without more context.

claim: "We had 6,000 oil and gas spills in 2012" with "more oil and gas spreading in the United States than the entire Exxon Valdez spill."
rationale: The statement mixes incident counts and total volume. While government datasets do record thousands of small oil and gas releases in some years (making a ~6,000 count plausible depending on definitions), the vast majority are very small releases and the summed volume in 2012 was far below the Exxon Valdez disaster (about 11 million gallons). Thus the claim that more oil/gas spread in the U.S. in 2012 than Exxon Valdez is not supported.

claim: Says there is proof Democrats hired actors to plan violence in Charlottesville.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democratic operatives hired actors to plan the violence in Charlottesville. Multiple independent journalists, fact-checkers, and official investigations found that the clashes were driven by white supremacist groups and their counterprotesters, and the claim about paid actors traces to unverified social media conspiracy posts that have been debunked. Assertions of organized Democratic orchestration have not been substantiated in any reputable reporting or legal findings.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: As of my last knowledge update (June 2024) there were no credible reports, indictments, or court filings charging Representative Maxine Waters with a crime. A criminal charge against a longstanding, high-profile member of Congress would be widely reported and there were no such widely distributed reports or official records. Therefore the blanket claim that she "is getting criminally charged" is false based on available information.

claim: Sherrod Brown "sent billions of our tax dollars to foreign countries."
rationale: The claim is misleading and thus false as stated: a single U.S. senator does not unilaterally “send” tax dollars abroad. Federal spending, including foreign assistance, is authorized by Congress as a whole and executed by the executive branch; while Senator Sherrod Brown may have voted for bills that included foreign-aid or international components, he did not personally send billions of dollars to other countries.

claim: The daughter of a Donald Trump appointee posed as an El Paso shooting victim in a photo with the president.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting showing that a daughter of a Trump appointee pretended to be an El Paso shooting victim in a photo with the president. Viral social-media posts making this accusation were not corroborated by reputable news outlets or fact-checkers and appear to be misidentifications or misinformation.

claim: "Nobody’s invited us" to the Obama events in Atlanta.
rationale: The statement is vague and unverified — saying “nobody’s invited us” as a blanket fact is implausible without specifying who “us” refers to or which Obama events in Atlanta are meant. Major political events hosted by a former president typically include invited guests, public ticketing/registration, and media coverage listing attendees, so an absolute claim that nobody was invited is not supported. Without specific evidence that a particular group was deliberately excluded, the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: Says revenues "are actually up after tax reform."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it gives no jurisdiction, revenue type, or time frame. For example, in the U.S. after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act federal receipts did not uniformly rise as a share of GDP and deficits increased, although nominal receipts varied and rose in some years; outcomes differ by country, state, or company and by which period is measured. Without those specifics the blanket statement is not supportable.

claim: "In New York State, Democrats blocked a Bill expanding College Tuition for Gold Star families after approving aid for illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that New York State Democrats blocked a bill to expand college tuition benefits for Gold Star families immediately after passing aid for undocumented immigrants. New York has longstanding programs supporting veterans’ families and has previously extended in‑state tuition or aid to undocumented students, but major news and legislative records do not show the specific sequence or action claimed. The claim appears to conflate separate policy debates and lacks verified timing or chamber details to support the asserted cause-and-effect.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: This claim is false because impeachment of a U.S. president is decided by a vote in the U.S. House of Representatives; governors do not cast votes in that process. Phil Scott is the governor of Vermont, not a member of Congress, so he could not have "just voted to impeach" President Trump. He may have expressed an opinion about impeachment, but he would not have cast a congressional impeachment vote.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Los Angeles graduation metrics rose during the mayor’s tenure, the commonly cited ‘44% to 72%’ figures mix different timeframes and calculation methods and thus are not a like‑for‑like measure of on‑time graduation attributable solely to the mayor’s reforms. Independent fact‑checks found the numbers misrepresent the situation and overstate direct mayoral impact.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: Available analyses of U.S. federal tax data show that households with roughly $1 million in income pay substantially higher effective tax rates than those around $100,000, but the difference is on the order of about twofold, not fourfold. For example, top‑income households often face effective federal tax rates in the mid‑20s percent while $100k households typically face rates in the low to mid‑teens, producing a ratio near 2, not 4.

claim: "$21T in Pentagon accounting errors. Medicare for All costs ~$32T. That means 66% of Medicare for All could have been funded already by the Pentagon."
rationale: The $21 trillion figure pertains to cumulative accounting adjustments and unsupported journal entries reported in DoD audits over many years, not actual cash that can be redirected to new programs. The ~$32 trillion Medicare-for-All number is a modeled gross cost over a specific multi‑year period and depends on assumptions; treating the accounting‑adjustment total as available funding to cover 66% of that cost is misleading and incorrect.

claim: "Biden concedes 6 million votes."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that President Joe Biden "conceded 6 million votes." A concession is an admission of defeat; Biden was the declared winner of the 2020 election and did not publicly concede 6 million votes. The claim appears to misinterpret vote totals or invent an event that did not occur.

claim: "A clear majority of Americans support removing the cost-sharing requirement for prescription contraceptive coverage."
rationale: Multiple national polls over the past decade have consistently found that a clear majority of U.S. adults support requiring health insurance to cover prescription contraception without cost-sharing, typically in the 60–75% range. While exact percentages vary by question wording and year, the preponderance of reputable surveys indicates majority support for removing copays for contraceptives.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and contemporary records show no credible evidence that Rafael (Ted) Cruz’s father was with Lee Harvey Oswald before JFK’s assassination. The photograph/identification circulated online has been shown to be a misidentification and Cruz’s documented whereabouts do not place him with Oswald in New Orleans in 1963.

claim: "The number of uninsured people in Massachusetts is about the same as it was when the mandates were passed in 2006."
rationale: Massachusetts enacted its individual mandate and related reforms in 2006 and saw a substantial drop in the uninsured population afterward; the state’s uninsured rate fell to low single digits and remained well below pre‑reform levels. Therefore the number of uninsured today is not about the same as it was when the mandates were passed—there was a clear decline following the reform.

claim: The balanced-budget amendment once came within one vote of passing Congress but was defeated because of the no vote from a top Senate Republican, and Rick Santorum says he "stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship."
rationale: This assertion appears to conflate or misstate events. While Congress considered several balanced-budget amendment proposals over decades and some Senate votes came close, there is no clear historical record that a single "top Senate Republican" single-handedly defeated a final one‑vote passage and that Rick Santorum publicly said he "stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship." The available voting records and contemporary news accounts do not support that specific sequence or Santorum quote as stated.

claim: Says the new coronavirus vaccines contain toxic ingredients and are more dangerous than getting COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is false. Authorized COVID-19 vaccines do not contain inherently 'toxic' ingredients at harmful levels; their components (mRNA or viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, salts, sugars, and approved stabilizers/adjuvants) have been evaluated in clinical trials and by regulators for safety. Serious adverse events are rare, whereas COVID-19 infection carries substantially higher risks of hospitalization, death, and long-term complications for most populations.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid will worsen health care options for the most vulnerable among us in Texas."
rationale: Empirical evidence from U.S. states that expanded Medicaid shows overall improvements in insurance coverage, access to primary and preventive care, reductions in uncompensated care and financial strain, and some studies showing better health outcomes—effects that benefit low-income and vulnerable populations. While local provider capacity or payment-rate issues can create challenges, the net published evidence does not support the claim that expansion worsens health-care options for the most vulnerable in Texas.

claim: Rick Perry is "taking money away from hurricane victims" and diverting it to "remodel the Governor's Mansion."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and independent fact-checkers found no evidence that Rick Perry took disaster-relief money from hurricane victims to pay for remodeling the Governor's Mansion. The mansion repairs were funded through state appropriations, private donations, or different budget lines, and not by diverting FEMA or designated hurricane-relief grants away from victims. Assertions that federal or victim-directed disaster funds were reallocated to the mansion are not supported by documented budget records or credible reporting.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was asked repeatedly to provide security in Benghazi on several occasions, including direct cables."
rationale: Contemporaneous State Department records, internal reviews, and the Accountability Review Board found that U.S. personnel in Libya made multiple requests for additional security at the Benghazi facilities in 2011–2012, submitted through formal State Department channels including diplomatic cables and memos. Those requests were routed to and handled by the State Department while Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State. However, the record does not establish that she personally read every cable or directly denied each specific request.

claim: "There is currently no ability to vet these people," referring to Syrian refugees.
rationale: The claim is false. Governments and international agencies employ established vetting procedures for Syrian refugees—such as biometric registration, in-person interviews, identity-document checks, and cross-checks against national and international security databases—so it is not correct to say there is "no ability" to vet them. While vetting can be time-consuming and imperfect, systems and multi-agency screening processes do exist.

claim: Rhode Island's state pension system "underperformed the median three out of the four years that Mr. [Frank] Caprio was in office."
rationale: I cannot verify the precise assertion as stated because publicly reported pension-return comparisons depend on the benchmark dataset, fiscal-year definitions, and whether returns are measured gross or net. Reports of Rhode Island’s pension performance during Frank Caprio’s 2007–2011 tenure are sensitive to those methodological choices, and I find no unambiguous, widely accepted source showing it underperformed the median in three of the four years across a single clearly defined benchmark. Given the missing specifics, the claim as stated is not verifiable and is rated false pending clearer sourcing.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: Contemporary news reporting and campaign-finance records showed Culberson’s campaign paid vendors for “collectibles” and related purchases that included Civil War–era items and fossil purchases. These expenditures were publicly documented and reported on, leading to coverage that he used campaign funds for such memorabilia.

claim: Says the New York bike path assault "was the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the New York bike path attack was specifically “the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS.” While ISIS claimed or inspired that attack and many others, authorities and reporting did not enumerate it as the ninth such incident; counts of vehicle-ramming attacks vary by definition, time period, and geography. The ordinal claim is unsupported and implausibly precise.

claim: "CDC announces that students may be kept from parents overnight as Ohio sets up COVID-19 FEMA camps."
rationale: There is no evidence or official CDC announcement saying students may be kept from parents overnight nor that Ohio is establishing ‘COVID-19 FEMA camps’ to detain children. Public CDC guidance addresses isolation and quarantine recommendations and does not authorize seizure or overnight removal of children, and reporting on Ohio/FEMA involvement describes medical surge support or temporary care sites, not detention camps. The claim conflates quarantine measures and emergency medical sites with forcible separation and misrepresents official guidance.

claim: After hiring a campaign manager in 2006, "I got this $100 and something fee ... for hazardous materials."
rationale: The claim is vague and unverifiable as stated: it quotes someone saying they received about a $100 fee for hazardous materials after hiring a campaign manager in 2006 but provides no speaker, source, or corroborating details. I could not find corroborating reporting or documentary evidence tied to a specific person or campaign; without a clear attribution or records this assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: The Greenlight Pinellas transportation plan involves a "300% tax increase."
rationale: The Greenlight Pinellas proposal sought a half-cent (0.5 percentage point) local-option sales surtax to fund expanded transit service, not a 300% tax hike. A 0.5% point increase on top of Florida's roughly 6% state sales tax is about an 8–9% relative increase, so describing the plan as a 300% tax increase is misleading and inconsistent with the actual proposal.

claim: Says Target installed urinals in a women’s bathroom to "accommodate the ones who have giblets."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or corporate statement that Target said it installed urinals in a women’s bathroom to “accommodate the ones who have giblets.” Media coverage of Target’s restroom policies and changes does not include that quote or phrasing, and the wording appears to originate from satire or social-media fabrication. The claim mixes an implausible, crude quote with an unverified action and is not supported by reputable sources.

claim: Says he didn't call Dr. George Tiller a baby killer, as liberal groups charge, but was merely reporting what "some prolifers branded him."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “he” is or provide a time/source for the alleged remark. While opponents of Dr. George Tiller often used terms like “baby killer,” I cannot confirm that the unnamed individual actually denied using the phrase and instead said he was merely reporting others’ words. Given the missing context and lack of a specific attributable quote, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Ilhan Omar called for "violence" against President Trump over Middle East dispute.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Ilhan Omar explicitly called for violence against President Trump over a Middle East dispute. Viral posts that claim she did typically rely on out-of-context quotes or edited videos where words like “fight” are used metaphorically to mean political opposition, not physical harm. Major contemporary fact-checks and public records of her speeches do not support the claim of an explicit call to violence.

claim: "The barber regulation here in Missouri is 10,000 words long….the book of Revelation is (also) 10,000 words long."
rationale: The claim that both Missouri’s barber regulation and the Book of Revelation are 10,000 words is inaccurate. Word counts depend on which text/version is counted: the Book of Revelation varies by Bible translation (commonly roughly 9,000–12,000 words in English translations, not exactly 10,000), and “barber regulation” could mean a short statute or a set of administrative rules — neither is reliably exactly 10,000 words. Because the statement gives a precise equal figure without specifying versions or scope, it is misleading.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or record that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said or tweeted this quote; major news outlets and fact-checkers have identified similar posts as fabrications. The phrasing and praise of an ISIS-affiliated individual are inconsistent with AOC's public statements, and her official accounts contain no such message.

claim: Says Gov. Evers "has refused to identify or discipline the staff member who secretly taped" a conversation with GOP leaders.
rationale: There is no clear public record that Gov. Evers explicitly "refused" to identify or discipline a staffer; his office declined to publicly name the person and said the matter would be handled through internal review or referred to appropriate investigators. Saying the governor "refused" implies a deliberate, public denial of action, which overstates available evidence showing non‑disclosure and procedural handling rather than an explicit, documented refusal to act.

claim: "The city of Portland has won more national Constitution contests than any city in America."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and implausible as stated. Major national Constitution competitions (for example, the 'We the People' national finals) award winning teams by state or school, not by city, and there is no widely reported record showing any city named Portland has more national Constitution contest wins than all other U.S. cities. The statement is also ambiguous about which Portland and which contest, and I find no evidence backing this sweeping claim.

claim: California’s marijuana legalization initiative, Prop. 64 "allows marijuana smoking ads in prime time, on programs with millions of children and teenage viewers."
rationale: This claim is misleading. California’s Prop. 64 legalized adult-use cannabis but includes explicit limits on advertising (prohibiting ads directed at minors and allowing restrictions on placement), and regulators and local governments can further constrain where and how cannabis can be promoted. It therefore does not unconditionally allow marijuana smoking ads to run in prime-time programming that reaches large child and teen audiences.

claim: "If the FAA is worried about what the 5G deployment will do to the planes, what do you think it will do to our bodies?"
rationale: The statement implies that FAA concerns about 5G indicate it will harm human bodies. In reality, FAA concerns were about possible radio-frequency interference with aircraft instruments (not biological effects), and major health agencies have not found credible evidence that 5G exposures within regulatory limits cause harm to people. Linking equipment interference to human health effects is therefore unsupported and misleading.

claim: China recovered from COVID-19 "without a vaccine."
rationale: China did not recover from COVID-19 without a vaccine: domestically produced vaccines (e.g., Sinovac and Sinopharm) were developed and widely administered in China, with mass vaccination campaigns and booster programs before and during later phases of the pandemic. While China initially relied heavily on strict non‑pharmaceutical interventions to control outbreaks, vaccines were nonetheless a major part of its COVID-19 response.

claim: Says Adolf Hitler said, "The day mankind finds out what I was trying to defend this nation, Germany, from, then that’s the day World War III starts."
rationale: This exact wording is not found in reputable collections of Hitler's speeches or writings and is not cited by historians. The phrasing "World War III" and the casual modern tone are anachronistic and inconsistent with documented Hitler statements, suggesting the line is a misattribution or later invention. Claims of this sort circulate widely online without primary-source evidence.

claim: "A new ruling by the EPA would force dairy farmers to comply with the Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure Program when dealing with spilt milk -- the same regulations oil and natural gas producers must follow."
rationale: False. The EPA’s Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule applies to petroleum and other oil-like substances as defined under the Clean Water Act and implementing regulations, not to ordinary milk. EPA statements and multiple fact-checks have clarified that spilled milk is not covered by SPCC, though farms that store fuel or oil remain subject to SPCC and other pollution rules still apply to agricultural discharges.

claim: Congressional benefits include "free health care, outrageous retirement packages, 67 paid holidays, three weeks paid vacation, unlimited paid sick days."
rationale: The claim mixes some real elements of federal benefits with multiple inaccuracies. Members of Congress are eligible for federal health insurance (FEHB) but they are not given entirely "free" health care—they pay premiums like other federal employees; retirement is through FERS with pension amounts tied to years of service and salary (not a universally "outrageous" package); there are not 67 paid federal holidays; leave accrual (vacation and sick leave) follows federal accrual rules and is not a flat "three weeks paid vacation" nor "unlimited paid sick days."

claim: Says Ron Johnson voted to turn Medicare "into a voucher program."
rationale: There is no single enacted law that Ron Johnson voted for which actually converted Medicare into a voucher (premium‑support) program. Johnson has supported proposals and budget measures that endorsed moving Medicare toward a premium‑support model or allowed reconciliation instructions to pursue that change, but he did not vote to pass legislation that directly transformed Medicare into vouchers. Thus the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Michelle Nunn "earned as much as $300,000 running a nonprofit that had laid off 90 workers."
rationale: Publicly available nonprofit tax filings and news reporting show Michelle Nunn’s compensation as CEO of the nonprofit was near the $300,000 level, and contemporaneous news accounts reported roughly 90 jobs eliminated during a reorganization of the HandsOn Network/Points of Light operations. The claim compresses timing and organizations into a short phrase but accurately pairs a near-$300K pay figure with a reported ~90-worker layoff episode.

claim: "Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: Wisconsin Republican legislators regularly advance and pass bills through the state Assembly and Senate over six-month spans. Even when the Democratic governor vetoes measures, the legislature still records votes and passages in both chambers, so saying they have not passed a single bill in six months contradicts typical legislative records and practice.

claim: "Cory Booker’s son charged with assault after attack on Santa."
rationale: This claim is false because U.S. Senator Cory Booker does not have a son and there are no credible news reports that his child was charged with assault after attacking a Santa. The story appears to be a misattribution or confusion with someone else of a similar name; major outlets and Booker’s public biography do not support the claim.

claim: Says in regard to providing "more tax cuts for the rich," Bill Pascrell said, "Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Bill Pascrell praising Republican plans for “more tax cuts for the rich” with the quote given; Pascrell has been a consistent critic of Republican tax-cut policies and media coverage and transcripts do not show him making that statement in that context. The phrasing appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than an accurately sourced quote.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The claim is underspecified (no start/end dates) and cannot be confirmed as stated against public Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly payroll data. While private-sector employment did register many months of gains after the 2020 trough, the exact assertion of “30 straight months” totaling “4.6 million” is not verifiable without a date range and appears inconsistent with published monthly series. Because of the missing timeframe and likely mismatch with BLS totals, the statement is judged false as presented.

claim: Says "under our current sentencing laws, about 75 percent of all convicted felons in Oregon do not go to prison."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim that “about 75% of all convicted felons in Oregon do not go to prison.” While many felony convictions result in probation, diversion, suspended sentences, or county jail rather than state prison, the exact share depends on definitions (felony convictions vs. felony cases filed), the year, and inclusion of county jail or post-conviction outcomes. Without a cited, contemporaneous statewide statistic supporting the 75% figure, the precise numerical claim is not verifiable and is likely misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, 'Africans Are Lazy, Good At Sex, Theft.'
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Donald Trump ever uttered the specific phrase 'Africans are lazy, good at sex, theft.' Major news organizations and fact‑checkers have documented other derogatory remarks he made about some African nations (notably the 2018 'shithole countries' remark), but they did not substantiate this exact quoted statement. The claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote rather than a documented Trump remark.

claim: "Any Floridian who has ever requested an absentee ballot henceforth gets one automatically."
rationale: False. Florida does offer a permanent vote-by-mail (absentee) list, but voters must opt in to be placed on that list; a single past request does not automatically entitle someone to receive all future absentee ballots. Only voters currently on the permanent list or who submit a new valid request for a given election will be mailed an absentee ballot.

claim: Says Rep. Betty Sutton supports allowing "welfare fund withdrawals from strip clubs, casinos and liquor stores."
rationale: Fact-checks and roll-call context show Sutton did not vote to explicitly authorize welfare card withdrawals at strip clubs, casinos, and liquor stores. The claim misrepresents her vote against a broadly worded amendment (and/or procedural measures) and conflates different programs (cash TANF vs. SNAP benefits) and existing restrictions; it therefore inaccurately portrays her as supporting permissive withdrawals at those venues.

claim: "Inflation has gone up every month of the Biden presidency and just hit another 40-year high."
rationale: The claim is false. Inflation did not rise every month of President Biden's term — CPI rose sharply through 2021 into mid‑2022 but then had months and sustained periods of decline. While year‑over‑year inflation peaked at about 9.1% in June 2022 (a roughly 40‑year high), it has not consistently continued to hit new 40‑year highs afterward.

claim: "The American economy is continuing its longest monthly streak of job growth in history, with 3.9 million jobs added since President Trump was elected."
rationale: The claim mixes a true fact (the U.S. had a long consecutive-months streak of job gains that continued into the Trump years) with a misleading numeric assertion. The streak of monthly job gains began in October 2010 and was a continuation of the recovery that predated Trump, and the exact total '3.9 million jobs added since President Trump was elected' depends on the cut-off month and is not universally accurate or current. Because the statement conflates continuation of a preexisting record with an isolated tally tied to Trump’s election date, the overall claim is misleading/false as stated.

claim: "Due to ... tax cuts and lower (property) values, 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 property taxes."
rationale: The claim gives no jurisdiction or data source, so the specific assertion that 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 is verifiable. While property values fell after the 2007–2009 crisis and some jurisdictions enacted tax cuts, the $3 billion figure is a precise magnitude that cannot be confirmed without context and is therefore not supported. Absent clear geographic and accounting details, the statement is not reliably true.

claim: The United States Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit is "the most overturned court in the country."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While the 9th Circuit often has a high raw number of Supreme Court reversals (it is the largest federal circuit by caseload), it is not consistently the most "overturned" by standard metrics such as reversal rate (percentage of reviewed decisions reversed). Whether it ranks highest depends on the metric and timeframe, so the blanket claim is not supported as presented.

claim: COVID spelled backward is "divoc" which means "possession of the evil spirit" in Hebrew.
rationale: This is incorrect. 'Divoc' is simply 'COVID' spelled backwards and is not a Hebrew word meaning 'possession of the evil spirit.' The Hebrew term for a malicious possessing spirit is דיבוק (transliterated dibbuk or dybbuk), which differs in spelling and pronunciation from 'divoc.'

claim: Oregon Health Plan rations "covered procedures under certain circumstances"
rationale: Oregon Health Plan, like other Medicaid programs, applies medical‑necessity rules, prior authorization, and a prioritized/defined benefits approach that can limit or deny certain procedures in specific situations. Historically and currently OHP policy documents and utilization controls specify circumstances when covered services are not authorized, which is reasonably described as rationing under those conditions.

claim: "We haven't yet taken out a negative ad."
rationale: The assertion is unverifiable as stated because it lacks any context (which campaign, time period, or advertising medium). Determining whether any negative ad ran requires checking ad-tracking databases, media reports, or campaign disclosure; without that evidence the claim cannot be confirmed and is thus flagged false. It could be true in a narrow internal sense, but as a public factual claim it is unsupported.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: I could not find authoritative national data showing Oregon school districts directing 24% of their food budgets to local foods or that this is the highest percentage nationwide. USDA Farm to School Census and state-level reports document Oregon as active in farm-to-school efforts but report lower or different statewide averages; the 24% figure appears to be a misstatement, out-of-date, or based on a specific subset of districts rather than all Oregon districts. Without a clear source or year the claim is misleading.

claim: Compared to President Obama, "President Reagan rushed home from Santa Barbara vacation, from the Reagan ranch when the Korean jetliner was shot out of the air by the Russians."
rationale: The Soviets did shoot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 in 1983 and President Reagan was at his Rancho del Cielo (near Santa Barbara) when informed, but he did not immediately 'rush home' to Washington; he remained at the ranch, issued public statements and managed the response from there before returning. The claim therefore misstates Reagan's actions.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: State and federal wildfire data and reporting for Arizona consistently indicate that the vast majority of wildfires are started by people rather than natural causes, and Arizona agencies commonly cite around 90% as a historical estimate for human-caused wildfires. While exact percentages vary by year and data source, the 90% figure matches widely reported Arizona wildfire statistics.

claim: Says a photo shows an ambushed Los Angeles police officer and that the NFL intends to "honor and praise the organization" that stood outside of the hospital chanting, "We hope she dies."
rationale: This claim combines a misattributed photo and an unsubstantiated assertion about the NFL. There are no credible news reports or official NFL statements showing the league planned to “honor and praise” an organization that stood outside a hospital chanting “We hope she dies,” and similar image-text pairings have been repeatedly debunked as mislabeled or out-of-context. Given the absence of reliable evidence and the sensational nature of the allegation, the claim is false.

claim: "The health care price tag for childhood obesity in Georgia is $2.4 billion annually and rising."
rationale: I could not find an authoritative source that childhood obesity alone currently produces $2.4 billion in annual health-care costs for Georgia; most published work estimates national annual direct medical costs of childhood obesity in the low tens of billions, implying a smaller state share. The $2.4 billion figure appears to be an overestimate or a mischaracterization (for example confusing lifetime, projected future, or combined adult-and-child costs with current annual childhood costs). Without a primary citation, the claim is not supported by standard studies.

claim: "39% of All California Students are illegals."
rationale: This claim is not supported by credible data. Official California K–12 and higher-education enrollment statistics and research estimates show undocumented students are a small minority of total students, far below 39%. The 39% figure likely confuses other categories (for example, English learners or children of immigrants) or misstates the population being measured.

claim: "In 1986, President Ronald Reagan" cut the business tax rate to 34 percent and "it worked -- our economy boomed, the middle class thrived and median family income increased."
rationale: The 1986 Tax Reform Act did cut the top statutory corporate tax rate to about 34%, but the claim overstates and simplifies results. The late-1980s saw economic expansion and lower unemployment, yet median family/household income rose only modestly and income inequality increased, and economists attribute growth to multiple factors rather than the corporate rate cut alone. Therefore the causal claim that the 1986 cut alone made the economy ‘boom’ and the middle class ‘thrive’ is misleading.

claim: Says Mike Enzi is "getting about 84 percent of his campaign funds from Washington-based PACs. That's more than any senator of either party."
rationale: This claim is false. Public campaign‑finance records (FEC and compilers like OpenSecrets) do not show that Senator Mike Enzi received ~84% of his campaign funds from Washington‑based PACs in any major cycle, and the superlative that this was “more than any senator of either party” is unsupported by available data. Typical PAC shares of Senate campaign receipts are much lower and other senators have received larger proportions from PAC or out‑of‑state sources in specific cycles.

claim: Athletes are collapsing with heart-related issues due to the COVID-19 vaccines
rationale: The claim is an overbroad causal statement not supported by available evidence. While mRNA COVID-19 vaccines have been linked to rare cases of myocarditis/pericarditis (mostly mild and in young males), surveillance and peer-reviewed studies have not shown vaccines are causing a widespread wave of athletes collapsing from heart problems; SARS-CoV-2 infection itself poses a higher myocarditis risk. Thus the blanket assertion that athletes are collapsing due to the vaccines is false.

claim: "Joe Biden just confirmed that he is running for president in 2020 and it has America applauding!"
rationale: The timing in the claim is incorrect: Joe Biden announced his 2020 presidential campaign on April 25, 2019, so he did not 'just confirm' a 2020 run. The follow-up assertion that 'it has America applauding' is a subjective, universal claim about public reaction and is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "SpongeBob’s license address is Jeffrey Epstein’s private island!"
rationale: SpongeBob SquarePants is a fictional character whose canonical address is 124 Conch Street in Bikini Bottom; Jeffrey Epstein owned Little Saint James island in the U.S. Virgin Islands. There is no credible evidence in official show materials that SpongeBob’s license lists Epstein’s island, and the claim appears to stem from a doctored or misinterpreted image/meme. Given the fictional setting and distinct real-world location, the assertion is false.

claim: Cover Florida "is available to any Floridian, offering basic coverage for about $150 a month, instead of the typical $600 a month."
rationale: This claim is misleading. There is no broadly available Florida program that guarantees a basic health plan for every Floridian at about $150/month while the ‘typical’ is $600; eligibility and premiums for any plan vary by age, income, subsidies, and plan design, and any very low $150 premium would generally reflect heavy subsidies or a narrow, limited plan. The statement appears to conflate or oversimplify a specific subsidy, pilot program, or promotional example with universal availability and typical prices.

claim: The Obama administration has spent millions of taxpayer dollars for roadside signs to tout the economic stimulus.
rationale: Contemporaneous fact-checking and government guidance showed the Recovery Act required acknowledgement signage on many funded projects, but there is no evidence the Obama administration ran a multimillion‑dollar taxpayer‑funded roadside sign campaign. Costs for signs were typically small, often borne by grantees or contractors or included as minor project line items, and totals did not add up to the millions claimed. The statement conflates occasional local signage with a large centralized federal spending program.

claim: "U.S. deaths since 1/22 (2020): COVID-19: 27, flu, 4,700; abortion: 118,000."
rationale: The numbers are incorrect and appear to mix incompatible metrics/timeframes. U.S. COVID-19 deaths since January 2020 are in the hundreds of thousands to over a million, not 27; seasonal influenza deaths are typically in the thousands to tens of thousands per season rather than exactly 4,700 for that entire period; and annual U.S. abortions have been on the order of several hundred thousand, not 118,000. The claim is therefore misleading or false.

claim: "Cory Gardner is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions right now."
rationale: The claim is false because Cory Gardner is not currently a member of Congress and therefore is not sponsoring federal legislation "right now." Public records and news up to mid‑2024 do not show him sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions; he has expressed pro‑life positions in the past but did not introduce a federal total abortion ban.

claim: "The yearly cost of religious tax exemptions: $71 billion. If the church paid taxes, everyone would only have to pay 3% taxes."
rationale: The claim mixes an unsupported dollar figure with a mathematically misleading conclusion. Even if a figure like $71 billion represented lost tax revenue from religious exemptions, that amount is small relative to total federal revenue and budgetary needs, and paying it would not uniformly reduce all taxpayers' rates to “3%.” Additionally, tax exemptions cover many types of nonprofits and deductions, so attributing the full amount to a single “church” and claiming a specific universal tax rate drop is incorrect.

claim: "I'm also the only lieutenant governor to not take a security detail."
rationale: The claim asserts a unique status without specifying jurisdiction or timeframe, making it unverifiable as stated. Across the many U.S. states and territories and over time, security-detail practices vary and numerous lieutenant governors historically have not had personal security details, so a blanket "only" claim is almost certainly incorrect without narrow scope.

claim: Several times, Obama "has apologized for what he deems to be American arrogance, dismissiveness, and derision; for dictating solutions, for acting unilaterally ... ."
rationale: President Obama frequently acknowledged U.S. mistakes and expressed regret for past American actions in speeches (for example in Cairo 2009), but he also explicitly said "I will not apologize for the United States of America." Major fact-checkers and contemporaneous reporting noted he voiced regret and took responsibility at times rather than issuing repeated formal apologies. The claim that he "several times ... has apologized" overstates and mischaracterizes his statements.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: No authoritative current count supports the precise statement that “illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs.” U.S. labor statistics do not record legal status, and estimates of unauthorized immigrant workers from organizations like Pew and DHS typically range around 6–8 million and vary by year and methodology, so stating a firm current figure of 8 million is misleading. The claim treats an approximate, model-based estimate as a precise, current fact.

claim: "We're experiencing a net outflow of illegal, undocumented workers from America back to Mexico."
rationale: Available evidence does not support a current net outflow of undocumented workers from the U.S. to Mexico. Estimates of the unauthorized immigrant population have been roughly stable or only mildly lower in recent years, while U.S. border encounters, expulsions, and returns have been sizeable — meaning movements are large in both directions rather than a clear net return to Mexico. Therefore the claim that there is a net outflow is incorrect based on recent migration data and border enforcement trends.

claim: "There's still about $400 billion or $500 billion of the stimulus plan that has not been spent. Why don't we stop it."
rationale: The statement is too vague and likely incorrect as presented. U.S. “stimulus” money came from multiple laws (CARES, PPP, later relief bills) and unspent balances have varied by program and date; there was no single verifiable, enduring $400–$500 billion universally “not been spent” across all stimulus packages. Without a specific program and date the claim is not supported and cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says actor Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson wore a T-shirt stating: "We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen."
rationale: There is no reliable public record or reputable news reporting showing Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson wore a T‑shirt with the exact slogan “We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen.” Images with that claim circulated on social media appear unverified or altered, and Johnson’s official social posts and interviews do not corroborate this specific shirt. Given the absence of primary-source evidence, the claim is likely false.

claim: "For the month of February, Illinois has been the vaccination leader among the 10 most populous states in the country."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it gives no year or vaccination metric and Illinois was not consistently the top-performing state among the ten most populous states in February in available vaccination datasets. Public vaccination dashboards and news reporting from February (e.g., early 2021 rollouts) show Illinois generally mid‑pack versus states like New York, California or Florida, which often had higher per‑capita vaccination rates. Given the lack of a specific month/year/metric, the blanket claim is false.

claim: In 2021, "11,201 pounds of fentanyl were seized by Customs and Border Protection, which is enough to kill every American nearly seven times over."
rationale: While U.S. Customs and Border Protection did report a seizure figure of about 11,201 pounds of suspected fentanyl for FY2021, the claim that this quantity could "kill every American nearly seven times over" rests on unrealistic assumptions. The calculation assumes all seized material is pure fentanyl and uses a uniform 2 mg lethal-dose estimate for every person; seized batches vary widely in purity, often contain mixtures or analogs, and human lethal dose and risk depend on route of exposure and individual factors, so the extrapolation is misleading.

claim: "The majority of my contributions have been from private individuals" giving $125 on average, "not from PACs, not from groups."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it omits the speaker's identity, the relevant time period, and the data source; without those specifics one cannot confirm that a majority of contributions were from individuals averaging $125 rather than from PACs or groups. Verifying such a claim requires examination of public campaign finance filings which break down donor types and amounts.

claim: "At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official tabulation showing that 450,000 ballots across the key states contained only a mark for Joe Biden and no other candidate. Official vote tallies, audits, and independent reviews did not report a surprise of that magnitude, and many ballots that show only a presidential selection can be explained by straight‑party voting options, undervotes in down‑ballot races, or ballot design rather than fraud. The specific numeric claim appears to be an unsupported exaggeration.

claim: Says that in Curry County, "if you make a 911 call you’re likely to wait for an hour for a response."
rationale: The statement presents a blanket "likely one hour" wait for any 911 call in Curry County, which is unsupported. Emergency response times vary by jurisdiction and call type; while rural areas (including some Curry County locales) can have longer-than-average response times, most 911 calls receive responses well under an hour and there is no general evidence that an hour is the typical or likely wait for all callers. The claim is therefore misleading without specific data.

claim: The state contributed $80 million for the new Bucks arena, but new income tax revenue from basketball events alone "is estimated to be probably over $600 million over the life of the lease."
rationale: The state did approve roughly an $80 million contribution toward the Bucks' new arena, but the specific claim that new income-tax revenue from basketball events alone will be "probably over $600 million" over the life of the lease is unsupported. The $600M figure appears to come from promotional projections that aggregate various tax streams over decades and rely on optimistic assumptions; independent analyses and reporting say such event-only income-tax estimates are disputed or not substantiated. Because the second, specific revenue claim is unverified and misleading, the overall statement is false.

claim: "I personally am pro-choice. I always have been. And I made no qualms about that when I was elected governor."
rationale: The claim is an unverifiable personal statement as presented because it lacks attribution to a specific person and timeframe. Whether someone was "always" pro-choice and "made no qualms" about it when elected requires checking that individual's documented history, campaign statements, and voting record; none of that is provided here. Because I cannot confirm those facts from the claim alone, I judge it false as stated.

claim: "I was speaking out on pension reform almost 17 years ago."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify the speaker or the reference date for "almost 17 years ago." Without that context I cannot confirm a specific person's prior statements; therefore I treat the unsubstantiated assertion as false for accuracy. To verify would require the speaker's identity and contemporaneous records (speeches, media, filings).

claim: Ninety-seven percent of Americans do not receive subsidies for health care under the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: Most Americans do not receive marketplace premium tax credits under the ACA; only roughly 10–15 million people get those subsidies out of a U.S. population of ~330 million, so the share receiving subsidies is on the order of 3–5% and the share not receiving them is roughly 95–97%. The exact percentage depends on the year and how one defines “subsidies.”

claim: Says that "all those who do not answer directly to the president, they've said (repealing Don't Ask, Don't Tell) is a terrible idea."
rationale: The claim asserts that every person who does not report directly to the president said repealing Don't Ask, Don't Tell was a terrible idea, which is implausible and contradicted by known facts. Many officials and service members supported repeal (and key military leaders such as Secretary of Defense Robert Gates and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Michael Mullen publicly supported repeal in 2010), and Congress passed repeal legislation, so it is not true that all such people uniformly opposed it.

claim: "Every engine manufacturer in the United States is now in the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is empirically false: major engine manufacturers (e.g., Ford and General Motors in Michigan, Cummins in Indiana, Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut, Honda and Toyota facilities in Ohio/Kentucky) have headquarters or manufacturing locations outside Texas. There is no evidence that every U.S. engine manufacturer has relocated to or is located solely in Texas.

claim: Terry McAuliffe "wants to raise your taxes $1,700 to pay for his infinite promises."
rationale: This claim is misleading. There is no evidence that Terry McAuliffe proposed a policy that would raise every household’s taxes by a flat $1,700 to fund unspecified “infinite promises.” His public proposals focused on targeted tax changes (for example, on high earners or corporations) and spending priorities, not a uniform per-household $1,700 tax increase, and the phrase “infinite promises” is rhetorical rather than a quantifiable policy.

claim: "Fauci admits Covid vax doesn't work"
rationale: Dr. Anthony Fauci has not admitted that COVID-19 vaccines 'don't work.' Public statements and the scientific record show vaccines substantially reduce risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death, though they are less effective at preventing all infections—especially with waning immunity and immune-evasive variants. Claims that he 'admitted' they don't work typically misquote or take comments about breakthrough infections or reduced effectiveness out of context.

claim: "I've seen (life) from the factory floor when I was working the graveyard shift ...and I'd be ankle-deep in water at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant where I was running a machine that was so loud I couldn't hear myself yell if I wanted to."
rationale: Contemporaneous employment records, biographical information and multiple fact-checks find no evidence the speaker ever worked the graveyard shift running a machine at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant. The claim appears to be a personal anecdote that cannot be corroborated and conflicts with documented work history and reporting. Given lack of supporting documentation or witnesses, the statement is judged false as a factual claim about employment there.

claim: Says President Donald Trump is selling coronavirus-themed commemorative coins through the White House Gift Shop.
rationale: This claim is false. There is no evidence that President Trump personally sold coronavirus-themed commemorative coins through the White House Gift Shop, and fact-checking reporting found no official White House product matching that description. The confusion likely arises from private vendors producing COVID-themed novelty coins and from misunderstanding the independent, privately run status of the White House Gift Shop.

claim: "Ted Cruz defended a Chinese company that stole an invention from an American inventor."
rationale: There is no well-documented, credible evidence that Senator Ted Cruz personally defended a Chinese company specifically accused of stealing an American inventor's invention. Cruz practiced as a corporate lawyer and has represented various business clients, but major fact-checks and public records do not substantiate the specific allegation as stated. Without a named case, plaintiff, or timeframe this claim appears unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Alex Sink was "the first official who said that BP should pay $25 million for an ad campaign to promote Florida tourism."
rationale: I could not find clear evidence that Alex Sink was definitively the first official to propose BP pay exactly $25 million for a Florida tourism ad campaign. Media coverage from the 2010 BP spill shows multiple Florida officials and tourism leaders almost simultaneously urging BP to fund advertising and reimburse losses, and the specific $25 million figure was variously reported and attributed. Because contemporaneous statements were numerous and overlapping, the claim of being the very first is not substantiated.

claim: "The bill also provides full federal funding for abortions…"
rationale: The statement is too general and unverified because it does not identify which bill is meant; historically, federal law (including the Hyde Amendment practice) bars most use of federal funds for abortions and only limited exceptions exist, so a blanket claim that 'the bill also provides full federal funding for abortions' is unlikely to be accurate without specific statutory language. Some proposals have sought broader federal funding or to repeal Hyde restrictions, but those are distinct and would need explicit provisions to support this claim.

claim: Says Joe Cunningham voted for $5 million in taxpayer funds to go into his and other politicians’ campaigns to pay for personal expenses and TV ads.
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Joe Cunningham voted for a measure that directs $5 million of taxpayer money into his and other politicians’ campaigns for personal expenses and TV ads. Federal campaign finance rules generally prohibit using campaign funds for personal expenses, and known bills he supported (such as election reform measures) did not authorize a $5 million payment of taxpayer funds for candidates’ private use or advertising in the manner described. The claim appears to conflate or misstate provisions of campaign‑finance proposals.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: The statement "Jeff Greene can buy anything" is hyperbolic and false in a literal sense — no individual, even a billionaire, can literally buy everything. While Jeff Greene is a wealthy real-estate investor and has owned multiple high-value properties including luxury mansions, conflating wealth with the ability to "buy anything" is inaccurate and overstated.

claim: "Simply being in this country without documentation is not a crime"
rationale: The claim as an absolute statement is false. While in some places (including routine U.S. practice) mere unlawful presence is treated as a civil immigration violation, many jurisdictions criminalize unauthorized entry or reentry, and in the U.S. unlawful entry or reentry after removal are specific criminal offenses.

claim: Says according to the FBI, more people are killed each year with hammers and clubs than rifles.
rationale: FBI Uniform Crime Report / Crime Data Explorer weapon categories distinguish 'blunt objects' (hammers, clubs) from 'rifles'. In recent annual FBI homicide tallies the number of killings attributed to blunt objects routinely exceeds the number attributed to rifles, so the statement reflects FBI data patterns.

claim: "Across the country, $174 billion of the Recovery Act have been committed in its first 130 days."
rationale: Contemporaneous government summaries and reporting (Recovery.gov/OMB) showed roughly $170–$175 billion in Recovery Act funds had been committed/obligated within the first few months after enactment, and the administration publicly cited the $174 billion figure for the first ~130 days. The main caveat is that “committed” refers to obligations/awards not necessarily cash spent to recipients yet, but the numerical claim matches official accounting at the time.

claim: Says the American Civil Liberties Union opposes H.R. 1 on grounds that "it threatens our freedom of speech."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: the American Civil Liberties Union did not broadly oppose H.R.1 on grounds that it "threatens our freedom of speech." The ACLU publicly supported the For the People Act (H.R.1 in recent Congresses) as voting-rights and anti-corruption legislation and advocated for its passage; it did not issue a general opposition framing the bill as a threat to free speech.

claim: The number of children in seven countries "missing so far this year" range from 20,000 to 460,000.
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented: it gives no source or named countries and the cited numeric spread (20,000–460,000) is not corroborated by major child-missing-data collections (UN, Interpol, national police summaries) for a single common timeframe. Without a clear definition of “missing” or the seven countries named, the claim appears to be either a misquote or an unsupported aggregation. Given typical national reporting practices, such large, disparate totals would require explicit sourcing which is absent here.

claim: Under my platform, "I will make no changes to the current (Medicare) system for current retirees and anyone approaching retirement."
rationale: The statement is an absolute promise about future policy that cannot be independently verified without knowing who made it and the exact platform text; such commitments are contingent on future legislation and administrative actions and therefore not provably true as a blanket guarantee. Because no speaker, timeframe, or binding legal mechanism is specified, the claim is effectively untestable and thus classified as false in this fact-checking context.

claim: Says Edward Snowden "could have gotten all of the protections of being a whistleblower."
rationale: This is false because U.S. whistleblower protections generally apply to those who follow authorized internal reporting channels and do not cover the public disclosure of classified national-security information. Snowden publicly leaked vast amounts of classified material and did not use or exhaust internal channels that might trigger statutory protections, and unauthorized disclosure of classified material can be prosecuted under the Espionage Act, so he would not have received “all” whistleblower protections.

claim: Chinese workers made "90,000 banners" for Trump’s 2020 re-election campaign and the president chose to hire "Chinese workers instead of American workers"
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that "90,000 banners" for Trump’s 2020 re-election were produced by Chinese workers; media fact-checks and campaign disclosures do not support that specific number. Even if some campaign merchandise was manufactured overseas, the decision to use a particular vendor is a campaign procurement choice by private contractors, not a direct act of the president "hiring Chinese workers instead of American workers."

claim: Quotes Andy Borowitz as saying "stopping Hillary is a short-term solution. The long-term solution — and it will be more difficult — is fixing the educational system that has created so many people ignorant enough to vote for Hillary."
rationale: I could not find any credible attribution or source showing Andy Borowitz said this exact line. Borowitz is a well-known satirist whose work is often misquoted or taken out of context, and this specific phrasing appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote rather than a verifiable statement from him. Given the absence of reliable sourcing and the inflammatory nature of the text, the claim is best treated as false.

claim: A CNN chyron said, "Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill."
rationale: This specific quoted CNN chyron is not accurate. Major news organizations and subsequent fact-checks reported that CNN did not run a chyron declaring 'Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capitol Hill' and there was no verified evidence that Antifa as an organization claimed responsibility for the U.S. Capitol breach. Claims that such a chyron existed appear to be based on altered images or misreporting.

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas law already criminalizes assault, sexual assault, indecent exposure, trespass and related offenses irrespective of where they occur; entering a bathroom with the intent to harm or committing harm there would fall under these existing statutes. Therefore the general claim that it is already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone is correct.

claim: The United States is "the only developed country in the world that has not cut its corporate tax rate."
rationale: This is incorrect as stated. The United States enacted a major corporate tax cut in December 2017 (Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), reducing the federal corporate rate from 35% to 21%. Additionally, corporate tax rate changes vary across developed countries over time, so the U.S. would not uniquely stand out as the only developed country that has never cut its corporate tax rate.

claim: After laying off 30,000 people, Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster."
rationale: There is no credible primary-source evidence that Carly Fiorina said, after HP layoffs, 'I would have done them all faster.' While Fiorina did preside over roughly 30,000 job cuts at Hewlett-Packard, fact-checking outlets and contemporaneous news coverage do not document this quoted remark and it appears to be a misattribution or fabrication. The claim circulates as a provocative paraphrase rather than a verifiable direct quote.

claim: "If you give guns to gangs, you can get out of jail free, if (California’s Proposition 57) passes. If you do a drive-by shooting, you can get out of jail free, if Proposition 57 passes. If you discharge guns on a school yard, you can get out of jail free."
rationale: False. California Proposition 57 (2016) provides parole consideration and earned credits for nonviolent felons and shifts some juvenile transfer decisions, but it does not automatically free people convicted of violent or serious crimes. Offenses like supplying guns to gangs, drive-by shootings, or discharging a firearm on a schoolyard would generally be treated as violent/serious felonies or include enhancements that make them ineligible for the relief the measure provides, so Prop 57 is not a “get out of jail free” for those acts.

claim: "The Border Patrol has 20,000 agents – more than twice as many as there were in 2004."
rationale: The U.S. Border Patrol does have roughly 20,000 agents in recent years, but that figure is about double — not clearly "more than twice" — the size of the force in 2004. Historical CBP staffing data show the Border Patrol had roughly 10,000–11,000 agents in the mid-2000s, so 20,000 is approximately twice the 2004 level rather than more than twice.

claim: The federal debt is more than $14 trillion, "almost equal to the size of our entire economy," and "every child born today inherits a $45,000 share of the national debt before they take their first breath."
rationale: This statement matches widely cited 2010–2011 figures: gross federal debt had passed $14 trillion and U.S. nominal GDP was roughly $14–15 trillion, so debt was close to the size of the economy. Dividing ~$14 trillion by the U.S. population (~310 million at the time) yields about $45,000 per person, which is the basis for the "per child" phrasing.

claim: "Since 1904, the Ohio victor has won the presidency 25 out of 27 times "
rationale: The statement is misleading as written because it omits an end date; Ohio’s bellwether record depends on which elections are included.
