Organizational changes for a Division of Emergency Management are typically documented in executive orders, directives, or press releases; without those records this specific assertion is unverified and best treated as false until substantiated.

claim: Says the United States has the "highest corporate tax rate in the world."
rationale: This is false. After the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act the U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut to 21% (with additional state-level taxes bringing combined rates typically into the mid-20s), far from the highest in the world. Even before 2018 the U.S. had one of the higher combined statutory rates among rich countries but was not unambiguously the single highest globally.

claim: "As your Lieutenant Governor…I cut your taxes."
rationale: The claim is too vague and implausible as stated: a lieutenant governor does not typically have unilateral authority to 'cut your taxes' and tax changes are enacted through legislation or executive action by a governor. Without identifying which lieutenant governor, which taxes, and what specific actions were taken, the statement cannot be verified and is likely misleading. If a particular lieutenant governor supported or signed tax legislation, that context would be needed to judge accuracy.

claim: "Our economy is so much stronger than when (Barack Obama and Joe Biden) took office. Nearly 15 million new private-sector jobs."
rationale: The statement is misleading and the specific figure is inaccurate without a clear endpoint. BLS payroll data show private‑sector employment rose by roughly 11–12 million during Obama’s two terms (Jan 2009–Jan 2017) and by about 20–22 million by Feb 2020 (pre-pandemic), so “nearly 15 million” does not accurately describe either common comparison period.

claim: John McCain's health care plan "leaves you on your own to pay McCain’s health insurance tax."
rationale: This is incorrect: McCain’s 2008 health proposal did not create a new ‘‘health insurance tax’’ that people were forced to pay. His plan centered on refundable tax credits to help individuals buy private insurance and policies such as allowing purchase across state lines, not a federal tax on insurance premiums; critics sometimes argued it left people to bear premiums themselves, but that is not the same as imposing a named ‘‘health insurance tax.’’

claim: "Snitker has been virtually ignored by the major media."
rationale: The claim that “Snitker has been virtually ignored by the major media” is not supported by observable coverage. As the manager of a high‑profile MLB team he has received national attention in sports and mainstream outlets, including game broadcasts, postgame interviews, profiles and national commentary. Saying he was “virtually ignored” overstates the case and ignores routine media coverage of his team and role.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The exact sentence does not appear in the published text of The Art of the Deal. While the book contains advice about aggressive dealmaking, publicity, and projecting strength, the pointed line "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated." is a later paraphrase or attribution rather than a verbatim quote from the book.

claim: "Over the last 40 years, real wage growth has been flatlined because of the policies of the Federal Reserve ... It was all driven by the Federal Reserve."
rationale: This is incorrect because although the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy affects inflation and unemployment (and thus can influence real wages), it is not the sole or primary driver of forty years of median real-wage dynamics. Long-term real-wage trends reflect many forces — productivity growth, the labor share of income, globalization and trade, technological change and automation, declining unionization, fiscal and tax policies, and corporate/market power — so attributing the flatlining entirely to the Fed is an oversimplification unsupported by broad empirical evidence.

claim: "California Democrat Maxine Waters charged on 3 counts."
rationale: There is no reliable public record or mainstream reporting up to mid‑2024 that Rep. Maxine Waters has been criminally charged on three counts. News and official court records would report such charges prominently; instead she has not faced criminal indictment. Claims asserting three counts appear to be unverified or misleading.

claim: "Black Lives Matter, who are attacking law enforcement officers" -- Barack Obama "had them to the White House."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Obama saying the phrase “Black Lives Matter, who are attacking law enforcement officers” or labeling the movement that way. While the Obama White House did host meetings and discussions with community activists, police chiefs, and some individuals associated with racial-justice activism about policing and reform, it did not endorse a characterization of Black Lives Matter as attackers of law enforcement nor publicly invite the movement with that description. The claim mixes an unverified quote with a misleading portrayal of routine meetings and dialogues the administration convened.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Carter "hasn’t held a town hall in five years."
rationale: Available public records and local news coverage through mid‑2024 indicate Rep. John Carter held constituent meetings and at least occasional town‑hall style events within the five years prior to the claim, so the blanket statement that he “hasn’t held a town hall in five years” is inaccurate. The claim also lacks a clear date of assertion and a definition of “town hall,” which makes the assertion misleading without additional context.

claim: The omicron variant’s name is evidence the coronavirus pandemic is a hoax.
rationale: The name 'omicron' is part of the WHO's Greek-letter naming system for SARS-CoV-2 variants and is a neutral label, not an assertion about the virus's reality. Variants are identified by genetic sequencing and epidemiological data showing real, measurable differences in virus lineages and spread, so the name itself is not evidence of a hoax.

claim: "Woodrow Wilson borrowed $30 billion to fund World War I in 1917. That money has not been paid back. And we are still paying interest on it."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. The U.S. financed World War I largely with Liberty Bonds and other borrowing that raised on the order of $20–25 billion across 1917–1919 (not a single $30 billion loan in 1917), and those bond issues were paid, redeemed, or rolled into later federal debt rather than remaining as unpaid WWI-era loans. Current federal interest payments are on outstanding modern debt instruments, not on an unpaid $30 billion WWI loan from Wilson’s administration.
